extraction.body: A romantic relationship between a CEO and a vice president who reports directly to him could create a serious conflict of interest. When that relationship is allegedly undisclosed and the executive holds authority over the subordinate's career, compensation, and responsibilities, it becomes a governance problem , not a personal one. The New York Times, citing five people who worked at Nvidia and spoke anonymously, reported that Jensen Huang allegedly had an extramarital relationship with Kimberly Powell, Nvidia's vice president of health care, who reportedly reports to him. Both Huang and Powell are married to other people, according to the Times. Two of the five anonymous sources told the Times that Huang and Powell were captured on video appearing affectionate at a San Jose hotel during Nvidia's GTC developer conference in March. The Times stated it had not viewed the video, and its existence should not be treated as established. The responses from all three parties were notable mostly for what they were not. Nvidia declined to comment to the Times. Powell did not respond to a request for comment. When the Times reached Huang directly, he said "I don't think you should be talking to me directly" and ended the call. Huang did not expressly deny the allegation in that exchange. This allegation is distinct from the separate matter in which Huang acknowledged being unfaithful to his wife in a message to Nvidia employees, according to the BBC. That admission concerned a different alleged relationship, with Alice Huang. U.S. officials reportedly assessed Alice Huang to be a Chinese intelligence asset , an assessment China has denied. Nvidia's board retained Wachtell, Lipton, Rosen and Katz to conduct an independent investigation into that matter, according to CNBC. Whether the scope of that investigation covers the Powell allegation is not public. Nvidia's own code of conduct, as characterized in Times reporting, instructs employees to avoid situations that create conflicts of interest, including those involving personal relationships, and states that the company investigates misconduct reports promptly. A reporting relationship between a CEO and a vice president is exactly what those rules exist to prevent. The available evidence does not confirm whether Nvidia's policies include explicit provisions for the chief executive, but the conflict-of-interest framework applies broadly to the company's workforce. The allegation and the footage described by anonymous sources both remain without independent confirmation. Whether the alleged relationship affected Powell's career trajectory, pay, or responsibilities at Nvidia has not been publicly confirmed. Powell joined Nvidia in 2008 and advanced to vice president of government health care after earlier roles in AI business development . No reporting establishes a connection between that progression and the alleged relationship. Nvidia shares fell more than 3% in after-hours trading after the Times published its report, according to CNBC, though that decline likely reflects the cumulative weight of multiple ongoing concerns. The more consequential question is not on a stock ticker. Five people inside Nvidia allegedly knew enough about a reported relationship between the CEO and a direct report to speak with a reporter. Whether any internal process addressed that situation before a law firm was retained for a separate investigation is not established by the available reporting. Nvidia's board faces a governance structure that was not built to scrutinize the person who built the company, and that gap is exactly what an independent review should now examine.

extraction.body: A romantic relationship between a CEO and a vice president who reports directly to him could create a serious conflict of interest. When that relationship is allegedly undisclosed and the executive holds authority over the subordinate's career, compensation, and responsibilities, it becomes a governance problem , not a personal one. The New York Times, citing five people who worked at Nvidia and spoke anonymously, reported that Jensen Huang allegedly had an extramarital relationship with Kimberly Powell, Nvidia's vice president of health care, who reportedly reports to him. Both Huang and Powell are married to other people, according to the Times. Two of the five anonymous sources told the Times that Huang and Powell were captured on video appearing affectionate at a San Jose hotel during Nvidia's GTC developer conference in March. The Times stated it had not viewed the video, and its existence should not be treated as established. The responses from all three parties were notable mostly for what they were not. Nvidia declined to comment to the Times. Powell did not respond to a request for comment. When the Times reached Huang directly, he said "I don't think you should be talking to me directly" and ended the call. Huang did not expressly deny the allegation in that exchange. This allegation is distinct from the separate matter in which Huang acknowledged being unfaithful to his wife in a message to Nvidia employees, according to the BBC. That admission concerned a different alleged relationship, with Alice Huang. U.S. officials reportedly assessed Alice Huang to be a Chinese intelligence asset , an assessment China has denied. Nvidia's board retained Wachtell, Lipton, Rosen and Katz to conduct an independent investigation into that matter, according to CNBC. Whether the scope of that investigation covers the Powell allegation is not public. Nvidia's own code of conduct, as characterized in Times reporting, instructs employees to avoid situations that create conflicts of interest, including those involving personal relationships, and states that the company investigates misconduct reports promptly. A reporting relationship between a CEO and a vice president is exactly what those rules exist to prevent. The available evidence does not confirm whether Nvidia's policies include explicit provisions for the chief executive, but the conflict-of-interest framework applies broadly to the company's workforce. The allegation and the footage described by anonymous sources both remain without independent confirmation. Whether the alleged relationship affected Powell's career trajectory, pay, or responsibilities at Nvidia has not been publicly confirmed. Powell joined Nvidia in 2008 and advanced to vice president of government health care after earlier roles in AI business development . No reporting establishes a connection between that progression and the alleged relationship. Nvidia shares fell more than 3% in after-hours trading after the Times published its report, according to CNBC, though that decline likely reflects the cumulative weight of multiple ongoing concerns. The more consequential question is not on a stock ticker. Five people inside Nvidia allegedly knew enough about a reported relationship between the CEO and a direct report to speak with a reporter. Whether any internal process addressed that situation before a law firm was retained for a separate investigation is not established by the available reporting. Nvidia's board faces a governance structure that was not built to scrutinize the person who built the company, and that gap is exactly what an independent review should now examine.

extraction.body: Sean Duffy, the transportation secretary, said the airspace was now open and the problem had been identified Airport chaos continues after FAA lifts ground stop – live updates Sean Duffy, the transportation secretary, said the airspace was now open and the problem had been identified Airport chaos continues after FAA lifts ground stop – live updates The Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) has lifted a nationwide ground stop that was declared Friday afternoon, delaying or canceling more than 11,000 US flights, according to aviation tracker FlightAware , and throwing airports into sudden chaos. The FAA confirmed the airspace was open in an advisory on its website . “So at 8.15 tonight, Eastern Time, we’ve opened up the airspace,” Sean Duffy, the US transportation secretary, said. “But it’s going to take us some time to unwind what’s happened this afternoon .” Duffy said that the federal government has “identified the problem” that brought down the US air traffic control system on Friday and the system “is operational right now”. The White House briefing Friday evening with Duffy and Markwayne Mullin, the homeland security secretary, quickly turned into a plea for funding from Congress to “fully fund a full build of a brand new air traffic control system”. “What we have is an incredibly old air traffic control system,” Duffy said. “Our routers actually got overloaded with data, and … they started to give us inconsistency in the data from those routers. And because of that, we shut the system down,” he added. Earlier Friday, Duffy said in a social media post that the stoppage was due to “a communication issue impacting all Air Route Traffic Control Centers” and that the FAA’s technicians are looking into the matter. A notice from the FAA said the ground stop was being imposed “due to extraordinary circumstances and for reasons of safety”. Duffy said that more than 3,500 airplanes were in the air when the ground stop was issued. Mullin said in a news conference that preliminary investigations into the stoppage did not indicate that it was tied to a “nefarious attack”. “There’s no indication as of yet that this was a nefarious attack against it. It’s just a telecommunications outage as of right now,” he told reporters. As news of the airspace reopening trickled down to airline passengers, not all greeted the news with joy. A woman at John F Kennedy airport in New York who gave her name as simply Lola said she was frustrated. She had already rebooked her flight to Atlanta for another day and was going home. “I don’t like it,” she said. Amid the earlier confusion at US airports, the California governor, Gavin Newsom, called the Trump administration to offer more clarity to passengers who are trying to get to their destinations. “Americans are stuck at airports across the country. They deserve answers, clear updates, and a plan to get home safely. Instead, the Trump Administration is correcting reporters on AI’s “preferred name”. These are not serious people,” Newsom wrote in a post on X, in reference to Mullin correcting a reporter’s use of the term AI earlier in the day. In an interview on CNN, US congressman Ro Khanna said that he is waiting to be briefed on what exactly led to the technical issues and sparked the ground stoppage and for more public-facing communications from the transportation secretary. “There’s a lot of nervousness,” Khanna said of the feeling among passengers. “We’re waiting to be briefed in Congress about what, exactly, has happened. Airport chaos continues after FAA lifts ground stop – live updates

The Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) has lifted a nationwide ground stop that was declared Friday afternoon, delaying or canceling more than 11,000 US flights, according to aviation tracker FlightAware , and throwing airports into sudden chaos.

The FAA confirmed the airspace was open in an advisory on its website . “So at 8.15 tonight, Eastern Time, we’ve opened up the airspace,” Sean Duffy, the US transportation secretary, said. “But it’s going to take us some time to unwind what’s happened this afternoon .”
Duffy said that the federal government has “identified the problem” that brought down the US air traffic control system on Friday and the system “is operational right now”.

The White House briefing Friday evening with Duffy and Markwayne Mullin, the homeland security secretary, quickly turned into a plea for funding from Congress to “fully fund a full build of a brand new air traffic control system”.

“What we have is an incredibly old air traffic control system,” Duffy said. “Our routers actually got overloaded with data, and … they started to give us inconsistency in the data from those routers. And because of that, we shut the system down,” he added.

Earlier Friday, Duffy said in a social media post that the stoppage was due to “a communication issue impacting all Air Route Traffic Control Centers” and that the FAA’s technicians are looking into the matter.
A notice from the FAA said the ground stop was being imposed “due to extraordinary circumstances and for reasons of safety”.
Duffy said that more than 3,500 airplanes were in the air when the ground stop was issued.
Mullin said in a news conference that preliminary investigations into the stoppage did not indicate that it was tied to a “nefarious attack”.
“There’s no indication as of yet that this was a nefarious attack against it. It’s just a telecommunications outage as of right now,” he told reporters.

As news of the airspace reopening trickled down to airline passengers, not all greeted the news with joy. A woman at John F Kennedy airport in New York who gave her name as simply Lola said she was frustrated. She had already rebooked her flight to Atlanta for another day and was going home. “I don’t like it,” she said.
Amid the earlier confusion at US airports, the California governor, Gavin Newsom, called the Trump administration to offer more clarity to passengers who are trying to get to their destinations.

“Americans are stuck at airports across the country. They deserve answers, clear updates, and a plan to get home safely. Instead, the Trump Administration is correcting reporters on AI’s “preferred name”. These are not serious people,” Newsom wrote in a post on X, in reference to Mullin correcting a reporter’s use of the term AI earlier in the day.

In an interview on CNN, US congressman Ro Khanna said that he is waiting to be briefed on what exactly led to the technical issues and sparked the ground stoppage and for more public-facing communications from the transportation secretary.

“There’s a lot of nervousness,” Khanna said of the feeling among passengers. “We’re waiting to be briefed in Congress about what, exactly, has happened. We just need communication from them. If they were there every hour briefing the American public, it would help and give us a sense of a timeline.”

According to CNN, the FAA told airlines that the outages are the result of router malfunctions that are believed to have originated at Chicago Midway international airport and rippled across the rest of the US.
Amid the uncertainty, San Francisco international airport announced in a social media post that flights bound for Hawaii and Asia were cleared to depart.
John F Kennedy airport posted on its social media that travelers should confirm flight status with the airline before heading to the airport.

British Airways cancelled a flight to New York that had been due to take off from Heathrow at 10.30pm on Friday night, and a spokesperson for Manchester airport confirmed three US-bound flights scheduled to leave on Saturday morning – all operated by Virgin Atlantic – were likely to be affected if the issue was not resolved soon.
A ground-stop order by the FAA requires that aircraft remain on the ground and bars them from taking off. Planes already in the air are usually allowed to remain in the air.

This is the third time all departing flights have been grounded in the US. The first time was on 9/11; the other was in January 2023, when the FAA paused all ⁠domestic departures for less than two hours after a pilot notification system malfunctioned.
The FAA has more than 14,000 air traffic controllers who handle the more than 44,000 flights that take off from airports across the US each day, according to FAA data.

Last week, the FAA announced that the first digital air traffic control towers in the US were officially operational in Alaska and Florida, as part of a modernization project intended to reduce flight delays and improve the flow of air traffic.
Last year, ​Congress ​approved $12.5bn to fix ​the FAA’s ageing communications system, and ​on Friday ‌the FAA ​and ​White House asked Congress for another $30.1bn to address other issues.

Sean Duffy, the transportation secretary, said the airspace was now open and the problem had been identified
Airport chaos continues after FAA lifts ground stop – live updates

The Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) has lifted a nationwide ground stop that was declared Friday afternoon, delaying or canceling more than 11,000 US flights, according to aviation tracker FlightAware , and throwing airports into sudden chaos.

The FAA confirmed the airspace was open in an advisory on its website . “So at 8.15 tonight, Eastern Time, we’ve opened up the airspace,” Sean Duffy, the US transportation secretary, said. “But it’s going to take us some time to unwind what’s happened this afternoon .”
Duffy said that the federal government has “identified the problem” that brought down the US air traffic control system on Friday and the system “is operational right now”.

The White House briefing Friday evening with Duffy and Markwayne Mullin, the homeland security secretary, quickly turned into a plea for funding from Congress to “fully fund a full build of a brand new air traffic control system”.

“What we have is an incredibly old air traffic control system,” Duffy said. “Our routers actually got overloaded with data, and … they started to give us inconsistency in the data from those routers. And because of that, we shut the system down,” he added.

Earlier Friday, Duffy said in a social media post that the stoppage was due to “a communication issue impacting all Air Route Traffic Control Centers” and that the FAA’s technicians are looking into the matter.
A notice from the FAA said the ground stop was being imposed “due to extraordinary circumstances and for reasons of safety”.
Duffy said that more than 3,500 airplanes were in the air when the ground stop was issued.
Mullin said in a news conference that preliminary investigations into the stoppage did not indicate that it was tied to a “nefarious attack”.
“There’s no indication as of yet that this was a nefarious attack against it. It’s just a telecommunications outage as of right now,” he told reporters.

As news of the airspace reopening trickled down to airline passengers, not all greeted the news with joy. A woman at John F Kennedy airport in New York who gave her name as simply Lola said she was frustrated. She had already rebooked her flight to Atlanta for another day and was going home. “I don’t like it,” she said.
Amid the earlier confusion at US airports, the California governor, Gavin Newsom, called the Trump administration to offer more clarity to passengers who are trying to get to their destinations.

“Americans are stuck at airports across the country. They deserve answers, clear updates, and a plan to get home safely. Instead, the Trump Administration is correcting reporters on AI’s “preferred name”. These are not serious people,” Newsom wrote in a post on X, in reference to Mullin correcting a reporter’s use of the term AI earlier in the day.

In an interview on CNN, US congressman Ro Khanna said that he is waiting to be briefed on what exactly led to the technical issues and sparked the ground stoppage and for more public-facing communications from the transportation secretary.

“There’s a lot of nervousness,” Khanna said of the feeling among passengers. “We’re waiting to be briefed in Congress about what, exactly, has happened. We just need communication from them. If they were there every hour briefing the American public, it would help and give us a sense of a timeline.”

According to CNN, the FAA told airlines that the outages are the result of router malfunctions that are believed to have originated at Chicago Midway international airport and rippled across the rest of the US.
Amid the uncertainty, San Francisco international airport announced in a social media post that flights bound for Hawaii and Asia were cleared to depart.
John F Kennedy airport posted on its social media that travelers should confirm flight status with the airline before heading to the airport.

British Airways cancelled a flight to New York that had been due to take off from Heathrow at 10.30pm on Friday night, and a spokesperson for Manchester airport confirmed three US-bound flights scheduled to leave on Saturday morning – all operated by Virgin Atlantic – were likely to be affected if the issue was not resolved soon.
A ground-stop order by the FAA requires that aircraft remain on the ground and bars them from taking off. Planes already in the air are usually allowed to remain in the air.

This is the third time all departing flights have been grounded in the US. The first time was on 9/11; the other was in January 2023, when the FAA paused all ⁠domestic departures for less than two hours after a pilot notification system malfunctioned.
The FAA has more than 14,000 air traffic controllers who handle the more than 44,000 flights that take off from airports across the US each day, according to FAA data.

Last week, the FAA announced that the first digital air traffic control towers in the US were officially operational in Alaska and Florida, as part of a modernization project intended to reduce flight delays and improve the flow of air traffic.
Last year, ​Congress ​approved $12.5bn to fix ​the FAA’s ageing communications system, and ​on Friday ‌the FAA ​and ​White House asked Congress for another $30.1bn to address other issues.

Open-weight artificial intelligence could lose one of its most influential supporters following the board-led ouster of Nvidia co-founder Jensen Huang, potentially changing the direction of an industry in which the chipmaker has championed alternatives to closed AI systems. The push for openly available AI model weights is one of several efforts Huang helped organize that could suffer after his resignation following his admission of an extramarital affair, TechCrunch argued . Nvidia makes open-weight models available alongside open-source tools for AI agents and security. These models give businesses more choices and can help reduce costs. In July, Huang coordinated a letter in favor of open-weight models that attracted hundreds of signatures. The effort followed reported lobbying by Anthropic and OpenAI for restrictions on Chinese open-weight models. TechCrunch identified Microsoft CEO Satya Nadella as another prominent supporter, though the outlet observed that Nadella hasn't organized the industry around the issue as visibly as Huang. Beyond supporting open-weight models, Huang helped finance the infrastructure needed to power AI. According to Bloomberg reporting cited in the analysis, Nvidia had committed to $750 billion in deals by July in which its investments helped companies expand and purchase its chips. That expansion has consequences for the energy grid: Data centers need electricity to run processors and cooling equipment. TechCrunch posited that his departure weakens that approach by removing its most visible champion. Another initiative looks to move some AI work onto personal computers. extraction.body: The open source community just lost one of its strongest advocates. Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang resigned Thursday after he admitted to an affair with an alleged Chinese spy, raising concerns about U.S. national security and the motives behind the executive’s support for softer chip export controls on China. Huang has been a staunch supporter of open source AI, framing the ecosystem as good for safety, innovation, diffusion, and sovereignty. And as frontier AI labs increasingly move to reduce their reliance on Nvidia and build their own chips, supporting open source is also a good way for the company to diversify its customer base by selling chips to nation-states, enterprises, and any organization that wants to own its own models. Still, Huang’s resignation raises questions about whether Nvidia will carry on his legacy by continuing to support the open model community. Jensen no longer being CEO would be very very bad for the open model cause in the US. Huang’s departure also comes as Nvidia has yet to finalize a deal to acquire open source platform Hugging Face for $13 billion . Hugging Face CEO Clem Delangue said in a post on X that the company would continue to fight for open source , whatever happens next. Nvidia also agreed to pay $6 billion for a non-exclusive license for open AI coding startup Poolside’s technology. Within Nvidia, Huang pushed for the development of the Nemotron family of open-weight AI models built for long-running agentic AI systems and reasoning workloads — potential competitors to closed frontier models. One company insider told TechCrunch that they don’t expect a change in leadership to have an impact on Nemotron development. Huang also backed companies that would make American open models more competitive, investing in startups like Reflection AI and Thinking Machines Lab. Huang’s influence extended beyond Nvidia’s investments and product roadmap. He also emerged as one of the most prominent voices pushing back against Washington’s efforts to restrict the open AI ecosystem. Earlier this year, Huang wrote an open letter signed by 25 companies, including Microsoft, Meta, IBM, and Palantir, urging the U.S. government not to over-restrict open-weight AI models, many of which come from China. The impetus for that letter was Washington’s debate over how the U.S. should respond to allegations that Chinese AI labs are stealing intellectual property from American counterparts like Anthropic and OpenAI, both of which have reportedly appealed directly to Washington on the matter, urging stronger protections. That combination of Huang’s personal visibility and Nvidia’s market power made him the strongest counterweight to arguments from closed-model providers like Anthropic and OpenAI, which have advocated for greater restrictions on advanced AI models due to safety reasons. Without Huang, the concern among open source community members is that whoever takes over will be more cautious. Nvidia has named CFO Colette Kress as interim CEO. It’s not clear how Kress will approach the Hugging Face deal or support for the open model ecosystem, but founder-driven priorities tend to get a downgrade when leadership changes. Huang’s exit could also strengthen the arguments of those in Washington who are arguing for tougher restrictions on Chinese AI companies, particularly as the scandal surrounding his relationship with Alice Huang, the Megaspeed executive and alleged spy, puts renewed scrutiny on his efforts to loosen chip export controls. Restrictions on open-weight models from China could kneecap competition for American companies, the most powerful of which have kept their models closed. Still, supporting open source isn’t simply a passion project Huang pursued out of idealism. It’s increasingly central to Nvidia’s business strategy. As some of Nvidia’s biggest customers, including Google and OpenAI, develop their own chips, Nvidia has an incentive to cultivate a much broader ecosystem of AI developers and customers. More players training, fine-tuning, and running models mean more GPUs sold, and less dependence on a handful of frontier labs. Huang may be gone, but Nvidia still needs an open AI ecosystem. The question now is whether that commitment can survive without the man who made it a priority. TechCrunch has reached out to Nvidia for comment. Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang resigned Thursday after he admitted to an affair with an alleged Chinese spy, raising concerns about U.S. national security and the motives behind the executive’s support for softer chip export controls on China.

Huang has been a staunch supporter of open source AI, framing the ecosystem as good for safety, innovation, diffusion, and sovereignty. And as frontier AI labs increasingly move to reduce their reliance on Nvidia and build their own chips, supporting open source is also a good way for the company to diversify its customer base by selling chips to nation-states, enterprises, and any organization that wants to own its own models.
Still, Huang’s resignation raises questions about whether Nvidia will carry on his legacy by continuing to support the open model community.
Jensen no longer being CEO would be very very bad for the open model cause in the US.

Huang’s departure also comes as Nvidia has yet to finalize a deal to acquire open source platform Hugging Face for $13 billion . Hugging Face CEO Clem Delangue said in a post on X that the company would continue to fight for open source , whatever happens next.
Nvidia also agreed to pay $6 billion for a non-exclusive license for open AI coding startup Poolside’s technology.

Within Nvidia, Huang pushed for the development of the Nemotron family of open-weight AI models built for long-running agentic AI systems and reasoning workloads — potential competitors to closed frontier models. One company insider told TechCrunch that they don’t expect a change in leadership to have an impact on Nemotron development.
Huang also backed companies that would make American open models more competitive, investing in startups like Reflection AI and Thinking Machines Lab.

Huang’s influence extended beyond Nvidia’s investments and product roadmap. He also emerged as one of the most prominent voices pushing back against Washington’s efforts to restrict the open AI ecosystem.

Earlier this year, Huang wrote an open letter signed by 25 companies, including Microsoft, Meta, IBM, and Palantir, urging the U.S. government not to over-restrict open-weight AI models, many of which come from China.

The impetus for that letter was Washington’s debate over how the U.S. should respond to allegations that Chinese AI labs are stealing intellectual property from American counterparts like Anthropic and OpenAI, both of which have reportedly appealed directly to Washington on the matter, urging stronger protections.

That combination of Huang’s personal visibility and Nvidia’s market power made him the strongest counterweight to arguments from closed-model providers like Anthropic and OpenAI, which have advocated for greater restrictions on advanced AI models due to safety reasons.

Without Huang, the concern among open source community members is that whoever takes over will be more cautious. Nvidia has named CFO Colette Kress as interim CEO. It’s not clear how Kress will approach the Hugging Face deal or support for the open model ecosystem, but founder-driven priorities tend to get a downgrade when leadership changes.

Huang’s exit could also strengthen the arguments of those in Washington who are arguing for tougher restrictions on Chinese AI companies, particularly as the scandal surrounding his relationship with Alice Huang, the Megaspeed executive and alleged spy, puts renewed scrutiny on his efforts to loosen chip export controls.
Restrictions on open-weight models from China could kneecap competition for American companies, the most powerful of which have kept their models closed.
Still, supporting open source isn’t simply a passion project Huang pursued out of idealism. It’s increasingly central to Nvidia’s business strategy.
As some of Nvidia’s biggest customers, including Google and OpenAI, develop their own chips, Nvidia has an incentive to cultivate a much broader ecosystem of AI developers and customers.
More players training, fine-tuning, and running models mean more GPUs sold, and less dependence on a handful of frontier labs.
Huang may be gone, but Nvidia still needs an open AI ecosystem. The question now is whether that commitment can survive without the man who made it a priority.
TechCrunch has reached out to Nvidia for comment.

extraction.body: Nvidia’s former chief executive Jensen Huang (젠슨 황) has stepped down following a board decision, raising expectations that a significant vacuum could emerge across the AI industry.On Tuesday, tech media outlet TechCrunch said the matter goes beyond a simple management scandal and could shake Nvidia’s role in driving AI policy and coordinating the industry.The key point is that Huang has served as a leading external channel for the AI industry, beyond his role as Nvidia CEO. Nvidia has pushed multiple agendas at once, including open-weight models, safety for AI agents, AI PCs and data centre investment structures, rather than acting only as a semiconductor supplier. Huang’s exit is seen as removing the central axis that connected and drove these agendas at the same time.First, some have raised the possibility that momentum behind open-weight models could weaken. Huang is seen as one of the most active advocates for the need for open-weight models in discussions with the tech industry and policymakers. Nvidia has provided not only its own models but also open-source technology tied to agents and AI security, and it has already agreed to acquire Hugging Face for $12.9 billion. The deal is expected to close in the first half of next year, subject to regulatory approval.After reports in July that Anthropic and OpenAI had asked the Trump administration to ban Chinese open-weight models, Huang organised an industry-wide letter of support. He advanced the argument that open-weight models give companies choice and lower costs. But a key variable is that there may be no clear figure to lead this push in an organised way at the industry level going forward.Debates on regulating AI agents could also be affected. Huang has publicly argued several times this year that, while security incidents involving AI agents have been revealed, the industry does not yet need regulation and safety issues can be solved through technology. He rallied the industry again as it was reviewing whether it needed an audit framework or a supervisory body similar to financial industry regulators. Nvidia brought together more than 100 companies to launch an Open Agent Safety Platform. The open-source-based project set out the goal of reducing problems involving agents that go out of control.The industry’s view of AI could also change. Huang has defined AI as an engineering system that produces products and stressed it can be controlled like other engineering systems. That contrasts with a trend among some large AI labs to highlight model autonomy or the possibility of consciousness. TechCrunch said Huang’s exit would, for the time being, weaken the voice representing that opposing view.Nvidia’s strategy in the AI PC market is also being put to the test. Huang recently persuaded several PC manufacturers to join Nvidia’s CPU strategy. He has also prepared a premium line of AI PCs that run AI agents on the device itself. The new products are due for release ahead of the year-end shopping season.The issue is that Huang’s personal symbolism has played an important role in product marketing. TechCrunch said Huang was no longer a suitable figure to promote these devices as an alternative to the Mac mini. It said Huang’s exit introduced a variable into efforts to build awareness for the new products and into strategies to expand the market.Confidence in AI data centre investment and financing structures could also be shaken. As a data centre construction boom continued, Huang directly designed large-scale financial structures centred on Nvidia. Critics have also raised claims that Nvidia approved circular transactions in which it supports customer expansion through equity investment and those customers then buy Nvidia chips. Citing a Bloomberg report, the outlet said the company had committed about $750 billion in such transactions through July.In August, Nvidia decided to provide support akin to loss compensation for $105 billion in funding for an OpenAI data centre in Ohio, and in the same month major private equity firms and financial companies including Apollo, BlackRock, Blackstone, Brookfield, Goldman Sachs and KKR decided to invest up to $500 billion in data centre construction. Huang has promised that Nvidia GPUs can serve as collateral that guarantees value preservation, presenting Nvidia as “investable infrastructure”.The issue is that Huang’s exit could affect confidence in these financing ideas themselves. Wall Street is already worried about the possibility of a sharp drop in Nvidia’s share price and the fallout, while fatigue over AI infrastructure investment has also grown. TechCrunch wrote, “Nvidia has ultimately lost its top salesman, and the AI industry has lost its strongest ‘hype man’.”After Huang’s exit, Nvidia now faces the task of building new leadership beyond a founder-centric management system. External variables also remain, including the possibility of additional political investigations. Whether Nvidia can replace Huang’s personal influence and maintain leadership of the AI industry has emerged as a key point to watch for the industry.

extraction.body: Michael Dell described Jensen Huang as a "visionary of the AI age." Deutsche Telekom CEO Tim Höttges said a photo with the Nvidia CEO produced more media coverage for his company than its iPhone launch. During the keynote of his annual Dreamforce conference, Salesforce's Marc Benioff said, "Jensen, we're all following you, bro," as the two paced through the audience. Follow CNBC's live coverage of Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang's resignation His fame extended way beyond tech. In May, Huang joined President Donald Trump on Air Force One for a trip to China to meet with President Xi Jinping . Three months later, Huang gathered six of the biggest names at the Nasdaq to announce on CNBC a proposed $500 billion artificial intelligence buildout plan, cementing his central role at the intersection of Wall Street and Silicon Valley. As Nvidia became the first company to rip past a $5 trillion market cap, bending the laws of physics with its advanced graphics processing units and pushing the AI boom to seemingly endless bounds, the now 63-year-old Huang, clad in a black leather jacket, traversed the globe as the face of the brand powering the next industrial revolution. Over the past week it all came crashing down. Following two reported extramarital affairs — one with an alleged Chinese spy and another with an employee — Huang is leaving the company he co-founded 33 years ago in crisis, and thrusting the AI market into chaos. The board is now left to pick a successor for a company that's been run by a singular figure with no second-in-command. Chief Financial Officer Colette Kress has been named interim CEO. Harvey Jones has been appointed chairman. Nvidia has not responded to multiple requests for comment. "How companies handle a crisis determines their future," former Cisco CEO John Chambers, now a startup investor, told CNBC's " Fast Money " on Wednesday. "How they handle this will determine if they're a great company and a great leadership team beyond one person." It had been a tumultuous stretch for Nvidia, even before the Huang saga led the board to launch an investigation of the CEO's behavior and the potential national security implications. The stock is on pace for its sixth straight weekly drop, which would be the longest losing streak since 2012. That includes a 9% slump last week after the midterm elections resulted in sweeping Democratic victories in both chambers of Congress, and the passage of dozens of ballot measures that could slow the buildout of new data centers. Nvidia is scheduled to report quarterly results on Tuesday, and expectations remain high, with analysts projecting 92% year-over-year revenue growth to $109.2 billion, according to LSEG. That's up 18-fold from the same quarter in 2022, just before OpenAI launched ChatGPT and kicked off the generative AI era. It's a historic level of growth for any business, and particularly notable for a company that spent most of its first few decades as a niche technology provider for video games. Huang founded Nvidia to make chips for computer graphics, both for video games and rendering. In the early 2000s, he and other executives saw an opportunity to put GPUs to work for computationally intense projects. That technology eventually turned Nvidia into the most important player in AI and a key American asset for national defense. In the process, Huang became the ultimate decider, choosing how, when and where GPUs get allocated. The biggest buyers were the hyperscalers — Amazon, Google , Meta and Microsoft — which needed the chips to build their own AI services and make them available to cloud customers. OpenAI , meanwhile, was snapping up GPUs for its powerful models and consumer apps. Oracle gobbled up billions of dollars worth of GPUs, going heavily into debt in the process. Elon Musk's xAI, now part of SpaceX , did the same to build its Grok model, before eventually starting to rent out excess capacity to Anthropic and Google. Huang wanted the world standardizing on Nvidia. Last year he demanded that Oracle buy additional Nvidia networking hardware if it wanted allocation to its state-of-the-art Grace Blackwell chips, said two people familiar with the deal who asked not to be named because the negotiations were private. In August, Nvidia said it will provide up to $105 billion in financing for an OpenAI data center in Ohio that could be the largest of its kind in the world. "He created the product that started the industry," said Chris Miglino, CEO of neocloud Axe Compute . " Without his leadership we may be many years behind where we are today with AI chip technology, which is the driving force behind the neocloud market." When it comes to investing cash in fledgling startups, Huang is known to host entrepreneurs at Nvidia's Silicon Valley headquarters. While there could be 30 Nvidia employees in the room for the pitch meeting, only Huang asks questions, according to people with knowledge of the matter, who requested anonymity because they're not authorized to speak publicly about it. One source told CNBC that key aspects of project finance are so reliant on Huang's sign-off that, when he travels, those involved in the deal are forced to wait for his plane to land before learning if they can go forward or if terms have to be renegotiated. Huang's ambitions extended well beyond the U.S. He wanted to be a force in China, which became a difficult market for Nvidia during the Biden administration and was virtually off-limits after Trump implemented strict export controls in his second term. Huang's aggressive pursuit of China may have been his undoing. The woman, with whom the Nvidia CEO had a romantic affair, was identified by U.S. intelligence as having been recruited by China's Ministry of State Security to gather information on Huang, according to people briefed on the intelligence cited by The New York Times. She has business ties to Megaspeed International, a Singapore-based cloud computing firm and an Nvidia customer that's facing scrutiny over suspicions that it facilitated billions of dollars of restricted Nvidia chips to China. U.S. lawmakers are up in arms, with many demanding investigations as well as Huang's resignation. Senate Banking Committee member Kevin Cramer , R-N.D., vocalized his concerns on Wednesday. "What bothers me at the end of it is what we don't know is what she knows about him that can be utilized," Cramer told CNBC, right before Huang resigned and referring to the affair. "This is a guy that's right now so vulnerable to extortion, blackmail. I just don't think, as a national security matter, we can run the risk." But industry experts are quick to emphasize how important Huang was to the health and growth of the broad AI ecosystem. He had the leading names on Wall Street on speed dial as he tried to turn GPUs into what he called an "investable asset" with an expanded roster of financial backers, and he had personal relationships with all the key figures in AI like OpenAI's Sam Altman and SoftBank's Masayoshi Son. On the deal-making side, Huang's top lieutenants were Kress and Vishal Bhagwati, head of corporate development, sources said, though they add that all the big decisions were made by the CEO. And when seeking a financial backstop, the person behind Huang was Nico Caprez, the CEO's son-in-law and the company's vice president of global AI infrastructure growth, three people said. Executives at numerous Nvidia customers, partners and portfolio companies told CNBC that Huang frequently emailed or called CEOs to offer his help in challenging times. Tomás Puig, founder and CEO of enterprise AI startup Alembic, said that following the collapse of Silicon Valley Bank in 2023, his company was "down to weeks of cash and Nvidia was our biggest customer." "I emailed Jensen, and they prepaid two years of invoices so we could keep the lights on and people kept their jobs," Puig told CNBC. That approach persisted, as recently as this week. On Monday, a day after publicly apologizing for being unfaithful to his wife, Huang emailed the CEO of AI infrastructure startup Fireworks AI, according to a person with knowledge of the matter. Fireworks, which Nvidia first backed in 2024, was dealing with a series of high-profile cyberattacks. Huang, whose name was suddenly front-page news for all the wrong reasons, was checking in, the person said, just to see if he could help. — CNBC's Lora Kolodny, Jordan Novet and Seema Mody contributed to this report.

sources.title: Jensen Huang’s exit puts Nvidia’s support for open source in question
passages: Without Huang, the concern among open source community members is that whoever takes over will be more cautious.
Nvidia has named CFO Colette Kress as interim CEO.
It’s not clear how Kress will approach the Hugging Face deal or support for the open model ecosystem, but founder-driven priorities tend to get a downgrade when leadership changes.
Huang’s departure also comes as Nvidia has yet to finalize a deal to acquire open source platform Hugging Face for $13 billion .
Still, supporting open source isn’t simply a passion project Huang pursued out of idealism.
It’s increasingly central to Nvidia’s business strategy.
Huang has been a staunch supporter of open source AI, framing the ecosystem as good for safety, innovation, diffusion, and sovereignty.
Huang’s influence extended beyond Nvidia’s investments and product roadmap.
He also emerged as one of the most prominent voices pushing back against Washington’s efforts to restrict the open AI ecosystem.

Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang resigned Thursday after he admitted to an affair with an alleged Chinese spy, raising concerns about U.S. national security and the motives behind the executive’s support for softer chip export controls on China.
Nvidia also agreed to pay $6 billion for a non-exclusive license for open AI coding startup Poolside’s technology.
The question now is whether that commitment can survive without the man who made it a priority.

Within Nvidia, Huang pushed for the development of the Nemotron family of open-weight AI models built for long-running agentic AI systems and reasoning workloads — potential competitors to closed frontier models.
As some of Nvidia’s biggest customers, including Google and OpenAI, develop their own chips, Nvidia has an incentive to cultivate a much broader ecosystem of AI developers and customers.
Huang also backed companies that would make American open models more competitive, investing in startups like Reflection AI and Thinking Machines Lab.
TechCrunch has reached out to Nvidia for comment.
This article has been updated with information from an Nvidia employee.

And as frontier AI labs increasingly move to reduce their reliance on Nvidia and build their own chips, supporting open source is also a good way for the company to diversify its customer base by selling chips to nation-states, enterprises, and any organization that wants to own its own models. Still, Huang’s resignation raises questions about whether Nvidia will carry on his legacy by continuing to support the open model community. Jensen no longer being CEO would be very very bad for the open model cause in the US. Huang’s departure also comes as Nvidia has yet to finalize a deal to acquire open source platform Hugging Face for $13 billion . Hugging Face CEO Clem Delangue said in a post on X that the company would continue to fight for open source , whatever happens next. Nvidia also agreed to pay $6 billion for a non-exclusive license for open AI coding startup Poolside’s technology. Within Nvidia, Huang pushed for the development of the Nemotron family of open-weight AI models built for long-running agentic AI systems and reasoning workloads — potential competitors to closed frontier models. One company insider told TechCrunch that they don’t expect a change in leadership to have an impact on Nemotron development. Huang also backed companies that would make American open models more competitive, investing in startups like Reflection AI and Thinking Machines Lab. Huang’s influence extended beyond Nvidia’s investments and product roadmap. He also emerged as one of the most prominent voices pushing back against Washington’s efforts to restrict the open AI ecosystem. Earlier this year, Huang wrote an open letter signed by 25 companies, including Microsoft, Meta, IBM, and Palantir, urging the U.S. government not to over-restrict open-weight AI models, many of which come from China. It’s not clear how Kress will approach the Hugging Face deal or support for the open model ecosystem, but founder-driven priorities tend to get a downgrade when leadership changes. More players training, fine-tuning, and running models mean more GPUs sold, and less dependence on a handful of frontier labs. Huang may be gone, but Nvidia still needs an open AI ecosystem. sources.title: Nvidia without Jensen Huang raises questions for AI industry as CEO exit brings five ripple effects
passages: Nvidia’s former chief executive Jensen Huang (젠슨 황) has stepped down following a board decision, raising expectations that a significant vacuum could emerge across the AI industry.On Tuesday, tech media outlet TechCrunch said the matter goes beyond a simple management scandal and could shake Nvidia’s role in driving AI policy and coordinating the industry.The key point is that Huang has served as a leading external channel for the AI industry, beyond his role as Nvidia CEO.
Nvidia has pushed multiple agendas at once, including open-weight models, safety for AI agents, AI PCs and data centre investment structures, rather than acting only as a semiconductor supplier.

Citing a Bloomberg report, the outlet said the company had committed about $750 billion in such transactions through July.In August, Nvidia decided to provide support akin to loss compensation for $105 billion in funding for an OpenAI data centre in Ohio, and in the same month major private equity firms and financial companies including Apollo, BlackRock, Blackstone, Brookfield, Goldman Sachs and KKR decided to invest up to $500 billion in data centre construction.
Nvidia has provided not only its own models but also open-source technology tied to agents and AI security, and it has already agreed to acquire Hugging Face for $12.9 billion.
Nvidia brought together more than 100 companies to launch an Open Agent Safety Platform.
Huang recently persuaded several PC manufacturers to join Nvidia’s CPU strategy.
Critics have also raised claims that Nvidia approved circular transactions in which it supports customer expansion through equity investment and those customers then buy Nvidia chips.
Wall Street is already worried about the possibility of a sharp drop in Nvidia’s share price and the fallout, while fatigue over AI infrastructure investment has also grown.
The open-source-based project set out the goal of reducing problems involving agents that go out of control.The industry’s view of AI could also change.

extraction.body: Nvidia’s former chief executive Jensen Huang (젠슨 황) has stepped down following a board decision, raising expectations that a significant vacuum could emerge across the AI industry.On Tuesday, tech media outlet TechCrunch said the matter goes beyond a simple management scandal and could shake Nvidia’s role in driving AI policy and coordinating the industry.The key point is that Huang has served as a leading external channel for the AI industry, beyond his role as Nvidia CEO. Nvidia has pushed multiple agendas at once, including open-weight models, safety for AI agents, AI PCs and data centre investment structures, rather than acting only as a semiconductor supplier. Huang’s exit is seen as removing the central axis that connected and drove these agendas at the same time.First, some have raised the possibility that momentum behind open-weight models could weaken. Huang is seen as one of the most active advocates for the need for open-weight models in discussions with the tech industry and policymakers. Nvidia has provided not only its own models but also open-source technology tied to agents and AI security, and it has already agreed to acquire Hugging Face for $12.9 billion. The deal is expected to close in the first half of next year, subject to regulatory approval.After reports in July that Anthropic and OpenAI had asked the Trump administration to ban Chinese open-weight models, Huang organised an industry-wide letter of support. He advanced the argument that open-weight models give companies choice and lower costs. But a key variable is that there may be no clear figure to lead this push in an organised way at the industry level going forward.Debates on regulating AI agents could also be affected. Huang has publicly argued several times this year that, while security incidents involving AI agents have been revealed, the industry does not yet need regulation and safety issues can be solved through technology. He rallied the industry again as it was reviewing whether it needed an audit framework or a supervisory body similar to financial industry regulators. Nvidia brought together more than 100 companies to launch an Open Agent Safety Platform. The open-source-based project set out the goal of reducing problems involving agents that go out of control.The industry’s view of AI could also change. Huang has defined AI as an engineering system that produces products and stressed it can be controlled like other engineering systems. That contrasts with a trend among some large AI labs to highlight model autonomy or the possibility of consciousness. TechCrunch said Huang’s exit would, for the time being, weaken the voice representing that opposing view.Nvidia’s strategy in the AI PC market is also being put to the test. Huang recently persuaded several PC manufacturers to join Nvidia’s CPU strategy. He has also prepared a premium line of AI PCs that run AI agents on the device itself. The new products are due for release ahead of the year-end shopping season.The issue is that Huang’s personal symbolism has played an important role in product marketing. TechCrunch said Huang was no longer a suitable figure to promote these devices as an alternative to the Mac mini. It said Huang’s exit introduced a variable into efforts to build awareness for the new products and into strategies to expand the market.Confidence in AI data centre investment and financing structures could also be shaken. As a data centre construction boom continued, Huang directly designed large-scale financial structures centred on Nvidia. Critics have also raised claims that Nvidia approved circular transactions in which it supports customer expansion through equity investment and those customers then buy Nvidia chips. Citing a Bloomberg report, the outlet said the company had committed about $750 billion in such transactions through July.In August, Nvidia decided to provide support akin to loss compensation for $105 billion in funding for an OpenAI data centre in Ohio, and in the same month major private equity firms and financial companies including Apollo, BlackRock, Blackstone, Brookfield, Goldman Sachs and KKR decided to invest up to $500 billion in data centre construction. Huang has promised that Nvidia GPUs can serve as collateral that guarantees value preservation, presenting Nvidia as “investable infrastructure”.The issue is that Huang’s exit could affect confidence in these financing ideas themselves. Wall Street is already worried about the possibility of a sharp drop in Nvidia’s share price and the fallout, while fatigue over AI infrastructure investment has also grown. TechCrunch wrote, “Nvidia has ultimately lost its top salesman, and the AI industry has lost its strongest ‘hype man’.”After Huang’s exit, Nvidia now faces the task of building new leadership beyond a founder-centric management system. External variables also remain, including the possibility of additional political investigations. Whether Nvidia can replace Huang’s personal influence and maintain leadership of the AI industry has emerged as a key point to watch for the industry.

Duffy and Department of Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin insisted during a news conference that the nation's "old" communications system became "overloaded," prompting the Federal Aviation Administration to shut down flights out of caution just before 4 p.m. on Friday. Mullin started the briefing by insisting the ground stoppage had nothing to do with a Microsoft outage a day earlier. "I want to make sure everybody understands there is no connection between this and Microsoft. I know a lot of people are making that jump. This is — so far, what we've seen, there was actually no cyberattack," Mulling told reporters at the White House late Friday. "We did it out of an abundance of caution," Mullin said of the ground stoppage, insisting there was no terrorism at play and adding, "All your loved ones are safe." Duffy said the ground stoppage was issued after experts saw "instability for our radar and our communications in our centers and our coms across the country." That "instability" prompted the decision to get planes on the ground immediately, he said. "We had over 3,500 airplanes in the air, they all engaged," said Duffy, who announced airspace had been opened as of 8:15 p.m. while warning it would take a while for things to return to normal. "Does that mean every flight will open up? It's going to be slow. If you're watching at an airport check with your airline. It depends on do we have crews available? Do we have pilots and flight attendants available to fly your flight? "We're going to try to move as many of those as we can tonight, if we have capacity with crews to move those flights. If not, we're going to start tomorrow morning with our airline partners moving those aircraft, but it's going to take us some time to unwind what's happened this afternoon." By the time Duffy announced the reopening of the airspace, at least JetBlue and United Airlines had already announced they'd canceled most of their remaining flights Friday. "This is an emergency. This is an emergency. I want Congress to give us emergency funding. This is bipartisan. This is American, I want $50 billion," he said. The Federal Aviation Administration ordered a nationwide ground stop at U.S. airports Friday, November 13.
U.S. Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy attributed the stoppage to a “communication issue.”
“FAA technicians are investigating the issue,” he said in a statement, noting that the problem affected all Air Route Traffic Control Centers.

The advisory issued to airports by the Air Traffic Control System Command Center said, “Due to extraordinary circumstances and for reasons of safety, attention all aircraft operations, by order of the Federal Aviation Command Center, all airports are ground stopped. All departing traffic should remain ground stopped until further notice.”

About five hours later, the ground stop was lifted. Trump administration officials said something overloaded the old copper-based ATC systems, causing intermittent radar and communications issues. Although the issue appeared resolved, they weren’t confident it wouldn’t happen again and said it could take days or weeks for flight schedules to normalize.
It was the third-ever nationwide halt. Previous ground stops came after the September 11, 2001, terrorist attacks and during a January 11, 2023, computer outage.

The 2023 outage disabled the FAA’s NOTAM system, which provides safety information to flight crews. The agency paused domestic departures while it checked the integrity of flight and safety information.

An FAA investigation found that contractors accidentally deleted files while trying to synchronize the system’s main database with a backup. The agency said in its January 19, 2023, statement that it had found no evidence of a cyberattack or malicious intent.

That ground stop lasted only about an hour and a half, but disruptions continued. By that afternoon, about 9,000 flights had been delayed and 1,300 canceled, according to the agency’s historical account.

The September 11 shutdown went further. The FAA halted civilian takeoffs nationwide and then ordered aircraft already in the air to land at the nearest airport as soon as practical. More than 4,500 aircraft were flying under instrument flight rules when the landing order came.
Previously, air traffic was restricted nationwide for planned drills during the Cold War.

extraction.body: Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy slammed Congress and demanded $50 billion to upgrade America's aviation systems as he announced a sudden nationwide ground stoppage on all flights had been lifted after more than four hours. Duffy and Department of Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin insisted during a news conference that the nation's "old" communications system became "overloaded," prompting the Federal Aviation Administration to shut down flights out of caution just before 4 p.m. on Friday. Mullin started the briefing by insisting the ground stoppage had nothing to do with a Microsoft outage a day earlier. "I want to make sure everybody understands there is no connection between this and Microsoft. I know a lot of people are making that jump. This is — so far, what we've seen, there was actually no cyberattack," Mulling told reporters at the White House late Friday. "We did it out of an abundance of caution," Mullin said of the ground stoppage, insisting there was no terrorism at play and adding, "All your loved ones are safe." Duffy said the ground stoppage was issued after experts saw "instability for our radar and our communications in our centers and our coms across the country." That "instability" prompted the decision to get planes on the ground immediately, he said. "We had over 3,500 airplanes in the air, they all engaged," said Duffy, who announced airspace had been opened as of 8:15 p.m. while warning it would take a while for things to return to normal. "Does that mean every flight will open up? It's going to be slow. If you're watching at an airport check with your airline. It depends on do we have crews available? Do we have pilots and flight attendants available to fly your flight? "We're going to try to move as many of those as we can tonight, if we have capacity with crews to move those flights. extraction.body: Takeoffs from airports throughout the US largely stopped on Friday after the FAA issued a national ground stop at 3:44PM ET “due to extraordinary circumstances and for reasons of safety,” while planes in the air will be allowed to land. The FAA tweeted just after 5PM ET that, “There has been a temporary telecommunications outage - out of an abundance of caution all flights have been halted. Every flight has been accounted for and international flights will be handled on a case by case basis.” More than four hours after the stop was issued, officials announced it was lifted at 8:15PM ET and that flights will resume. It’s unclear how many flights will be able to take off and when, as they now face problems of overloaded airports and flight crews that have run out of time to operate the planes, meaning many people will be stuck where they are for the time being and more flights will be delayed or canceled. In a press conference announcing that the stop had been lifted, Transportation Secretary Ryan Duffy blamed an aging air traffic control system that he is pursuing funds to replace, saying that the TRACONs (Terminal Radar Approach Control) in the air traffic control centers “started to have inconsistency in the data from the radars and the communications from airplanes.” He said that the devices that had the issue were analog telecom devices, where the switches / routers “got overloaded with data” and started to show inconsistency. An earlier report from CBS News cited multiple sources who said that an update to the air traffic control system’s private communications network, operated by L3Harris, caused a system reboot and the subsequent outage. The flight tracking site FlightAware lists 9,124 US flights as delayed and 5,901 flights canceled as of 8:39PM ET. According to CNN, the last nationwide ground stop in 2023 lasted for about 90 minutes after the NOTAM (Notice to Air Missions) system for pilots went down, and the last one prior to that was after the attacks on September 11th, 2001. Air Space Intelligence (ASI), the company that designed the system and was awarded a 12-year $875 million contract in June to deploy it, denied any connection, tweeting “The current ground stop is not based on or a result of the SMART system, any product of ASI or our integration with FAA and ATC.” Jon Ostrower of The Air Current reports that the outage began with the Chicago air traffic control center, followed by centers in Boston, Washington, New York, and Minneapolis, and as the FAA issued a ground stop for aircraft flying east, more facilities began reporting problems.

extraction.body: The US federal aviation regulator has lifted a nationwide ground stop for all airports. Trump administration officials blame "overloaded" and "outdated" systems for the hourslong halt to departures. The US Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) canceled a ground stop on all national flights hours after stopping departures at US airports on Friday. "We have old switches, old routers, we use 1980s old copper lines. We use an old system," US Secretary of Transportation Sean Duffy said. "It was a legacy network problem." Even with the order being lifted, airlines will not be able to immediately return to normal operations as many of their planes and crews are out of position. "It's going to be slow," Duffy told reporters at the White House. Officials said they think the system will be back to normal in time for Thanksgiving on November 26, one of the busiest times to travel in the US. It was the first nationwide ground stop since January 2023, when the FAA dealt with a system outage. Prior to that, the last ground stop was after the September 11, 2001 terror attacks . US Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin said there was no indication the communications breakdown resulted from a cyberattack or artificial intelligence and that the ⁠public ​was ​never ​in danger. Over 4,500 flights were canceled Friday and about 700 for Saturday and over 10,000 flights within, into, or out of the United States were delayed, according to the FlightAware aviation tracker. "All departing traffic should remain groundstopped until further notice," the FAA had said earlier Friday. The agency said the ground stop was "due to extraordinary circumstances and reasons for safety." The FAA cited a temporary telecommunication outage and said, "Every flight has been accounted for and international flights will be handled on a case by case basis." The agency said flights were halted "out of abundance of caution." In a post on X, Duffy said the stop was due to a communication issue impacting all Air Route Traffic Control Centers. "FAA technicians are investigating the issue. We will provide immediate updates as we have them," he wrote. The FAA ground stop order came a day after Duffy asked Congress for $30 billion to upgrade and modernize the US Air Traffic Control System. "This investment is critical to complete the modernization of our national airspace — delivering a resilient telecommunications backbone for air traffic controllers, modern hardware and software, state-of-the-art control towers, and world-class airport infrastructure," Duffy and Office of Management and Budget Director Russell Vought wrote in a letter to lawmakers. The European Organisation for the Safety of Air Navigation, Eurocontrol, urged airlines to issue delay notices for flights that had initially been unable to take off. Eurocontrol had earlier said that all flights departing for US airports from its 42 member states were suspended following a request from the FAA. It has since removed that note from its website. Canada's air navigation service provider, NAV Canada, said it is closely monitoring the US ground stop and later said, "It was implementing traffic management measures at Toronto Pearson, Montreal-Trudeau, Calgary and Vancouver to safely manage traffic volumes." "Travelers should expect delays and check with their airline. Our systems are operating normally," NAV Canada added.

extraction.body: Takeoffs from airports throughout the US largely stopped on Friday after the FAA issued a national ground stop at 3:44PM ET “due to extraordinary circumstances and for reasons of safety,” while planes in the air will be allowed to land. The FAA tweeted just after 5PM ET that, “There has been a temporary telecommunications outage - out of an abundance of caution all flights have been halted. Every flight has been accounted for and international flights will be handled on a case by case basis.” More than four hours after the stop was issued, officials announced it was lifted at 8:15PM ET and that flights will resume. It’s unclear how many flights will be able to take off and when, as they now face problems of overloaded airports and flight crews that have run out of time to operate the planes, meaning many people will be stuck where they are for the time being and more flights will be delayed or canceled. In a press conference announcing that the stop had been lifted, Transportation Secretary Ryan Duffy blamed an aging air traffic control system that he is pursuing funds to replace, saying that the TRACONs (Terminal Radar Approach Control) in the air traffic control centers “started to have inconsistency in the data from the radars and the communications from airplanes.” He said that the devices that had the issue were analog telecom devices, where the switches / routers “got overloaded with data” and started to show inconsistency. An earlier report from CBS News cited multiple sources who said that an update to the air traffic control system’s private communications network, operated by L3Harris, caused a system reboot and the subsequent outage. The flight tracking site FlightAware lists 9,124 US flights as delayed and 5,901 flights canceled as of 8:39PM ET. According to CNN, the last nationwide ground stop in 2023 lasted for about 90 minutes after the NOTAM (Notice to Air Missions) system for pilots went down, and the last one prior to that was after the attacks on September 11th, 2001. Air Space Intelligence (ASI), the company that designed the system and was awarded a 12-year $875 million contract in June to deploy it, denied any connection, tweeting “The current ground stop is not based on or a result of the SMART system, any product of ASI or our integration with FAA and ATC.” Jon Ostrower of The Air Current reports that the outage began with the Chicago air traffic control center, followed by centers in Boston, Washington, New York, and Minneapolis, and as the FAA issued a ground stop for aircraft flying east, more facilities began reporting problems.

extraction.body: The US federal aviation regulator has lifted a nationwide ground stop for all airports. Trump administration officials blame "overloaded" and "outdated" systems for the hourslong halt to departures. The US Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) canceled a ground stop on all national flights hours after stopping departures at US airports on Friday. "We have old switches, old routers, we use 1980s old copper lines. We use an old system," US Secretary of Transportation Sean Duffy said. "It was a legacy network problem." Even with the order being lifted, airlines will not be able to immediately return to normal operations as many of their planes and crews are out of position. "It's going to be slow," Duffy told reporters at the White House. Officials said they think the system will be back to normal in time for Thanksgiving on November 26, one of the busiest times to travel in the US. It was the first nationwide ground stop since January 2023, when the FAA dealt with a system outage. Prior to that, the last ground stop was after the September 11, 2001 terror attacks . US Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin said there was no indication the communications breakdown resulted from a cyberattack or artificial intelligence and that the ⁠public ​was ​never ​in danger. Over 4,500 flights were canceled Friday and about 700 for Saturday and over 10,000 flights within, into, or out of the United States were delayed, according to the FlightAware aviation tracker. "All departing traffic should remain groundstopped until further notice," the FAA had said earlier Friday. The agency said the ground stop was "due to extraordinary circumstances and reasons for safety." The FAA cited a temporary telecommunication outage and said, "Every flight has been accounted for and international flights will be handled on a case by case basis." The agency said flights were halted "out of abundance of caution." In a post on X, Duffy said the stop was due to a communication issue impacting all Air Route Traffic Control Centers. "FAA technicians are investigating the issue. We will provide immediate updates as we have them," he wrote. The FAA ground stop order came a day after Duffy asked Congress for $30 billion to upgrade and modernize the US Air Traffic Control System. "This investment is critical to complete the modernization of our national airspace — delivering a resilient telecommunications backbone for air traffic controllers, modern hardware and software, state-of-the-art control towers, and world-class airport infrastructure," Duffy and Office of Management and Budget Director Russell Vought wrote in a letter to lawmakers. The European Organisation for the Safety of Air Navigation, Eurocontrol, urged airlines to issue delay notices for flights that had initially been unable to take off. Eurocontrol had earlier said that all flights departing for US airports from its 42 member states were suspended following a request from the FAA. It has since removed that note from its website. Canada's air navigation service provider, NAV Canada, said it is closely monitoring the US ground stop and later said, "It was implementing traffic management measures at Toronto Pearson, Montreal-Trudeau, Calgary and Vancouver to safely manage traffic volumes." "Travelers should expect delays and check with their airline. Our systems are operating normally," NAV Canada added.
