Nvidia co-founder and now former CEO Jensen Huang has never been as prone to controversy as AI leaders like OpenAI's Sam Altman or SpaceXAI's Elon Musk. But the 63-year-old industry kingpin recently admitted that he cheated on his wife of 40 years in affairs that could have ramifications beyond Huang's personal life and U.S. national security. U.S. officials believe that one of Huang's likely romantic interests, Megaspeed executive Alice Huang, is a Chinese spy who has been feeding information back to Beijing. (Alice Huang, a Chinese citizen, is of no relation to Jensen Huang.) Megaspeed is a Singapore-based AI infrastructure company that reportedly purchased $4.8 billion worth of Nvidia chips over the last two years. The U.S. and Singapore have both previously investigated Megaspeed over suspicions that the firm was illegally sharing chips with China. The Justice Department has since taken over the federal investigation into the company, The New York Times has reported. The story took a sudden turn on Wednesday. Citing five people who worked at Nvidia, the Times reported that Huang also had an extramarital relationship with Kimberly Powell, the company's vice president of healthcare, who reports directly to him. Nvidia, Huang and Powell have not confirmed the report. Reached by a Times reporter, Huang reportedly said, "I don't think you should be talking to me directly," before hanging up. By early Thursday morning, Huang was no longer CEO of the company he co-founded 33 years ago. Then, Thursday afternoon, Reuters dropped another bombshell, publishing a report alleging that Huang had yet another extramarital affair with another unnamed Nvidia employee. The U.S. and China are embroiled in a fierce technological arms race to build the most advanced AI infrastructure, which could shape each country's economic future, military prowess, and capacity for innovation. Nvidia is valuable in this competition as one of the world's largest makers of AI chips, which are essential for accelerating AI development. But as an American company, Nvidia faces government restrictions on the sale of its most powerful chips to Chinese entities. More reports continue to roll out that illustrate the shock and severity of Huang's resignation from Nvidia. Bloomberg reported that Huang looked "broken and shattered, his legendary energy depleted" by the time he surrendered his role on Wednesday night, uttering phrases like "whatever" and "I don't care." Separately, The Wall Street Journal reported that Huang had been critical of his CFO and current interim CEO, Colette Kress. Huang is said to have described Kress as "a deer in the headlights" during a presentation this summer, and he had described Kress as someone who could not help him steer strategy or decision-making. In a scathing letter sent to Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick, Representative Richard Neal (D-MA) and Senator Ron Wyden (D-OR) said they will investigate how the Trump administration handled Nvidia's chip sales to China, especially after Trump was briefed about Huang's relationship with a purported Chinese spy. "Although [Lutnick] and President Trump were reportedly briefed on this intelligence, the Administration did not appear to acknowledge this evident national security threat. On the contrary: despite reportedly learning of Mr. Huang's compromising relationship last fall, President Trump granted Nvidia permission to sell its advanced H200 AI chips to China in December 2025 in exchange for a cut of the export sales," the letter states. Nvidia said its board had accepted Huang's resignation on Wednesday. The company's current CFO, Colette Kress , will take over as interim CEO while still fulfilling her CFO duties. Nvidia is expected to conduct a larger search to determine a permanent successor to Huang. Harvey C. Jones, a managing partner of Square Wave Ventures and former CEO of Synopsys, was appointed as the company's first-ever chair of the board of directors. Jones has been on Nvidia's board since 1993. Later in the day, Huang confirmed that he would testify in Congress at some point before Thanksgiving, which falls on November 26. "Jensen and I have been very at odds as some of you already know on export controls, but Nvidia is a very important company to the United States of America," House Foreign Affairs Committee Chairman Brian Mast said to reporters. "I don't want to see anything hurt in Nvidia, but he has some very serious questions to answer." The testimony is expected to take place behind closed doors, but Mast believes the briefing will be recorded and transcribed. After reports of a second extramarital affair, Nvidia's board reportedly plans to meet to discuss Huang's future at the company, per The Wall Street Journal. Stock fell about 8% in after-hours trading on Wednesday and is down 11% in the past five days. Huang famously delegates very little and has about 60 direct reports, he has said . The company has not had an obvious successor or a succession plan. The New York Times reported that Jensen Huang also had an affair with Nvidia vice president of healthcare Kimberly Powell, who reports directly to the CEO. According to the report, Huang and Powell were captured on film "being affectionate" at a hotel during a conference earlier this year. Huang has not responded to a request from three Republican congressmen to appear for a closed-door briefing for questioning about his affair with an alleged Chinese spy. House China Committee Chairman John Moolenaar said Wednesday on Fox Business that if Huang doesn't agree to the briefing, he'll likely be subpoenaed . "I have not spoken to him about it. I just know he's a fine person, but you never know what's going on," Trump said. When asked if Huang should remain chief of Nvidia , Trump said, "I think so. Oh yeah, sure." Jensen Huang wrote in a letter to Nvidia employees — which was also published as a press release — that he cheated on his wife. "I owe my family and all of you an apology," Huang told his company. "I was unfaithful to my wife. My actions hurt her and our children. There is no excuse for what I did. I am deeply sorry." Huang did not mention Alice Huang by name in the message, but linked his infidelity to "the national security concerns raised in news reports." "Nvidia's Board of Directors has initiated an independent investigation. I support the investigation and will cooperate fully. I love our country and our company. I am committed to protecting Nvidia and supporting America's national security. I am proud and grateful to be an American," Huang wrote. Nvidia shares slid over 5% the following day. An Nvidia spokesperson denied that this relationship was something out of the ordinary. "Jensen's interactions with Ms. Huang are not unusual or unexpected. Meetings with customers are part of a CEO's job; Jensen talks with thousands of customer executives every year," Nvidia spokesperson John Rizzo said. He added that "if the U.S. government believes that any person is a threat to American industry, it would let us know." U.S. officials circulated a secret memo among policymakers that warned that Megaspeed's Alice Huang, who had a relationship with Jensen Huang, was a spy for China's Ministry of State Security. This memo was not public knowledge until it was later reported by the New York Times. Secretary of State Marco Rubio supervised the drafting of the memo. Megaspeed, a neocloud that used Nvidia chips, had been renting computing power to Chinese internet giant Alibaba and other Chinese companies, the Times reported. A Commerce Department official who had visited Megaspeed's data center in Malaysia in 2024 had found a hoard of Nvidia equipment that was still packed in boxes and the concern was that this equipment was being directly shipped somewhere else, like China, rather than installed and sold as a cloud service. Jensen Huang had been spotted socializing with Megaspeed executive Alice Huang as early as 2024 in Taiwan, where the Nvidia CEO was born. U.S. export controls restrict the most advanced of those chips from reaching China, a country competing directly with the United States in AI development. Those rules reflect bipartisan concern that advanced AI processors could accelerate China’s military and surveillance capabilities, which is what transforms the following sequence of events from a corporate personnel matter into a national-security concern. Jensen Huang leads Nvidia; Alice Huang ran operations at a firm built on Nvidia’s technology. Jensen Huang co-founded Nvidia in 1993 and has led it since. Alice Huang , also known as Huang Le, is a Chinese citizen and former senior executive at Megaspeed, a Singapore-based data-center company that rents computing capacity built on Nvidia processors. She is not related to Jensen Huang. Media accounts placed the pair together in Taiwan multiple times before any investigation became public. Those encounters later became relevant to intelligence reporting about the alleged operation, according to the cited reporting. No public statement about the relationship was identified in that reporting from either Nvidia or U.S. officials at the time. U.S. and Singapore authorities opened parallel inquiries into whether Nvidia chips reached China through a third-party operator. In October 2025 , U.S. and Singapore authorities reportedly examined whether Megaspeed had helped Chinese firms, including Alibaba, obtain Nvidia processors in potential violation of U.S. export restrictions. Export controls are rules that restrict the sale of certain advanced technology to designated countries, entities, or uses, sometimes requiring government licensing. Officials also questioned the disposition of Nvidia equipment observed at a Malaysian facility, according to the supplied reporting, as AI is making enforcement of such controls increasingly complex. The president learned of the intelligence months before it became public. Nvidia co-founder and now former CEO Jensen Huang has never been as prone to controversy as AI leaders like OpenAI's Sam Altman or SpaceXAI's Elon Musk. But the 63-year-old industry kingpin recently admitted that he cheated on his wife of 40 years in affairs that could have ramifications beyond Huang's personal life and U.S. national security. U.S. officials believe that one of Huang's likely romantic interests, Megaspeed executive Alice Huang, is a Chinese spy who has been feeding information back to Beijing. (Alice Huang, a Chinese citizen, is of no relation to Jensen Huang.) Megaspeed is a Singapore-based AI infrastructure company that reportedly purchased $4.8 billion worth of Nvidia chips over the last two years. The U.S. and Singapore have both previously investigated Megaspeed over suspicions that the firm was illegally sharing chips with China. The Justice Department has since taken over the federal investigation into the company, The New York Times has reported. The story took a sudden turn on Wednesday. Citing five people who worked at Nvidia, the Times reported that Huang also had an extramarital relationship with Kimberly Powell, the company's vice president of healthcare, who reports directly to him. Nvidia, Huang and Powell have not confirmed the report. Reached by a Times reporter, Huang reportedly said, "I don't think you should be talking to me directly," before hanging up. By early Thursday morning, Huang was no longer CEO of the company he co-founded 33 years ago. Then, Thursday afternoon, Reuters dropped another bombshell, publishing a report alleging that Huang had yet another extramarital affair with another unnamed Nvidia employee. The U.S. and China are embroiled in a fierce technological arms race to build the most advanced AI infrastructure, which could shape each country's economic future, military prowess, and capacity for innovation. Nvidia is valuable in this competition as one of the world's largest makers of AI chips, which are essential for accelerating AI development. But as an American company, Nvidia faces government restrictions on the sale of its most powerful chips to Chinese entities. More reports continue to roll out that illustrate the shock and severity of Huang's resignation from Nvidia. Bloomberg reported that Huang looked "broken and shattered, his legendary energy depleted" by the time he surrendered his role on Wednesday night, uttering phrases like "whatever" and "I don't care." Separately, The Wall Street Journal reported that Huang had been critical of his CFO and current interim CEO, Colette Kress. Huang is said to have described Kress as "a deer in the headlights" during a presentation this summer, and he had described Kress as someone who could not help him steer strategy or decision-making. In a scathing letter sent to Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick, Representative Richard Neal (D-MA) and Senator Ron Wyden (D-OR) said they will investigate how the Trump administration handled Nvidia's chip sales to China, especially after Trump was briefed about Huang's relationship with a purported Chinese spy. "Although [Lutnick] and President Trump were reportedly briefed on this intelligence, the Administration did not appear to acknowledge this evident national security threat. On the contrary: despite reportedly learning of Mr. Huang's compromising relationship last fall, President Trump granted Nvidia permission to sell its advanced H200 AI chips to China in December 2025 in exchange for a cut of the export sales," the letter states. Nvidia said its board had accepted Huang's resignation on Wednesday. The company's current CFO, Colette Kress , will take over as interim CEO while still fulfilling her CFO duties. Nvidia is expected to conduct a larger search to determine a permanent successor to Huang. Harvey C. Jones, a managing partner of Square Wave Ventures and former CEO of Synopsys, was appointed as the company's first-ever chair of the board of directors. Jones has been on Nvidia's board since 1993. Later in the day, Huang confirmed that he would testify in Congress at some point before Thanksgiving, which falls on November 26. "Jensen and I have been very at odds as some of you already know on export controls, but Nvidia is a very important company to the United States of America," House Foreign Affairs Committee Chairman Brian Mast said to reporters. "I don't want to see anything hurt in Nvidia, but he has some very serious questions to answer." The testimony is expected to take place behind closed doors, but Mast believes the briefing will be recorded and transcribed. After reports of a second extramarital affair, Nvidia's board reportedly plans to meet to discuss Huang's future at the company, per The Wall Street Journal. Stock fell about 8% in after-hours trading on Wednesday and is down 11% in the past five days. Huang famously delegates very little and has about 60 direct reports, he has said . The company has not had an obvious successor or a succession plan. The New York Times reported that Jensen Huang also had an affair with Nvidia vice president of healthcare Kimberly Powell, who reports directly to the CEO. According to the report, Huang and Powell were captured on film "being affectionate" at a hotel during a conference earlier this year. Huang has not responded to a request from three Republican congressmen to appear for a closed-door briefing for questioning about his affair with an alleged Chinese spy. House China Committee Chairman John Moolenaar said Wednesday on Fox Business that if Huang doesn't agree to the briefing, he'll likely be subpoenaed . "I have not spoken to him about it. I just know he's a fine person, but you never know what's going on," Trump said. When asked if Huang should remain chief of Nvidia , Trump said, "I think so. Oh yeah, sure." Jensen Huang wrote in a letter to Nvidia employees — which was also published as a press release — that he cheated on his wife. "I owe my family and all of you an apology," Huang told his company. "I was unfaithful to my wife. My actions hurt her and our children. There is no excuse for what I did. I am deeply sorry." Huang did not mention Alice Huang by name in the message, but linked his infidelity to "the national security concerns raised in news reports." "Nvidia's Board of Directors has initiated an independent investigation. I support the investigation and will cooperate fully. I love our country and our company. I am committed to protecting Nvidia and supporting America's national security. I am proud and grateful to be an American," Huang wrote. Nvidia shares slid over 5% the following day. An Nvidia spokesperson denied that this relationship was something out of the ordinary. "Jensen's interactions with Ms. Huang are not unusual or unexpected. Meetings with customers are part of a CEO's job; Jensen talks with thousands of customer executives every year," Nvidia spokesperson John Rizzo said. He added that "if the U.S. government believes that any person is a threat to American industry, it would let us know." U.S. officials circulated a secret memo among policymakers that warned that Megaspeed's Alice Huang, who had a relationship with Jensen Huang, was a spy for China's Ministry of State Security. This memo was not public knowledge until it was later reported by the New York Times. Secretary of State Marco Rubio supervised the drafting of the memo. Megaspeed, a neocloud that used Nvidia chips, had been renting computing power to Chinese internet giant Alibaba and other Chinese companies, the Times reported. A Commerce Department official who had visited Megaspeed's data center in Malaysia in 2024 had found a hoard of Nvidia equipment that was still packed in boxes and the concern was that this equipment was being directly shipped somewhere else, like China, rather than installed and sold as a cloud service. But the 63-year-old industry kingpin recently admitted that he cheated on his wife of 40 years in affairs that could have ramifications beyond Huang’s personal life and U.S. national security. U.S. officials believe that one of Huang’s likely romantic interests, Megaspeed executive Alice Huang, is a Chinese spy who has been feeding information back to Beijing. (Alice Huang, a Chinese citizen, is of no relation to Jensen Huang.) Megaspeed is a Singapore-based AI infrastructure company that reportedly purchased $4.8 billion worth of Nvidia chips over the last two years. The U.S. and Singapore have both previously investigated Megaspeed over suspicions that the firm was illegally sharing chips with China. The Justice Department has since taken over the federal investigation into the company, The New York Times has reported. The story took a sudden turn on Wednesday. Citing five people who worked at Nvidia, the Times reported that Huang also had an extramarital relationship with Kimberly Powell, the company’s vice president of healthcare, who reports directly to him. Nvidia, Huang and Powell have not confirmed the report. Reached by a Times reporter, Huang reportedly said, “I don’t think you should be talking to me directly,” before hanging up. By early Thursday morning, Huang was no longer CEO of the company he co-founded 33 years ago. Then, Thursday afternoon, Reuters dropped another bombshell, publishing a report alleging that Huang had yet another extramarital affair with another unnamed Nvidia employee. The U.S. and China are embroiled in a fierce technological arms race to build the most advanced AI infrastructure, which could shape each country’s economic future, military prowess, and capacity for innovation. Nvidia is valuable in this competition as one of the world’s largest makers of AI chips, which are essential for accelerating AI development. But as an American company, Nvidia faces government restrictions on the sale of its most powerful chips to Chinese entities. More reports continue to roll out that illustrate the shock and severity of Huang’s resignation from Nvidia. Bloomberg reported that Huang looked “broken and shattered, his legendary energy depleted” by the time he surrendered his role on Wednesday night, uttering phrases like “whatever” and “I don’t care.” Separately, The Wall Street Journal reported that Huang had been critical of his CFO and current interim CEO, Colette Kress. Huang is said to have described Kress as “a deer in the headlights” during a presentation this summer, and he had described Kress as someone who could not help him steer strategy or decision-making. In a scathing letter sent to Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick, Representative Richard Neal (D-MA) and Senator Ron Wyden (D-OR) said they will investigate how the Trump administration handled Nvidia’s chip sales to China, especially after Trump was briefed about Huang’s relationship with a purported Chinese spy. “Although [Lutnick] and President Trump were reportedly briefed on this intelligence, the Administration did not appear to acknowledge this evident national security threat. On the contrary: despite reportedly learning of Mr. Huang’s compromising relationship last fall, President Trump granted Nvidia permission to sell its advanced H200 AI chips to China in December 2025 in exchange for a cut of the export sales,” the letter states. Nvidia said its board had accepted Huang’s resignation on Wednesday. The company’s current CFO, Colette Kress , will take over as interim CEO while still fulfilling her CFO duties. Nvidia is expected to conduct a larger search to determine a permanent successor to Huang. Harvey C. Jones, a managing partner of Square Wave Ventures and former CEO of Synopsys, was appointed as the company’s first-ever chair of the board of directors. Jones has been on Nvidia’s board since 1993. After reports of a second extramarital affair, Nvidia’s board reportedly plans to meet to discuss Huang’s future at the company, per The Wall Street Journal. Stock fell about 8% in after-hours trading on Wednesday and is down 11% in the past five days. Huang famously delegates very little and has about 60 direct reports, he has said . The company has not had an obvious successor or a succession plan. The New York Times reported that Jensen Huang also had an affair with Nvidia vice president of healthcare Kimberly Powell, who reports directly to the CEO. According to the report, Huang and Powell were captured on film “being affectionate” at a hotel during a conference earlier this year. Huang has not responded to a request from three Republican congressmen to appear for a closed-door briefing for questioning about his affair with an alleged Chinese spy. House China Committee Chairman John Moolenaar said Wednesday on Fox Business that if Huang doesn’t agree to the briefing, he’ll likely be subpoenaed . The Nvidia CEO pulled out of upcoming speaking engagements at the ElevenLabs Summit and Anthropic CEO Forum. Alice Huang and her family reportedly built a network of companies in China and Singapore to acquire Nvidia chips, including founding a Chinese company called Shanghai Century Litong. Founded in 2023, it became an Nvidia-preferred cloud partner, giving it priority access to chips, The Information reported . The Information also reported that Shanghai Century Litong facilitated buying $7.5 billion worth of Nvidia’s chips, including banned chips. Nvidia’s head lawyer, Tim Teter, intervened in a 2025 U.S. government probe surrounding the suspected smuggling of AI chips by Megaspeed International, Bloomberg reported . Teter contacted Commerce Under Secretary Jeffrey Kessler asking questions about whether the Trump administration played a role in detaining Alice Huang. An Nvidia spokesperson denied that this relationship was something out of the ordinary. “Jensen’s interactions with Ms. Huang are not unusual or unexpected. Meetings with customers are part of a CEO’s job; Jensen talks with thousands of customer executives every year,” Nvidia spokesperson John Rizzo said. He added that “if the U.S. government believes that any person is a threat to American industry, it would let us know.” U.S. officials circulated a secret memo among policymakers that warned that Megaspeed’s Alice Huang, who had a relationship with Jensen Huang, was a spy for China’s Ministry of State Security. This memo was not public knowledge until it was later reported by the New York Times. Secretary of State Marco Rubio supervised the drafting of the memo. Megaspeed, a neocloud that used Nvidia chips, had been renting computing power to Chinese internet giant Alibaba and other Chinese companies, the Times reported. sources.title: OpenAI launches ChatGPT Wallet, allowing its 'dots' AI agents to make purchases for users - CNBC
passages: OpenAI on Friday announced ChatGPT Wallet, a new payment feature that enables its "dots" artificial intelligence agents to make purchases on behalf of users.
OpenAI introduced the dots agents during its annual developer conference in late September, shortly after Meta's Muse offering topped the App Store charts .
OpenAI's ChatGPT chatbot supports more than 1.2 billion weekly active users and nearly 100 million paying users as of the end of the third quarter.
With such a broad user base, Gebb said OpenAI can decide to "turn up the volume" on ChatGPT Wallet when it wants to.

With the initial launch, OpenAI is working to build relationships with merchants and position itself as a serious platform for shoppers, especially as vendors are beginning to experiment with personal agents.
ChatGPT Wallet is initially available to OpenAI's Pro subscribers in the U.S. who are over 18 years old.
The limited rollout is intentional, and the "right approach to make sure things are working," said Luke Gebb , executive vice president and global head of innovation at Amex.

OpenAI said Friday that agentic commerce is still in its "early days," and it published tools and guidance alongside its ChatGPT Wallet announcement to help businesses start to navigate the transition.
The company explained how merchants can make sure their websites aren't inadvertently blocking OpenAI's agents, for instance.
Eligible users enter their card information once, prompt their dot to find items to buy and approve each purchase with a security check.
OpenAI said its dots agents will never actually access a user's card details.
Instead, their payment networks will provide the dot with a "payment token," which contains a scoped card number, security code and expiration date that is specific to a given transaction.
OpenAI has pushed deeper into AI-enabled commerce over the last year, but some of its early attempts failed to take off.
The company introduced an " Instant Checkout " feature last fall, which it quickly pivoted away from.
By March, it had rolled out a revamped shopping experience that aimed to make it easier for users to find and compare products.

"Our goal here is to really focus on merchants and our network partners and start building out a really great foundation that's safe and easy to use," Chaya Nayak, who leads product for monetization and payments at OpenAI, told CNBC in an interview.

passages: OpenAI has launched ChatGPT Wallet, a payment feature that allows its artificial intelligence agents, called dots, to make purchases on behalf of users, CNBC reported on Friday.

The feature works only in conversations with dots and is not available in regular ChatGPT chats, Work or standalone Codex threads.
OpenAI said the agents do not receive access to users' actual card details.

CNBC reported that OpenAI is not taking a cut of transactions at launch, as it focuses on building relationships with merchants and payment partners.
The feature builds on the company's broader push into AI-enabled shopping and personal agents.

coreStoryFacts.text: OpenAI on Friday announced ChatGPT Wallet, a new payment feature that enables its "dots" artificial intelligence agents to make purchases on behalf of users.
OpenAI introduced the dots agents during its annual developer conference in late September, shortly after Meta's Muse offering topped the App Store charts .
OpenAI's ChatGPT chatbot supports more than 1.2 billion weekly active users and nearly 100 million paying users as of the end of the third quarter.
With such a broad user base, Gebb said OpenAI can decide to "turn up the volume" on ChatGPT Wallet when it wants to.

With the initial launch, OpenAI is working to build relationships with merchants and position itself as a serious platform for shoppers, especially as vendors are beginning to experiment with personal agents.
ChatGPT Wallet is initially available to OpenAI's Pro subscribers in the U.S. who are over 18 years old.
The limited rollout is intentional, and the "right approach to make sure things are working," said Luke Gebb , executive vice president and global head of innovation at Amex.

OpenAI said Friday that agentic commerce is still in its "early days," and it published tools and guidance alongside its ChatGPT Wallet announcement to help businesses start to navigate the transition.
The company explained how merchants can make sure their websites aren't inadvertently blocking OpenAI's agents, for instance.
Eligible users enter their card information once, prompt their dot to find items to buy and approve each purchase with a security check.
OpenAI said its dots agents will never actually access a user's card details.
Instead, their payment networks will provide the dot with a "payment token," which contains a scoped card number, security code and expiration date that is specific to a given transaction.
OpenAI has pushed deeper into AI-enabled commerce over the last year, but some of its early attempts failed to take off.
The company introduced an " Instant Checkout " feature last fall, which it quickly pivoted away from.
By March, it had rolled out a revamped shopping experience that aimed to make it easier for users to find and compare products.

"Our goal here is to really focus on merchants and our network partners and start building out a really great foundation that's safe and easy to use," Chaya Nayak, who leads product for monetization and payments at OpenAI, told CNBC in an interview.

There was also pressure on the Commerce Department to add it to the list, but separate reporting in the Financial Times said the department was delaying efforts to have the cloud computing firm included. extraction.body: Washington — Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick has agreed to testify before the Senate Banking Committee on Dec. 10, according to a U.S. official, amid intensifying scrutiny of the Commerce Department's oversight of the export of powerful AI chips following the resignation of Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang.A growing number of Republicans are calling on Lutnick to answer questions about the Commerce Department's apparent delay in adding Singapore-based company Megaspeed International to the U.S. government's Entity List, which would have restricted the company's ability to get access to advanced AI chips.Megaspeed was previously led by Alice Huang, the suspected Chinese spy who had an affair with Jensen Huang. The U.S. government suspects Megaspeed of directing advanced Nvidia chips to China, circumventing a U.S. export ban.GOP Sen. Jim Banks of Indiana, a member of the Senate Banking Committee, told Fox News on Thursday that "we know that the Department of Commerce, Secretary Lutnick, it appears, used loopholes to allow some of these chip sales to occur even though President Trump has directed his administration and the Department of Commerce not to allow that to happen."On Friday, Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent repeatedly emphasized that the Treasury Department and other parts of the executive branch had pushed for restrictions on Megaspeed, laying the blame for the delay at the feet of the Commerce Department."Treasury, War, [the U.S. Trade Representative] and State, they were in favor of putting Megaspeed on the Entity List for months, but Commerce has the pen," Bessent told CNBC. "And you will have to ask them about their internal processes."Bessent declined to comment on reported tensions between himself and Lutnick. The Commerce Department did not immediately respond to CBS News' request for comment.

extraction.body: US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent has blamed Howard Lutnick's Commerce Department for failing to properly oversee the export of high-spec AI chips, as the fallout from the Nvidia scandal widens to President Donald Trump's cabinet. Pressure is building on Lutnick from across the political spectrum to explain his department's actions. Jensen Huang was ousted as Nvidia CEO after revelations he had an affair with a businesswoman who was also allegedly a Chinese spy. Megaspeed, the firm she worked for, had been probed by US government agencies over suspicions it was smuggling Nvidia chips into China, reports said, but it is not on a list of firms US companies are prevented from working with. Bessent told CNBC several agencies "were in favour of putting Megaspeed on the entity list for months". "But Commerce has the pen... and you will have to ask them about their internal process," he added. Bessent's comments come after Lutnick was called to testify before the Senate Banking Committee next month over the Commerce Department's role in allowing Nvidia to export its advanced chips. Other congressional committees have asked both Lutnick and his department to retain all records relating to Nvidia and Huang. Bessent said he was "frustrated" by delays in putting the company on the export control list and reports of leakage of AI chips into China. "President Trump made it very clear that China should not receive any Nvidia chips above H100s, so any leakage is very frustrating because it hurts our great companies in the AI race, because it gives the Chinese an advantage," he said. Last year, the Commerce Department had been investigating Megaspeed over suspicions it had been smuggling some of Nvidia's advanced AI chips into China, according to the New York Times. Megaspeed has been contacted for comment. There was also pressure on the Commerce Department to add it to the list, but separate reporting in the Financial Times said the department was delaying efforts to have the cloud computing firm included. However, Bessent also pointed the finger at Nvidia. "The story has been thus far of Jensen Huang's personal foibles," he told CNBC's Squawk Box programme . "The real story here should be: Did Nvidia know their client, and was there a robust effort at Nvidia to make sure that there was no leakage and that they were selling to what were obviously pass-through shell companies? "It's important that anyone at the company there be held accountable for that." Bessent's pointed comments are a rare instance of internal debate within the Trump administration spilling out into the public view, although tensions have reportedly simmered between Bessent and Lutnick in the past. In 2024, the two reportedly jostled for the role of treasury secretary ahead of Trump's return to the White House, and last year the pair butted heads over the administration's tariff policy, accoprding to US media. Huang has been summoned to testify before the Senate Banking Committee about his alleged affair with the former Megaspeed executive, who is suspected of being a Chinese spy. The commerce secretary has also been summoned to appear before the committee in December. "Recent reports raise serious concerns about our national security and the protection of sensitive US technology," committee chairman, Republican Senator Tim Scott posted on X. Democrats on key congressional committees have asked the Commerce Department and Lutnick to keep all records relating to decisions to allow Nvidia to sell its advanced AI chips to Chinese companies, including all their communications with or about Nvidia and Jensen Huang. Ways and Means Committee Ranking Member Richard E Neal and Senate Finance Committee Ranking Member Ron Wyden are starting investigations into the way Nvidia was allowed to sell these chips. According to Neal and Wyden, Nvidia's advanced H200 chips could be sold to Chinese firms if they were first imported from their manufacturing facility in Taiwan into America for inspection. A 25% tariff - a levy that is paid to the federal government - was imposed on those chips, under a section of the Trade Act that Neal and Wyden say is meant to allow the US president to take action against imports that risk national security. "Trump's use of the statute appears to have done the opposite, undermining US national security and putting Americans at risk," they said. The scandal has cast a spotlight on Singapore's success as a chip hub - and a location for alleged illicit trade.

WASHINGTON (AP) — Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent said Friday he was frustrated with the Commerce Department’s delay in placing restrictions on Nvidia chip exports to a company led by an alleged Chinese spy. Bessent said on CNBC that his department, along with the departments of State and Defense and the U.S. Trade Representative, were in favor of adding Singapore-based Megaspeed International to an export control list for months but that the Commerce Department was in charge of the matter. “Commerce has the pen, and you will have to ask them about their internal processes,” Bessent said. “My deputy has been pushing this for months.” Bessent’s comments were an unusually public rebuke of a fellow Cabinet member, in this case Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick. Commerce oversees U.S. government controls over exports of sensitive, high-tech goods. The comments come as Nvidia’s ties to Megaspeed are prominent in the resignation of Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang . Huang allegedly had an affair with the CEO of Megaspeed, Alice Huang, who U.S. intelligence suspects is a Chinese spy, The New York Times has reported. China has denied allegations of spying. Lutnick has come under increasing scrutiny because of his reportedly close relationship with Huang. The ex-Nvidia CEO is also close to President Donald Trump and recently visited the White House Sept. 29 to discuss AI safety. The Times reported Thursday that Lutnick resisted placing greater limits on the sale of Nvidia’s more advanced chips to China. Chinese firms have accessed Nvidia’s chips through companies like Megaspeed, which has reportedly purchased more than $4 billion worth of Nvidia’s advanced semiconductors. The split in Trump’s Cabinet reflects the widespread fallout from the scandal that has engulfed Nvidia , one of the most valuable publicly-traded companies in the world. Nvidia’s computer chips play a central role in the buildout of artificial intelligence, powering AI models such as those developed by OpenAI and Anthropic. Just last month, Trump awarded the then-Nvidia CEO a National Medal of Science. Earlier this week, Trump defended Huang, noting that “he said he had absolutely no idea that the person in question was a spy.” The U.S. government has, since the Biden administration, sought to restrict the sale of the most advanced AI computer chips to China in an effort to protect U.S. technology companies’ lead. Yet China has at times retaliated, creating controversy over how far the U.S. should push its restrictions. The Commerce Department did not immediately respond to messages seeking comment. Bessent declined to comment Friday on the Times report that he confronted Lutnick last week in the White House’s situation room about Megaspeed. Separately, Axios reported this week that Lutnick received a classified memo this spring warning about Jensen Huang’s relationship with a suspected spy. Last year, Megaspeed was accused of illicitly shipping advanced Nvidia computer chips into China, but in December the company said there was “no evidence” of such exports. The Commerce Department’s Bureau of Industry and Security began investigating Megaspeed International in 2024. The bureau later handed off the investigation to the Justice Department. A person familiar with the bureau’s investigation denied any intervention from Nvidia. The person wasn’t authorized to discuss the matter publicly and spoke on condition of anonymity. Richard Neal, both Democrats, wrote Lutnick a letter demanding that he preserve all records related to decisions about Nvidia chip exports, pending an investigation. Wyden and Neal are the top Democrats on the Senate Finance and House Ways and Means committees, respectively. Trump’s approval of advanced Nvidia chip exports to China “raises critical questions about whether and to what extent political considerations are improperly influencing policy decisions made by the Administration,” Wyden and Neal wrote . And the chair of the House Foreign Affairs Committee wants Nvidia’s general counsel, Tim Teter, and a senior Commerce Department official to appear before Congress. Rep. Brian Mast, a Republican from Florida and the panel chair, sent a letter this week to Jeff Kessler, undersecretary of commerce for industry and security, seeking a Dec. 2 hearing on computer chip smuggling and “reported interference by private companies into export control policies and enforcement investigations.” Republican Sen. WASHINGTON (AP) — Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent said Friday he was frustrated with the Commerce Department’s delay in placing restrictions on Nvidia chip exports to a company led by an alleged Chinese spy.

Bessent said on CNBC that his department, along with the departments of State and Defense and the U.S. Trade Representative, were in favor of adding Singapore-based Megaspeed International to an export control list for months but that the Commerce Department was in charge of the matter.
“Commerce has the pen, and you will have to ask them about their internal processes,” Bessent said. “My deputy has been pushing this for months.”

Bessent’s comments were an unusually public rebuke of a fellow Cabinet member, in this case Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick. Commerce oversees U.S. government controls over exports of sensitive, high-tech goods. The comments come as Nvidia’s ties to Megaspeed are prominent in the resignation of Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang . Huang allegedly had an affair with the CEO of Megaspeed, Alice Huang, who U.S. intelligence suspects is a Chinese spy, The New York Times has reported. China has denied allegations of spying.

Lutnick has come under increasing scrutiny because of his reportedly close relationship with Huang. The ex-Nvidia CEO is also close to President Donald Trump and recently visited the White House Sept. 29 to discuss AI safety. The Times reported Thursday that Lutnick resisted placing greater limits on the sale of Nvidia’s more advanced chips to China. Chinese firms have accessed Nvidia’s chips through companies like Megaspeed, which has reportedly purchased more than $4 billion worth of Nvidia’s advanced semiconductors.

The split in Trump’s Cabinet reflects the widespread fallout from the scandal that has engulfed Nvidia , one of the most valuable publicly-traded companies in the world. Nvidia’s computer chips play a central role in the buildout of artificial intelligence, powering AI models such as those developed by OpenAI and Anthropic.

Just last month, Trump awarded the then-Nvidia CEO a National Medal of Science. Earlier this week, Trump defended Huang, noting that “he said he had absolutely no idea that the person in question was a spy.”

The U.S. government has, since the Biden administration, sought to restrict the sale of the most advanced AI computer chips to China in an effort to protect U.S. technology companies’ lead. Yet China has at times retaliated, creating controversy over how far the U.S. should push its restrictions.
The Commerce Department did not immediately respond to messages seeking comment.
Bessent declined to comment Friday on the Times report that he confronted Lutnick last week in the White House’s situation room about Megaspeed.
Separately, Axios reported this week that Lutnick received a classified memo this spring warning about Jensen Huang’s relationship with a suspected spy.
Last year, Megaspeed was accused of illicitly shipping advanced Nvidia computer chips into China, but in December the company said there was “no evidence” of such exports.
The Commerce Department’s Bureau of Industry and Security began investigating Megaspeed International in 2024. The bureau later handed off the investigation to the Justice Department.
A person familiar with the bureau’s investigation denied any intervention from Nvidia. The person wasn’t authorized to discuss the matter publicly and spoke on condition of anonymity.

The Justice Department’s national security division is investigating whether Megaspeed violated export control laws in an inquiry that will also include scrutiny of Alice Huang, according to a person familiar with the matter, The Associated Press reported Wednesday .

On Thursday, Megaspeed maintained it takes its obligation to comply with American export control laws “extremely seriously” — and that it was committed to working “constructively and transparently” with the U.S. government.
Numerous members of Congress have said they will investigate Lutnick’s actions and called for him to testify on Capitol Hill.

On Thursday, Oregon Sen. Ron Wyden and Massachusetts Rep. Richard Neal, both Democrats, wrote Lutnick a letter demanding that he preserve all records related to decisions about Nvidia chip exports, pending an investigation. Wyden and Neal are the top Democrats on the Senate Finance and House Ways and Means committees, respectively.

Trump’s approval of advanced Nvidia chip exports to China “raises critical questions about whether and to what extent political considerations are improperly influencing policy decisions made by the Administration,” Wyden and Neal wrote .
And the chair of the House Foreign Affairs Committee wants Nvidia’s general counsel, Tim Teter, and a senior Commerce Department official to appear before Congress.

Rep. Brian Mast, a Republican from Florida and the panel chair, sent a letter this week to Jeff Kessler, undersecretary of commerce for industry and security, seeking a Dec. 2 hearing on computer chip smuggling and “reported interference by private companies into export control policies and enforcement investigations.”
Republican Sen. John Kennedy of Louisiana, a member of the Senate Banking Committee, urged Lutnick to hold a press conference to explain what he knew.

“The Commerce Department greenlit $4 billion of sales of advanced chips to the company of the spy that Mr. Huang was having an affair with and I want to know why,” Kennedy said. “I want to know why the Commerce Department did it in light of the export controls, and everything I read indicates that this was a decision by the secretary himself.”
Kennedy added that Lutnick should testify before the Senate and should be subpoenaed if necessary.

Lutnick has come under increasing scrutiny because of his reportedly close relationship with Huang. The ex-Nvidia CEO is also close to President Donald Trump and recently visited the White House Sept. 29 to discuss AI safety. The Times reported Thursday that Lutnick resisted placing greater limits on the sale of Nvidia’s more advanced chips to China. Chinese firms have accessed Nvidia’s chips through companies like Megaspeed, which has reportedly purchased more than $4 billion worth of Nvidia’s advanced semiconductors. The split in Trump’s Cabinet reflects the widespread fallout from the scandal that has engulfed Nvidia , one of the most valuable publicly-traded companies in the world. Nvidia’s computer chips play a central role in the buildout of artificial intelligence, powering AI models such as those developed by OpenAI and Anthropic. Just last month, Trump awarded the then-Nvidia CEO a National Medal of Science. Earlier this week, Trump defended Huang, noting that “he said he had absolutely no idea that the person in question was a spy.”

The U.S. government has, since the Biden administration, sought to restrict the sale of the most advanced AI computer chips to China in an effort to protect U.S. technology companies’ lead. Yet China has at times retaliated, creating controversy over how far the U.S. should push its restrictions.

Last year, Megaspeed was accused of illicitly shipping advanced Nvidia computer chips into China, but in December the company said there was “no evidence” of such exports.
The Commerce Department’s Bureau of Industry and Security began investigating Megaspeed International in 2024. The bureau later handed off the investigation to the Justice Department.

Richard Neal, both Democrats, wrote Lutnick a letter demanding that he preserve all records related to decisions about Nvidia chip exports, pending an investigation. Bessent's comments come after Lutnick was called to testify before the Senate Banking Committee next month over the Commerce Department's role in allowing Nvidia to export its advanced chips.
Other congressional committees have asked both Lutnick and his department to retain all records relating to Nvidia and Huang.

Megaspeed, the firm she worked for, had been probed by US government agencies over suspicions it was smuggling Nvidia chips into China, reports said, but it is not on a list of firms US companies are prevented from working with.
Bessent told CNBC several agencies "were in favour of putting Megaspeed on the entity list for months".
However, Bessent also pointed the finger at Nvidia.

Bessent's pointed comments are a rare instance of internal debate within the Trump administration spilling out into the public view, although tensions have reportedly simmered between Bessent and Lutnick in the past.
Pressure is building on Lutnick from across the political spectrum to explain his department's actions.

"President Trump made it very clear that China should not receive any Nvidia chips above H100s, so any leakage is very frustrating because it hurts our great companies in the AI race, because it gives the Chinese an advantage," he said.

extraction.body: US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent has blamed Howard Lutnick's Commerce Department for failing to properly oversee the export of high-spec AI chips, as the fallout from the Nvidia scandal widens to President Donald Trump's cabinet. Pressure is building on Lutnick from across the political spectrum to explain his department's actions. Jensen Huang was ousted as Nvidia CEO after revelations he had an affair with a businesswoman who was also allegedly a Chinese spy. Megaspeed, the firm she worked for, had been probed by US government agencies over suspicions it was smuggling Nvidia chips into China, reports said, but it is not on a list of firms US companies are prevented from working with. Bessent told CNBC several agencies "were in favour of putting Megaspeed on the entity list for months". "But Commerce has the pen... and you will have to ask them about their internal process," he added. Bessent's comments come after Lutnick was called to testify before the Senate Banking Committee next month over the Commerce Department's role in allowing Nvidia to export its advanced chips. Other congressional committees have asked both Lutnick and his department to retain all records relating to Nvidia and Huang. Bessent said he was "frustrated" by delays in putting the company on the export control list and reports of leakage of AI chips into China. "President Trump made it very clear that China should not receive any Nvidia chips above H100s, so any leakage is very frustrating because it hurts our great companies in the AI race, because it gives the Chinese an advantage," he said. Last year, the Commerce Department had been investigating Megaspeed over suspicions it had been smuggling some of Nvidia's advanced AI chips into China, according to the New York Times. Megaspeed has been contacted for comment. There was also pressure on the Commerce Department to add it to the list, but separate reporting in the Financial Times said the department was delaying efforts to have the cloud computing firm included. However, Bessent also pointed the finger at Nvidia. "The story has been thus far of Jensen Huang's personal foibles," he told CNBC's Squawk Box programme . "The real story here should be: Did Nvidia know their client, and was there a robust effort at Nvidia to make sure that there was no leakage and that they were selling to what were obviously pass-through shell companies? "It's important that anyone at the company there be held accountable for that." Bessent's pointed comments are a rare instance of internal debate within the Trump administration spilling out into the public view, although tensions have reportedly simmered between Bessent and Lutnick in the past. In 2024, the two reportedly jostled for the role of treasury secretary ahead of Trump's return to the White House, and last year the pair butted heads over the administration's tariff policy, accoprding to US media. Huang has been summoned to testify before the Senate Banking Committee about his alleged affair with the former Megaspeed executive, who is suspected of being a Chinese spy. The commerce secretary has also been summoned to appear before the committee in December. "Recent reports raise serious concerns about our national security and the protection of sensitive US technology," committee chairman, Republican Senator Tim Scott posted on X. Democrats on key congressional committees have asked the Commerce Department and Lutnick to keep all records relating to decisions to allow Nvidia to sell its advanced AI chips to Chinese companies, including all their communications with or about Nvidia and Jensen Huang. Ways and Means Committee Ranking Member Richard E Neal and Senate Finance Committee Ranking Member Ron Wyden are starting investigations into the way Nvidia was allowed to sell these chips. According to Neal and Wyden, Nvidia's advanced H200 chips could be sold to Chinese firms if they were first imported from their manufacturing facility in Taiwan into America for inspection. A 25% tariff - a levy that is paid to the federal government - was imposed on those chips, under a section of the Trade Act that Neal and Wyden say is meant to allow the US president to take action against imports that risk national security. "Trump's use of the statute appears to have done the opposite, undermining US national security and putting Americans at risk," they said. The scandal has cast a spotlight on Singapore's success as a chip hub - and a location for alleged illicit trade.

Department of Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin said there was no indication the nationwide FAA disruption was a “nefarious attack,” saying a telecommunications outage prompted the rare move to issue ground stops at airports across the country. Stream NBC 5 for free, 24/7, wherever you are. The FAA issued a nationwide ground stop Friday afternoon, saying in an initial statement that the move was “due to extraordinary circumstances and for reasons of safety.” In an update, the agency said the alert followed “communication issues impacting multiple Air Route Traffic Control Centers.” The agency later said the issue stemmed from “a temporary telecommunications outage.” Speaking to reporters outside the White House, Mullin repeatedly emphasized that passengers and the public were safe, pushing back on comparisons to the Sept. 11 terrorist attacks. “As I want to make sure we say this again, there's no reason for the public to be afraid or scared for your loved ones,” he said. “This isn't another 9/11. I just can't repeat that enough...This is a telecommunication outage. This is much different.” Officials had not ruled out a cyberattack, but Mullin stressed that they did not yet know the cause and did not want to get ahead of the investigation. “Everybody's safe,” Mullin said. “There is no reason to be concerned about your loved ones if they're flying or anything like that. I just want to make sure everybody's at ease about that. As we investigate what caused this, you always got to assume that as many cyberattacks that take place, that you make that assumption. So, but as of right now, that's not known.” Moments before the nationwide ground stop, both major airports in Chicago were under ground stops due to an “equipment outage.” There was no timeline for restoring normal operations, with Mullin explaining that the outage would “take some time” to resolve. “...So this isn't going to just be resolved and, and turned around within the hour," he said. "This is, this is going to take, take some time. But once again, everybody is safe. The flights are accounted for, and there's no, there should be no fear to the public at all in this.” Only departing flights were affected, while arriving flights were expected to continue to their scheduled airports. One traveler at O’Hare Airport told NBC Chicago that airline employees said their flight was on hold “until further notice,” with no timeline provided for when it might depart. More than 250 flights were delayed between Chicago's O'Hare and Midway airports. “Every flight has been accounted for, and international flights will be handled on a case-by-case basis,” the FAA said. Further details about what caused the nationwide disruption were not immediately clear.

extraction.body: ‘FaceStealer’ scam tied to $400M+ theft, 900+ webcam recordings The US government on Thursday said it had obtained court authorization to seize or restrain use of over $1.2 billion stolen during last month's $6.3 billion Binance heist, as part of a larger effort to disrupt North Korea's ongoing cryptocurrency theft. The court also allowed the takedown of cloud-based infrastructure used in a Democratic People’s Republic of Korea (DPRK) social engineering scheme called “FaceStealer” that has amassed more than $400 million in the last 18 months. It’s called FaceStealer because it involved secretly recorded webcam videos. Victims are typically people working in the cryptocurrency and web3 industries, along with open source software developers and maintainers who DPRK hackers target in the hope of accessing the software repositories they control as the first step towards creating supply chain attacks. The FBI said it had seized more than 900 webcam videos belonging to these tech workers. First, the North Koreans send targets an invitation to join a video meeting. Those invitations come from hijacked accounts that the next intended victim may find familiar or credible. “You're going to think it's real because it's going to be based on either conversations or interests you've expressed in the past with this actual person,” said special agent Jeremy Robertson, who oversees counterintelligence and cyber investigations at FBI Los Angeles. “They're going to then send you a link to catch up, and it's usually a calendar invite, and it's going to have some typo-squatted URLs in there,” he told reporters on Thursday. The URL directs the victim to a fake Zoom or Teams meeting, and the cybercriminals record the target’s webcam video while playing a phony, prerecorded video of the person who purportedly sent the meeting invite. Sometimes the hackers also use deepfake videos of well-known individuals in the cryptocurrency and web3 industries, we’re told. “When you log in, whoever invited you – your friend or business associate – is going to be on the screen, but you're not going to hear any audio,” Robertson said. “But you're going to see their face, you're going to see them looking around, you're going to see them mouthing some words, and then in the text box you're going to receive some instructions.” The text box tells the victim that the person on the other end of the video call can’t hear them, they need to upgrade their software for the audio to work properly, and it sends a link to the supposed fix. Clicking to access the “fix” installs cryptocurrency-stealing malware on the victim’s computer and sends their contact list to the digital thieves to perpetuate the scam. The FBI attributes FaceStealer to a North Korea-linked group tracked as Sapphire Sleet , which is widely regarded as a Lazarus Group offshoot. Sapphire Sleet is also known as UNC1069, Stardust Chollima, APT38, and BlueNoroff. “The actors behind this activity, commonly referred to as Sapphire Sleet and other associated names, are part of a broader North Korean effort to generate revenue for the regime, to steal virtual assets, and gain access to networks and trusted online ecosystems,” Brett Leatherman, assistant director of the FBI's Cyber Division, told reporters. “North Korean hackers are increasingly blending cyber intrusion, social engineering, and emerging technologies such as deep fakes to make their impersonation efforts more convincing and scalable.” The FBI also provided an update on its efforts to recover the stolen assets from the October 29 attack on Binance. “When you log in, whoever invited you – your friend or business associate – is going to be on the screen, but you're not going to hear any audio,” Robertson said. “But you're going to see their face, you're going to see them looking around, you're going to see them mouthing some words, and then in the text box you're going to receive some instructions.”

The text box tells the victim that the person on the other end of the video call can’t hear them, they need to upgrade their software for the audio to work properly, and it sends a link to the supposed fix.
Clicking to access the “fix” installs cryptocurrency-stealing malware on the victim’s computer and sends their contact list to the digital thieves to perpetuate the scam.

The FBI attributes FaceStealer to a North Korea-linked group tracked as Sapphire Sleet , which is widely regarded as a Lazarus Group offshoot. Sapphire Sleet is also known as UNC1069, Stardust Chollima, APT38, and BlueNoroff.

The FBI also provided an update on its efforts to recover the stolen assets from the October 29 attack on Binance. The agency previously blamed the $6.3 billion heist on TraderTraitor, a North Korean hacking operation also linked to Lazarus Group.

Last week, Binance revealed the attackers laid the groundwork for their “ sophisticated, multi-stage campaign ” back in June, and said it involved social engineering during fake job interviews, malware downloads, compromised internal AI tooling, endpoint takeover, and an “advanced transaction-authorization method.”

Since the theft, federal investigators and private-sector partners have helped freeze more than $2.7 billion in stolen assets. The Justice Department's court authorization covers more than $1.2 billion of that haul.®

The hackers have aggressively targeted people in the cryptocurrency and Web3 industries, as well as workers in the development and maintenance of open-source software, the FBI said in a written statement. Web3, in general, describes internet applications that interact with a blockchain — a digital ledger that stores data. On Thursday, the FBI and Department of Justice announced the disruption of a cloud-based infrastructure used by the North Korean hackers, resulting in the seizure of more than 900 webcam videos of victims working in the crypto and Web3 industries worldwide. Before the operation was disrupted, the scheme resulted in the theft of more than $400 million over an 18-month period. Binance said it has replaced the stolen assets to its customers, but not recovered the stolen loot. Federal authorities said they have worked closely with private companies to recover the stolen funds, freezing more than $2.7 million and obtaining court approval to seize or restrict access to $1.2 billion of that amount. Separately, the Justice Department announced court authorization to seize or restrain more than $1.2 billion stolen from Binance, the cryptocurrency exchange hit by a roughly $6.3 billion theft last month .

“What we’ve seen over the last six months is a significant evolution in both the scale and sophistication of this operation,” said Justin Moore, director of adversary operations at Arctic Wolf, one of the firms that has assisted the FBI in its efforts to track the operation.

We’ve also seen the group’s social engineering playbook expand well beyond fake meetings into document-sharing platforms, identity verification requests, media content, and other trusted business workflows.”
The FBI attributed the theft to North Korea’s TraderTraitor group.

extraction.body: The FBI disrupted an elaborate North Korean hacking campaign that used secretly recorded videos of victims to impersonate them in online meetings, in a scheme that officials said Thursday has netted more than $400 million in stolen cryptocurrency and threatened widely used software. The operation , dubbed FaceStealer, tricks people into joining fake video calls with what appear to be familiar contacts, then installing malicious software disguised as a fix for an audio problem. Hackers use the resulting access to steal funds, take over accounts and approach the victim’s friends and colleagues. Authorities seized cloud infrastructure used in the campaign and more than 900 webcam videos of victims. The FBI also said hackers broke into the computer of a developer who maintains widely used software, then used that access to add malicious code that could reach people downloading it. The attack was detected and stopped before it widely spread. Separately, the Justice Department announced court authorization to seize or restrain more than $1.2 billion stolen from Binance, the cryptocurrency exchange hit by a roughly $6.3 billion theft last month . Officials said the two campaigns likely involved different North Korean actors. The FaceStealer operations build on relationships victims already trust. Invitations arrive through genuine accounts that hackers have taken over on services including Telegram, LinkedIn, Slack and Discord, officials say. Access to earlier conversations allows the attackers to make their messages sound familiar, Jeremy Robertson, special agent in charge at the FBI’s Los Angeles Field Office, told reporters. A meeting link directs the target to a website designed to look like Zoom or Microsoft Teams. Inside, the target sees a recording of someone they recognize. The attackers sometimes add other apparent participants, making the meeting more convincing. A message then tells the person their audio is not working and supplies instructions to fix it. Those steps — which can include running a script or pasting commands into the computer’s terminal — instead install malware capable of recording keystrokes, capturing screens and giving the hackers continued access. Meanwhile, the fake meeting records the new victim’s webcam. That footage, combined with stolen accounts and contact lists, helps the hackers repeat the process with someone else. The campaign highlights a unique degree of scale and creativity on the part of Pyongyang’s cryptocurrency theft operations that have not been publicly outlined before. “This is not something we can patch,” Robertson said, calling it a “very, very convincing” social engineering scheme. The targeting has also reached developers who maintain open-source software, which other organizations use to build their own applications. Earlier this year, a maintainer of a JavaScript software library joined a fake Teams meeting featuring someone they recognized and followed instructions that infected their computer, officials said. “What we’ve seen over the last six months is a significant evolution in both the scale and sophistication of this operation,” said Justin Moore, director of adversary operations at Arctic Wolf, one of the firms that has assisted the FBI in its efforts to track the operation. “Today, we’ve identified more than 677 targets across 58 countries. We’ve also seen the group’s social engineering playbook expand well beyond fake meetings into document-sharing platforms, identity verification requests, media content, and other trusted business workflows.” In the separate Binance case, public and private sector efforts have frozen more than $2.7 billion. The $1.2 billion covered by court orders is part of that total and not an additional recovery. A senior DOJ official said the government now has custody of the funds covered by those orders. Returning them would generally involve court proceedings to determine ownership, though the official cautioned it was too early to say exactly how that process would unfold. Binance previously said attackers used a fake job interview to compromise an engineer’s computer before reaching systems used to approve cryptocurrency transfers. The FBI attributed the theft to North Korea’s TraderTraitor group. Recovering more of the money is becoming harder as the hackers divide it into smaller amounts and distribute it among laundering networks, the senior DOJ official said. “These actors have gotten very good at laundering,” the official said. “They’ve learned from their past efforts and our efforts to interdict them.” NEXT STORY: Nvidia spying allegations test Washington’s defenses against tech espionage

extraction.body: North Korea 's Crypto Theft Operations: DOJ Seizes $1.2 Billion and Disrupts Hacker Infrastructure Gootloader Malware Disrupted After Infecting 25,000 Computers Unpatched Check Point Gateways Are Being Wiped exploiting PHP2Shell New SignDrop Exploit Can Abuse Windows Defender to Bypass Security Protections The School Bomb Threats Came From Accounts Already in Stolen Data Microsoft Cloud Outage Hits Outlook, Teams, Copilot and AI Services AI Pentest Tool AntiFox Abused To Steal AWS Credentials WhiteArmor Demands $5 Million from Maersk, Claims Theft of 100GB of Data Hackers Advertise a $1,000 Gmail Tool That Allegedly Survives Password Resets Google fixes the eighth actively exploited Chrome zero-day of 2026 Iris Ohyama data breach may expose personal information of 7.7 million people France Blames Iran for the Supermarket Fridge Attacks QNAP Warns Users as Plex2Shell Flaws Are Used to Hack NAS Devices The U.S. Department of Justice announced two separate but connected actions against North Korea ‘s cryptocurrency theft operations. The press release covers the seizure of infrastructure behind a social engineering scheme called FaceStealer and court-authorized seizures tied to the $6 billion Binance theft of October 29. Together, the two moves put more than $1.2 billion back under law enforcement control. “Today the Department of Justice announced coordinated actions against the Democratic People’s Republic of North Korea (DPRK) government’s schemes to fund its regime through the massive theft of cryptocurrency.” states the press release published by DoJ. “These actions include the seizure of cloud-based infrastructure used in the FaceStealer social engineering scheme that has resulted in the theft of more than $400 million worth of cryptocurrency and the court-authorized seizure and restraint of more than $1.2 billion worth of cryptocurrency recently stolen from Binance, a virtual currency exchange.” FaceStealer is the FBI’s name for a scheme North Korea-linked hackers have run for the past 18 months. The same actors go by Sapphire Sleet , BlueNoroff , APT38 and several other tracking names depending on who is writing the report. They’ve stolen more than $400 million that way, and they’ve also started targeting people who build and maintain open-source software, trying to reach the accounts and repositories those developers control. The process is quite specific. The hackers send meeting invitations from accounts they have already stolen. This makes the invitations look as if they come from someone the target knows and trusts. During the meeting, they play a recorded video of a previous victim or use a deepfake showing a well-known person in the cryptocurrency or Web3 industry. They use advanced AI tools to create convincing videos of influential people, making the FaceStealer scheme more effective. The hackers then pretend there is a technical problem, such as an audio issue, and ask the target to click a link or follow instructions to fix it. This leads to the installation of malware. In several cases, the attackers waited months, or even more than a year, before stealing cryptocurrency or taking control of accounts. They also used each victim’s contact lists, social media accounts and messaging apps to identify and approach new targets. Under a federal warrant, the FBI seized more than 900 webcam videos recorded from FaceStealer victims. “The FBI today published a report providing greater detail on the mechanics of the FaceStealer scheme, including best practices to protect against this scheme and steps victims can take in the event of a compromise. Additionally, the FBI created a website, www.fbi.gov/facestealer , to serve as a centralized hub for resources and information on the scheme.” continues the press release. “The effort to disrupt the FaceStealer campaign was led by Assistant U.S. Attorney Khaldoun Shobaki for the Central District of California and the FBI’s Los Angeles Field Office.” The operation to seize the infrastructure was led by the U.S. Attorney’s Office for the Central District of California and the FBI’s Los Angeles Field Office. The mechanics are specific. The hackers send meeting invitations from accounts stolen from earlier victims, so the invite looks like it comes from someone the target knows. Once in the meeting, the hackers play a pre-recorded video of a previous victim or use a deepfake of a well-known person in crypto or Web3 to simulate trusted contacts. “The North Korean hackers also use super intelligence (SI) to develop deepfake videos of well-known and influential individuals often in the cryptocurrency and web3 industries that make the FaceStealer scheme even more effective.” FBI continues. “Here again, they use the deepfake videos in the meetings with targets to gain the target’s trust.” Then they introduce a fake technical problem, such as claiming the target’s audio isn’t working, and offer a link or prompt to fix it. The fix installs malware. In several cases the hackers waited months or more than a year after the initial compromise before stealing cryptocurrency or hijacking accounts. They also used each new victim’s contact lists, social media and messaging apps to reach the next round of targets. The FBI seized more than 900 webcam videos from FaceStealer victims under a federal warrant. The U.S. Department of Justice announced two separate but connected actions against North Korea ‘s cryptocurrency theft operations. The press release covers the seizure of infrastructure behind a social engineering scheme called FaceStealer and court-authorized seizures tied to the $6 billion Binance theft of October 29. Together, the two moves put more than $1.2 billion back under law enforcement control.

“Today the Department of Justice announced coordinated actions against the Democratic People’s Republic of North Korea (DPRK) government’s schemes to fund its regime through the massive theft of cryptocurrency.” states the press release published by DoJ. “These actions include the seizure of cloud-based infrastructure used in the FaceStealer social engineering scheme that has resulted in the theft of more than $400 million worth of cryptocurrency and the court-authorized seizure and restraint of more than $1.2 billion worth of cryptocurrency recently stolen from Binance, a virtual currency exchange.”

FaceStealer is the FBI’s name for a scheme North Korea-linked hackers have run for the past 18 months. The same actors go by Sapphire Sleet , BlueNoroff , APT38 and several other tracking names depending on who is writing the report. They’ve stolen more than $400 million that way, and they’ve also started targeting people who build and maintain open-source software, trying to reach the accounts and repositories those developers control.

The process is quite specific. The hackers send meeting invitations from accounts they have already stolen. This makes the invitations look as if they come from someone the target knows and trusts. During the meeting, they play a recorded video of a previous victim or use a deepfake showing a well-known person in the cryptocurrency or Web3 industry. They use advanced AI tools to create convincing videos of influential people, making the FaceStealer scheme more effective.

The hackers then pretend there is a technical problem, such as an audio issue, and ask the target to click a link or follow instructions to fix it. This leads to the installation of malware. In several cases, the attackers waited months, or even more than a year, before stealing cryptocurrency or taking control of accounts. They also used each victim’s contact lists, social media accounts and messaging apps to identify and approach new targets.
Under a federal warrant, the FBI seized more than 900 webcam videos recorded from FaceStealer victims.

“The FBI today published a report providing greater detail on the mechanics of the FaceStealer scheme, including best practices to protect against this scheme and steps victims can take in the event of a compromise. The operation to seize the infrastructure was led by the U.S. Attorney’s Office for the Central District of California and the FBI’s Los Angeles Field Office.

Once in the meeting, the hackers play a pre-recorded video of a previous victim or use a deepfake of a well-known person in crypto or Web3 to simulate trusted contacts.

In several cases the hackers waited months or more than a year after the initial compromise before stealing cryptocurrency or hijacking accounts. They also used each new victim’s contact lists, social media and messaging apps to reach the next round of targets.
