coreStoryFacts.text: “The actors behind this activity, commonly referred to as Sapphire Sleet and other associated names, are part of a broader North Korean effort to generate revenue for the regime, to steal virtual assets, and gain access to networks and trusted online ecosystems,” Brett Leatherman, assistant director of the FBI's Cyber Division, told reporters.
“North Korean hackers are increasingly blending cyber intrusion, social engineering, and emerging technologies such as deep fakes to make their impersonation efforts more convincing and scalable.”
The FBI also provided an update on its efforts to recover the stolen assets from the October 29 attack on Binance.
The agency previously blamed the $6.3 billion heist on TraderTraitor, a North Korean hacking operation also linked to Lazarus Group.

Last week, Binance revealed the attackers laid the groundwork for their “ sophisticated, multi-stage campaign ” back in June, and said it involved social engineering during fake job interviews, malware downloads, compromised internal AI tooling, endpoint takeover, and an “advanced transaction-authorization method.”
First, the North Koreans send targets an invitation to join a video meeting.
Since the theft, federal investigators and private-sector partners have helped freeze more than $2.7 billion in stolen assets.
The FBI said it has disrupted a highly tailored, hard-to-detect cryptocurrency theft scheme by a North Korean hacking group that has managed to steal billions across the world in recent years.
Before the operation was disrupted, the scheme resulted in the theft of more than $400 million over an 18-month period.

Federal authorities said they have worked closely with private companies to recover the stolen funds, freezing more than $2.7 million and obtaining court approval to seize or restrict access to $1.2 billion of that amount.
FBI officials say the funds are used to bankroll its "rogue regime and illicit weapons program through cryptocurrency theft" and the videos are employed to impersonate and target more victims.
FBI officials said efforts to trace, freeze, seize and forfeit the stolen virtual assets are ongoing.

“Cryptocurrency unfortunately has become fertile ground for North Korea to defraud victims and fund its malign activities,” Bill Essayli, the top federal prosecutor for Los Angeles, said in a written statement.

The FBI disrupted an elaborate North Korean hacking campaign that used secretly recorded videos of victims to impersonate them in online meetings, in a scheme that officials said Thursday has netted more than $400 million in stolen cryptocurrency and threatened widely used software.

Separately, the Justice Department announced court authorization to seize or restrain more than $1.2 billion stolen from Binance, the cryptocurrency exchange hit by a roughly $6.3 billion theft last month .

“What we’ve seen over the last six months is a significant evolution in both the scale and sophistication of this operation,” said Justin Moore, director of adversary operations at Arctic Wolf, one of the firms that has assisted the FBI in its efforts to track the operation.
“Today, we’ve identified more than 677 targets across 58 countries.

We’ve also seen the group’s social engineering playbook expand well beyond fake meetings into document-sharing platforms, identity verification requests, media content, and other trusted business workflows.”
The FBI attributed the theft to North Korea’s TraderTraitor group.
“This is not something we can patch,” Robertson said, calling it a “very, very convincing” social engineering scheme.
The FaceStealer operations build on relationships victims already trust.
Invitations arrive through genuine accounts that hackers have taken over on services including Telegram, LinkedIn, Slack and Discord, officials say.
Access to earlier conversations allows the attackers to make their messages sound familiar, Jeremy Robertson, special agent in charge at the FBI’s Los Angeles Field Office, told reporters.
A meeting link directs the target to a website designed to look like Zoom or Microsoft Teams.

extraction.body: The FBI said it has disrupted a highly tailored, hard-to-detect cryptocurrency theft scheme by a North Korean hacking group that has managed to steal billions across the world in recent years. The hackers have aggressively targeted people in the cryptocurrency and Web3 industries, as well as workers in the development and maintenance of open-source software, the FBI said in a written statement. Web3, in general, describes internet applications that interact with a blockchain — a digital ledger that stores data. On Thursday, the FBI and Department of Justice announced the disruption of a cloud-based infrastructure used by the North Korean hackers, resulting in the seizure of more than 900 webcam videos of victims working in the crypto and Web3 industries worldwide. Before the operation was disrupted, the scheme resulted in the theft of more than $400 million over an 18-month period. FBI officials say the funds are used to bankroll its "rogue regime and illicit weapons program through cryptocurrency theft" and the videos are employed to impersonate and target more victims. “North Korea’s government bankrolls its rogue regime and illicit weapons program through cryptocurrency theft,” said Principal Deputy Assistant Atty. "The FBI attributes this activity to the North Korean hacking group commonly referred to in the private sector as Sapphire Sleet, UNC1069, Stardust Chollima, APT38, and BlueNoroff," the FBI said in a written statement. “Cryptocurrency unfortunately has become fertile ground for North Korea to defraud victims and fund its malign activities,” Bill Essayli, the top federal prosecutor for Los Angeles, said in a written statement. “Today’s seizure shows that America will continue the fight against rogue states who financially gain from cybercrime.” The federal agency said the hackers used several tactics to compromise victims, including a sophisticated social engineering scheme dubbed "FaceStealer." The scheme involves hijacking LinkedIn, Telegram, Slack and Discord accounts of people known to the victim, then impersonating those people to make contact and lure the victims into video calls using Zoom, Microsoft Teams and Google Meets. "Their objective is compromise of the software supply chain. By infiltrating accounts of trusted developers and maintainers, the threat actors can potentially distribute malicious code through widely used software, impacting millions of downstream users," the FBI said in its written statement. FBI Cyber Branch Operations Director Brett Leatherman said in a statement that the "North Korean regime relies on proceeds from large-scale cryptocurrency theft to fund its illicit weapons program, stealing billions of dollars in recent years." Separately from the FaceStealer scheme, members of the North Korean military, referred by the FBI as "TraderTraitor," stole more than $6 billion in cryptocurrency from the world's largest crypto exchange Binance on Oct. Binance said it has replaced the stolen assets to its customers, but not recovered the stolen loot. Federal authorities said they have worked closely with private companies to recover the stolen funds, freezing more than $2.7 million and obtaining court approval to seize or restrict access to $1.2 billion of that amount. FBI officials said efforts to trace, freeze, seize and forfeit the stolen virtual assets are ongoing.

extraction.body: The FBI disrupted an elaborate North Korean hacking campaign that used secretly recorded videos of victims to impersonate them in online meetings, in a scheme that officials said Thursday has netted more than $400 million in stolen cryptocurrency and threatened widely used software. The operation , dubbed FaceStealer, tricks people into joining fake video calls with what appear to be familiar contacts, then installing malicious software disguised as a fix for an audio problem. Hackers use the resulting access to steal funds, take over accounts and approach the victim’s friends and colleagues. Authorities seized cloud infrastructure used in the campaign and more than 900 webcam videos of victims. The FBI also said hackers broke into the computer of a developer who maintains widely used software, then used that access to add malicious code that could reach people downloading it. The attack was detected and stopped before it widely spread. Separately, the Justice Department announced court authorization to seize or restrain more than $1.2 billion stolen from Binance, the cryptocurrency exchange hit by a roughly $6.3 billion theft last month . Officials said the two campaigns likely involved different North Korean actors. The FaceStealer operations build on relationships victims already trust. Invitations arrive through genuine accounts that hackers have taken over on services including Telegram, LinkedIn, Slack and Discord, officials say. Access to earlier conversations allows the attackers to make their messages sound familiar, Jeremy Robertson, special agent in charge at the FBI’s Los Angeles Field Office, told reporters. A meeting link directs the target to a website designed to look like Zoom or Microsoft Teams. Inside, the target sees a recording of someone they recognize. The attackers sometimes add other apparent participants, making the meeting more convincing. A message then tells the person their audio is not working and supplies instructions to fix it. Those steps — which can include running a script or pasting commands into the computer’s terminal — instead install malware capable of recording keystrokes, capturing screens and giving the hackers continued access. Meanwhile, the fake meeting records the new victim’s webcam. That footage, combined with stolen accounts and contact lists, helps the hackers repeat the process with someone else. The campaign highlights a unique degree of scale and creativity on the part of Pyongyang’s cryptocurrency theft operations that have not been publicly outlined before. “This is not something we can patch,” Robertson said, calling it a “very, very convincing” social engineering scheme. The targeting has also reached developers who maintain open-source software, which other organizations use to build their own applications. Earlier this year, a maintainer of a JavaScript software library joined a fake Teams meeting featuring someone they recognized and followed instructions that infected their computer, officials said. “What we’ve seen over the last six months is a significant evolution in both the scale and sophistication of this operation,” said Justin Moore, director of adversary operations at Arctic Wolf, one of the firms that has assisted the FBI in its efforts to track the operation. “Today, we’ve identified more than 677 targets across 58 countries. We’ve also seen the group’s social engineering playbook expand well beyond fake meetings into document-sharing platforms, identity verification requests, media content, and other trusted business workflows.” In the separate Binance case, public and private sector efforts have frozen more than $2.7 billion. The $1.2 billion covered by court orders is part of that total and not an additional recovery. A senior DOJ official said the government now has custody of the funds covered by those orders. Returning them would generally involve court proceedings to determine ownership, though the official cautioned it was too early to say exactly how that process would unfold. Binance previously said attackers used a fake job interview to compromise an engineer’s computer before reaching systems used to approve cryptocurrency transfers. The FBI attributed the theft to North Korea’s TraderTraitor group. Recovering more of the money is becoming harder as the hackers divide it into smaller amounts and distribute it among laundering networks, the senior DOJ official said. “These actors have gotten very good at laundering,” the official said. “They’ve learned from their past efforts and our efforts to interdict them.” NEXT STORY: Nvidia spying allegations test Washington’s defenses against tech espionage

passages: Bloomberg reported that the FBI doesn't believe the outage was a cyberattack or criminal act, and that one line of inquiry is whether a software update caused it.
An update is a far more ordinary explanation than a hack, and in some ways a more uncomfortable one, because it means a national system can be taken down by its own maintenance.

The FAA then ordered a nationwide ground stop, telling airlines that "all departing traffic should remain groundstopped until further notice" and citing "extraordinary circumstances and reasons of safety." Planes already in the air were allowed to land, and international arrivals were handled case by case.
Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy said the fault hit every one of the FAA's en route air traffic control centers, and CBS News counted about 8,000 delays and 400 cancellations within hours.
Investigators haven't named the update, its author or a restart time.
In January 2023 the FAA's NOTAM system failure stopped departures nationwide for under two hours, and the agency said files were unintentionally deleted during work on its databases.
In July 2024 a faulty CrowdStrike update crashed about 8.5 million Windows machines, by Microsoft's estimate, and Delta alone said it lost around $500 million.
The pattern is the same each time: a small change, a wide blast radius, and no cheap way back.
Planes sat at gates from Chicago to New York on Friday while investigators asked whether a routine software change, not a hacker, knocked out the radios air traffic controllers depend on.
For now the facts are short: no named update, no confirmed cause, and no public timetable from the FAA for getting every departure moving again.

extraction.body: Passengers wait at Midway Airport as a nationwide ground stop brings flights to a halt. UPDATE: The Federal Aviation Administration has lifted the nationwide ground stop, but flight disruptions are expected to linger into the weekend. The Federal Aviation Administration released a new statement following a rare ground stop issued at all airports across the country. Stream NBC 5 for free, 24/7, wherever you are. In its original alert, the FAA said the ground stop was issued "due to extraordinary circumstances and for reasons of safety." In a newer statement, the agency said the alert followed "communication issues impacting multiple Air Route Traffic Control Centers." "FAA technicians are investigating the issue. We will provide updates," the FAA said in its statement. In a later message, the FAA said the issue stemmed from "a temporary telecommunications outage." "Out of an abundance of caution all flights have been halted. Every flight has been accounted for and international flights will be handled on a case by case basis," the statement read. A nationwide ground stop is exceptionally rare, experts say, with only one other such alert issued since 9/11. That ground stop took place in 2023 , when the FAA suffered an outage of the system that sends messages to pilots. According to the advisory from the FAA Friday, all aircraft operators were told "by order of the Federal Aviation Command Center" that airports were ground stopped and all departing traffic should remain grounded "until further notice." "Inbound flights will be managed on a case by case basis," the alert stated. Moments earlier, both major airports in Chicago were listed under a ground stop due to an "equipment outage." It remained unclear if that outage was connected to the ground stop, however. U.S. Secretary of Transportation Sean Duffy confirmed the ground stop, saying it was under investigation. The @FAAnews issued a nationwide ground stop for all U.S. airports following a communication issue impacting all Air Route Traffic Control Centers. FAA technicians are investigating the issue. We will provide immediate updates as we have them. U.S. Secretary of Homeland Security Markwayne Mullin Mullin said there was "no indication as of yet that this was a nefarious attack against us." "We were wanting to assure all the American people this isn't a safety to the American people or another 9/11," Mullin said. "I think that's what a lot of people are trying to make the comparison to, and that's not the case." The communications problems don’t appear to be linked to the FAA’s new AI-powered system the agency is rolling out to help predict problems in the sky, according to Mullin. The FAA’s SMART system is based in a single location near Washington, D.C., where a team of experts analyzes flight schedules, weather forecasts and hundreds of other streams of data. Then that office sends recommendations to the FAA’s command center that relays them to controllers across the country for consideration. The company that designed the system, ASI, said “the current ground stop is not based on or a result of the SMART system, any product of ASI or our integration with FAA and ATC.” More than 200 flights were delayed at Chicago's airports Friday afternoon. As of 3:11 p.m., the Chicago Department of Aviation reported 213 delays at O'Hare International Airport and another 55 at Midway International Airport. Former United Airlines pilot and aviation expert Steve Arroyo said the problem appeared similar to a regional air traffic control communication outage in September that snarled hundreds of flights across the Northeast, except this time on a nationwide scale. Arroyo said it could be linked to the outdated technology used by air traffic controllers. “If you don’t have that ability, whether it’s because the old wires that they have are just run down or for whatever reason, you’ve got to stop airplanes on the ground,” said Arroyo. “And not put them in the air where you’re going to risk not being able to communicate with them.” While still early in the investigation, multiple officials from multiple agencies told NBC News there is no indication that the incident has been caused by malicious activity. They said they haven’t seen the type of activity that would normally be associated with a cyber attack incident but cautioned that it is still early in the investigation and that information could still change. Three senior officials said there’s nothing that indicates a connection between the FAA incident and Thursday's Microsoft outage. Check back for more on this developing story.

The communications problems don’t appear to be linked to the FAA’s new AI-powered system the agency is rolling out to help predict problems in the sky, according to Mullin. extraction.body: At 12:54 p.m. Pacific on Friday, the FAA ordered every departing flight in America to stay exactly where it was, a move the agency had pulled only twice before: on September 11, 2001, and one January morning in 2023. The official reason, as of this writing, is a "temporary telecommunications outage" somewhere in the web of radios and radar that keeps airliners from meeting each other at 35,000 feet. That's a plausible explanation and, let's be honest, barely an explanation at all. The stop also landed just days after the agency took a new AI air-traffic planning tool nationwide, and the Homeland Security secretary says he isn't ruling anything out, though so far nothing ties the two together and officials say they see no sign of an attack. So here's what's known, what isn't, and which of the theories ricocheting around your feed deserve a raised eyebrow versus a full eye-roll (details current as of mid-afternoon Pacific on Friday, Nov. 13). The FAA's Air Traffic Control System Command Center posted the advisory at 12:54 p.m. Pacific, ordering all airports ground-stopped "due to extraordinary circumstances and for reasons of safety," according to the SF Standard . About 20 minutes later, Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy took to X to blame "a communication issue impacting all Air Route Traffic Control Centers," which, as ABC News explains, are the 22 facilities responsible for everything flying above 18,000 feet. He offered neither a cause nor an estimate of when flights would resume. The scale is hard to overstate. Roughly 11,000 flights were still scheduled to depart when the order came down, per aviation analytics firm Cirium, as CNBC reported. Flightradar24 counted 4,042 airborne flights bound for U.S. airports at that moment, all of which were allowed to land, and by press time Afar was citing FlightAware figures of more than 10,000 delays and 1,948 cancellations, both still climbing. So what actually broke? The aviation newsletter The Air Current reported, via Fast Company , that the command center told airlines radio frequencies and radar capabilities were affected and that it had no information on timing or cause. One pilot told Yahoo News the trouble started at Kansas City Center, which covers the middle of the country, and spread from there; that's a single account, not an FAA finding. ABC News noted both Chicago airports had already been grounded earlier in the afternoon for an equipment outage, and Newsweek counts this as only the third nationwide ground stop ever. Every Bay Area airport got caught in it. KQED confirmed that planes weren't departing from SFO, Oakland, San José Mineta or Sacramento, that SFO spokesperson Doug Yakel said inbound flights would keep landing, and that the Governor's Office said the state was "closely monitoring" the ground stop. Long ground stops can also leave crews at risk of reaching legal duty-hour limits. There was a sliver of good news by midafternoon. The SF Standard reported that Pacific-bound flights at SFO were cleared to resume about two hours in, with a plane lifting off around 2:30 p.m. and stranded travelers cheering a second takeoff before 3. The same report said the FAA later extended the broader stop to 8:30 p.m. Pacific, and that San José's airport told travelers it didn't know when operations would return to normal. SFO had already been having a day, with FAA wind-and-weather delays in place before any of this started, and SFist noticed the FAA's own status page was still blaming a 138-minute average delay on wind, with no mention of the national shutdown. A nationwide outage on top of the weather delays feels like piling on. The administration's message has been consistent, if thin. Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin told reporters there was "no indication as of yet that this was a nefarious attack against us," per The Hill , though he also said officials aren't "ruling out anything at this point," as GeekWire quoted him. Multiple officials from multiple agencies told NBC News they hadn't seen the kind of activity normally associated with a cyberattack, while cautioning it's early. Bloomberg, as relayed by MS NOW , reported the FBI doesn't believe a cyberattack or criminality was involved. Here's the awkward part. An airline source told CNN that controllers were on a crisis call with still no clear answer on the cause, and a congressional official told Scripps News that neither the White House nor the Pentagon knew what had happened. The cause remained unclear even as officials said they had seen no signs of a cyberattack. For what it's worth, Mullin said President Trump had been briefed, according to CNN . Here's the sequence, as best it can be pieced together. The FAA began using SMART, short for Strategic Management of Airspace, Routes and Trajectories, in a "limited mode" around Washington in September, per Bloomberg via AviationPros , then expanded it to all 22 centers, according to Airways , which cites a November 10 FAA statement. The SF Standard describes the expansion as coming a day before the outage, so the exact date is murky, but every account puts it ahead of Friday. SMART is an AI air-traffic planning tool, a different layer from the radios and radar reportedly affected Friday. Mullin said officials weren't "ruling out anything at this point," while the tool's maker said the stop "is not based on or a result of the SMART system," per NBC News . SMART had gone nationwide before Friday's stop, but whether the two are connected remains unclear. Nature abhors a vacuum, and the internet abhors an unexplained outage. As of this writing, we couldn't find any named public figure putting a specific accusation of sabotage or cover-up on the record; what we found instead was a lot of "just asking questions," which is how these things usually start. Everything in this section is unverified, and we've labeled it accordingly. The claim: Iran, or another adversary, took down air traffic control. Where it comes from: the U.S. and Israel went to war with Iran on February 28, and in April the FBI, CISA and NSA warned that Iran-affiliated hackers were disrupting American critical infrastructure, TechCrunch reported. Colin Clarke of the Soufan Group told Yahoo News he'd fielded several texts asking "This is the Iranians, right?" while saying he'd seen no evidence cyberterrorism was behind the stop. The reality check: officials say there's no indication of an attack, and Google threat analyst John Hultquist observed back in March that Iranian hackers often "fabricate and exaggerate their effects," per Defense One . And in 2023, the last nationwide stop also set off cyberattack fears before the FAA concluded contract workers had accidentally deleted files, as NPR reported. The dull explanation has a strong track record here, though "strong" is not the same as "always." The claim: the FAA's new AI system broke the airspace. Where it comes from: the timing laid out above, plus Mullin's refusal to rule it out, which GeekWire also reported. The reality check: Air Space Intelligence said the stop "is not based on or a result of the SMART system," in a statement NBC News quoted, and the FAA has said SMART makes recommendations facilities can accept or decline and can't take control of an aircraft, per Airways . On paper, a scheduling advisor shouldn't be able to knock out radios and radar, which are different layers of the system, though "on paper" has not been the FAA's strongest argument this year. Of course, a company denying fault is also what companies do, which is why the investigation matters. The claim: the FAA stoppage, Thursday's Microsoft 365 outage and a Friday-afternoon National Weather Service outage are one coordinated event. Where it comes from: the NWS said it was dealing with nationwide internet and communications problems, Reuters reported, and WND put "Coincidence?" in its headline over a roundup of social posts while acknowledging there was no confirmed link. Polymarket and Mario Nawfal flagged the weather outage alongside the ground stop, and Gunther Eagleman's post is a representative sample: 🚨 NOW: The National Weather Service is reportedly confirming a NATIONWIDE RADAR OUTAGE. This comes less than an hour after the FAA grounded every departing flight in America over a communication issue at every Air Route Traffic Control Center. That means TWO NATIONWIDE SYSTEMS went down on the same afternoon. Nobody has said yet whether the two are connected, and Americans deserve a straight answer fast. Washington needs to tell us exactly what is going on. — Gunther Eagleman™ (@GuntherEagleman) November 13, 2026 To be fair to the poster, the post doesn't claim a hack; it asks for answers, which is a reasonable thing to want. It does lean on the words "radar outage," which is slightly misleading: per News9 , the NWS problem involved its national radar website and other online products, and local offices kept issuing warnings and forecasts, as KESQ noted. The reality check: three senior officials told NBC News there's nothing to indicate a connection to the Microsoft outage, and Mullin dismissed the idea with "Those are separate issues," per Ticker News . IVN reports Microsoft attributed its outage to a network capacity upgrade followed by a network change, with no sign of malicious activity. What no one we found has addressed directly is the Weather Service overlap, and the SF Standard noted officials haven't confirmed whether those two outages are related, so that one is an open question rather than a conspiracy. The strongest version of the skeptic's argument goes like this: early official reads are sometimes wrong, and "no evidence of an attack" is only as good as the FAA's ability to see one. On that second point, the Government Accountability Office reported September 21 that the FAA hadn't completed formal risk assessments for seven of eight spectrum-dependent systems it reviewed and lacked comprehensive real-time detection of jamming and spoofing, so some incidents can only be investigated after someone reports them, per AvWeb . The agency concurred with all nine of the watchdog's recommendations, according to the GAO . To be clear, that report describes vulnerabilities, not an incident, and no one has tied it to Friday's stop. But it's the best evidence anywhere in this story that "we found nothing" and "nothing happened" are different statements. It cuts both ways, though: in each of the recent incidents we found, the dull explanation, a deleted file or a blown circuit, beat the dramatic one. Air traffic control wobbles have been the story of the past 18 months. In spring 2025, the Philadelphia facility that handles Newark's airspace lost radar for 90 seconds and radios for 30 on April 28, with several more outages in the following weeks, according to UPI . Newark's approach control had been moved to Philadelphia in July 2024 to address chronic understaffing, per AeroCorner . This year has been no better. On August 6, a dual equipment failure at the Minneapolis center knocked out radar and voice communications for roughly two hours and triggered ground stops across multiple states, according to AeroCorner . On September 21, a blown circuit in Philadelphia led to more than 1,000 canceled flights nationwide after FAA Administrator Bryan Bedford said officials discovered the backup line had already been cut, as ABC7 reported, with PhillyVoice reporting the FAA blamed an Amtrak crew for the damage. So much for redundancy. Which brings us to the money and the politics. Congress has approved $12.5 billion for the air traffic control overhaul, and the figure cited for what's still needed has ranged from about $20 billion in September reporting from AeroCorner to $30 billion in remarks from Duffy, per Scripps News . Sen. Tammy Duckworth, the top Democrat on the aviation subcommittee, said "The safety of our skies is built on redundancies" and promised to demand answers, according to CNN , while the Senate Commerce Committee's Republican staff said the stoppage underscores the need to modernize the centers, per Yahoo News . Quick note first: this is general information, not legal advice. Under DOT's automatic refund rule, a passenger whose flight is canceled or significantly changed is entitled to a refund if they don't accept the alternative flight or travel credit the airline offers, according to KOMO . "Significant" means a change of more than three hours domestically or six internationally, as Good Morning America explains, and the money is supposed to arrive without you asking, within seven days for a credit card and 20 days for other payment methods, per CNN via WHDH . The rule doesn't turn on whose fault the cancellation was, and there's no separate cash payout for the inconvenience itself, the way European passengers get, according to DeepArrival . Meals and hotels are murkier. Most major airlines have committed to give passengers meals after a long wait and hotel rooms for overnight disruptions, KOMO reports, but those promises live in each carrier's own customer-service plan and, as we understand it, generally apply when the airline is at fault. A nationwide FAA-ordered stop is about as far from "the airline's fault" as it gets, so check your carrier's plan before assuming a hotel voucher is coming; that's our read, not a ruling. Then there's the tarmac. DOT rules bar U.S. airlines from letting domestic flights sit on the tarmac more than three hours without offering passengers a chance to deplane (four hours for international), and require food and water after two hours, with exceptions for safety, security or air traffic control reasons, according to DOT . Whether a nationwide ground stop falls under the air-traffic-control exception is a question we expect lawyers will enjoy. For now, if you're stuck on a plane for hours, ask the crew what the plan is. The stop was extended to 8:30 p.m. Pacific per the SF Standard's reporting, though Latin Times reported it remained in effect with no lift timeline as of 5:45 p.m. Eastern, and Live and Let's Fly predicts Saturday will be messy even after departures resume. Beyond the logistics, keep an eye out for a named cause from the FAA or DOT, Duckworth's promised demand for answers, and whether anyone ever addresses the Weather Service overlap. Until then, check your airline's app, resist the urge to "just head to the airport," and be a little skeptical of anyone on X who sounds certain about anything at 3 p.m. on a Friday. extraction.body: LONDON — Unauthorized drone activity prompted a security response at an American base in Britain, but the situation has been “resolved,” U.S. and U.K. defense officials said Friday. Security forces at Royal Air Force Base Lakenheath in eastern England responded to suspected unauthorized drone activity, but no personnel, aircraft or infrastructure were affected, the U.S. Air Force in Europe said in a statement. “We continue to work closely with our host nation counterparts to ensure the safety and security of our U.S. service members, U.S. and host nation civilians, contractors, and all of our families,” the statement said. A spokesperson for the British Ministry of Defense said the incident has been “resolved.” U.S. Air Force security personnel had responded to the reports, and the U.K. ministry is working closely with the Americans to determine what happened, according to the spokesperson, who spoke on condition of anonymity to discuss sensitive security matters. The drone incident means that three U.S. bases in the United Kingdom have been affected by threats in recent weeks. Friday's security response at RAF Lakenheath comes just days after the U.S. moved more than a dozen aircraft from a different base just miles away in eastern England — RAF Mildenhall — because of a threat. During the plane exodus, RAF Mildenhall also raised its alert level to FPCON Charlie — the second-highest level, which is used when an incident occurs or intelligence is received indicating that some form of terrorist action targeting personnel or facilities is likely. A U.S. official said at the time that the decision to move the aircraft was proactive rather than reactive. Several weeks ago, a group of men was detained after three suspicious vans were spotted traveling toward RAF Fairford, roughly 150 miles (240 kilometers) west of Mildenhall and Lakenheath. British authorities linked the plot to Iran , and the U.S. withdrew its bombers that had been stationed there. The U.K.-owned base has been used by American bombers during decades of conflicts in the Middle East, including the Iran war . Other arrests followed, and at least three men have been charged with plotting to attack RAF Fairford. Also this week, a U.S. Army officer assigned to a NATO unit at a military base near Gloucester, England, was arrested on suspicion of spying for Russia. Police said the arrest was not related to other counterterrorism investigations, indicating no connection with the suspected terror plot linked to Iran at RAF Fairford, also near Gloucester.

Security forces at Royal Air Force Base Lakenheath in eastern England responded to suspected unauthorized drone activity, but no personnel, aircraft or infrastructure were affected, the U.S. Air Force in Europe said in a statement. “We continue to work closely with our host nation counterparts to ensure the safety and security of our U.S. service members, U.S. and host nation civilians, contractors, and all of our families,” the statement said. A spokesperson for the British Ministry of Defense said the incident has been “resolved.” U.S. Air Force security personnel had responded to the reports, and the U.K. ministry is working closely with the Americans to determine what happened, according to the spokesperson, who spoke on condition of anonymity to discuss sensitive security matters. The drone incident means that three U.S. bases in the United Kingdom have been affected by threats in recent weeks. Friday's security response at RAF Lakenheath comes just days after the U.S. moved more than a dozen aircraft from a different base just miles away in eastern England — RAF Mildenhall — because of a threat. During the plane exodus, RAF Mildenhall also raised its alert level to FPCON Charlie — the second-highest level, which is used when an incident occurs or intelligence is received indicating that some form of terrorist action targeting personnel or facilities is likely. A U.S. official said at the time that the decision to move the aircraft was proactive rather than reactive. Several weeks ago, a group of men was detained after three suspicious vans were spotted traveling toward RAF Fairford, roughly 150 miles (240 kilometers) west of Mildenhall and Lakenheath. British authorities linked the plot to Iran , and the U.S. withdrew its bombers that had been stationed there. The U.K.-owned base has been used by American bombers during decades of conflicts in the Middle East, including the Iran war . Other arrests followed, and at least three men have been charged with plotting to attack RAF Fairford. Also this week, a U.S. Army officer assigned to a NATO unit at a military base near Gloucester, England, was arrested on suspicion of spying for Russia. Police said the arrest was not related to other counterterrorism investigations, indicating no connection with the suspected terror plot linked to Iran at RAF Fairford, also near Gloucester.

sources.title: Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang’s ‘spy’ affair could spark Congress crackdown on AI export controls: ‘Massive earthquake’ - Yahoo
passages: Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang's affair with an alleged Chinese spy has sparked fears of a major clampdown on the AI industry – pitting China hawks against those who warn that an overreaction will put the US at a disadvantage versus Beijing, The Post has learned.

Lawmakers from both parties are scrutinizing past remarks from Jensen, who was the most influential voice pushing US officials to curb export controls on Nvidia chips — even as they assess whether his affair with Megaspeed executive Alice Huang compromised national security.

Meanwhile, Bloomberg reported Nvidia general counsel Tim Teter directly called Kessler, who oversees chip export controls, in the summer of 2025 to ask about the department's investigation into Megaspeed.

Ousting Huang himself, the source added, would be a "massive earthquake" during a fragile moment for the AI sector, which is already facing questions on Wall Street over whether it's a giant bubble ready to burst.
Nvidia CEO tries to act 'business as usual' in office return after 'China spy' affair bombshell: report

However, there are real concerns about Huang's ability to remain at the helm of Nvidia – despite the fact that many consider him irreplaceable to the company and the lack of any obvious successor within its ranks.
That argument seems unlikely to satisfy key lawmakers who were already concerned about China gaining access to Nvidia's best hardware – even before Huang's embarrassing misstep.
Elizabeth Warren (D-Mass.) called for legislation targeting "various pathways through which China accesses advanced chips."
One key loophole currently under the microscope is China's well-documented practice of accessing high-end Nvidia hardware housed in data centers based in Southeast Asia.

Nvidia initially replied that all of its chip sales were accurately recorded – even though Megaspeed had imported 50,000 more computer chips than what Nvidia linked to its data centers, Bloomberg reported.

Some DC sources believe the scandal will result in a bipartisan push for even stronger curbs on chip sales — with proponents concerned that Nvidia's cutting-edge chips will fuel greater inroads into AI by Chinese companies.

Bloomberg via Getty Images At the same time, some of them warn that ordering such a crackdown – for example banning a loophole allowing Chinese companies to rent access to Nvidia's high-end hardware through data centers located in Southeast Asia – would play right into China's hands, a source close to the situation said. "If they do that, it will just drive those foreign clouds to Huawei," the source told The Post, referring to the Chinese telecom giant that is aggressively pursuing AI business. "Ultimately, over time, those clouds will choose what's available to them. It becomes an economic question – do you want foreign clouds to have American technology or Huawei technology?" Ousting Huang himself, the source added, would be a "massive earthquake" during a fragile moment for the AI sector, which is already facing questions on Wall Street over whether it's a giant bubble ready to burst. That argument seems unlikely to satisfy key lawmakers who were already concerned about China gaining access to Nvidia's best hardware – even before Huang's embarrassing misstep. House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries (D-NY) said he "strongly supports" adding tougher chip controls to an annual year-end defense spending bill, while Sen. Jim Banks (R-Ind.) and Sen. Elizabeth Warren (D-Mass.) called for legislation targeting "various pathways through which China accesses advanced chips." "This is not, at this point, a partisan mud fight. This is bipartisan. We need answers about what happened here, what the FBI is looking into or already knew . We are in a bipartisan gathering phase." One key loophole currently under the microscope is China's well-documented practice of accessing high-end Nvidia hardware housed in data centers based in Southeast Asia. US officials have suspected Singapore-based Megaspeed – and alleged Chinese intelligence asset Alice Huang – of exploiting the loophole to smuggle AI chips to China. Nvidia has long resisted efforts to crack down on so-called "remote access," while key Commerce Department figures like Howard Lutnick and undersecretary Jeffrey Kessler, who oversees the Bureau of Industry and Security, have been reluctant to take action. Rush Doshi, a China policy expert and Senior Fellow at the Council on Foreign Relations, expects Democrats to push hard to close the "remote access" loophole. "If the reporting is right, it potentially reveals corruption and compromise in American China policy on one of the most important issues of our time, including in ways that undermine AI safety for Americans," Doshi said. "Democrats and Republicans alike are going to want to investigate what they see as the decision to sell off American national security and economic advantage and AI safety for profit." Nvidia declined to comment. Representatives for the White House and Commerce Department did not immediately return questions for comment. Aside from pursuing answers about Huang's personal conduct, lawmakers from both parties are sure to seek answers about the Trump administration's handling of the situation – specifically, its delay in taking action despite warnings months ago that the Nvidia boss was tangled up with an alleged Chinese spy, and the Commerce Department's dealings with Nvidia, Doshi added. Last year, US officials grew concerned that Megaspeed, the largest buyer of Nvidia chips in southeast Asia, was involved in chip smuggling and asked Nvidia to audit its dealings with the firm. Nvidia initially replied that all of its chip sales were accurately recorded – even though Megaspeed had imported 50,000 more computer chips than what Nvidia linked to its data centers, Bloomberg reported. Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick testifies during a subcommittee hearing with the Senate Committee on Appropriations in the Dirksen Senate Office Building on April 22, 2026 in Washington, DC. Getty Images Meanwhile, Bloomberg reported Nvidia general counsel Tim Teter directly called Kessler, who oversees chip export controls, in the summer of 2025 to ask about the department's investigation into Megaspeed. The report added that Commerce staffers were subsequently "muzzled in their ability to look into the company" and told to route requests on the matter through Kessler. "BIS conducts all enforcement strictly by the book," a spokesperson told the outlet. "BIS enforces aggressively across the board, including with respect to chip smuggling, and enforcement is at an all-time high." While the scandal is a major black eye for Nvidia, it's unlikely to completely upend the company's role as the linchpin of the AI movement, according to Daniel Newman, CEO of Futurum Group. The company's deal roadmap is already largely set through 2028, and companies can't easily find a replacement for Nvidia's advanced hardware even if they were inclined to. However, there are real concerns about Huang's ability to remain at the helm of Nvidia – despite the fact that many consider him irreplaceable to the company and the lack of any obvious successor within its ranks. "The big question is on the continuum of, is he a CEO that committed infidelity? I think he can survive that. That doesn't mean it's good," Newman said. "All the risks around intelligence stuff is not survivable. If any line was crossed beyond him just having an affair, the board is going to have to move." US officials say the disruption was caused by old equipment overloading and not a cyber-attack or a Microsoft outage.

passages: China warned the United States on Friday against putting additional export controls on semiconductors in the wake of the scandal surrounding AI chip giant Nvidia.
I’m in favour of limiting those exports,” House speaker Mike Johnson was quoted as saying.

China “has consistently opposed the abuse of export control measures, which disrupts the stability of global industrial and supply chains and serves no party’s interests,” foreign ministry spokeswoman Mao Ning told a regular briefing when asked about calls from US lawmakers to impose more limits on exports of chip equipment to China.
Reports allege the Commerce Department under Secretary Howard Lutnick may have failed to act on suspicions that Megaspeed was helping reroute restricted Nvidia technology to China.
US intelligence reportedly circulated a memo this spring alleging that Alice Huang — no relation to Jensen Huang — was an asset of China’s Ministry of State Security.
Beijing has rejected the allegations and on Thursday said that they are a “pretext to for imposing a technological blockade” to stop China advancing in artificial intelligence technology.
The furore comes ahead of a meeting expected next week between US President Donald Trump and Chinese counterpart Xi Jinping in Shenzhen in southern China at a APEC gathering.

sources.title: Democrats Demand Answers Over Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang's Alleged China Spy Scandal - Newsweek
passages: The abrupt resignation of Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang on Thursday comes as Democrats prepare to take control of Congress following sweeping victories in the midterm elections last week.

Judging by their reactions to his exit, which followed revelations of multiple affairs, including one with a suspected Chinese intelligence operative, Democrats intend to pursue answers well beyond his departure from the company.
"Despite Jensen Huang's resignation, Congress must demand answers from Mr.
Huang and others at Nvidia about how they may have put U.S. national security at risk," the New York Democrat wrote on X Thursday.

"I think it also raises a question, where we have these companies that are so powerful, whether it's Jensen Huang or Elon Musk, that they literally are driving national security policy," Warner told Newsweek .
Meanwhile, Democrats' demands for answers suggest the controversy could remain a focus of congressional oversight even after Huang's departure.

The national security implications loom large, given Nvidia's central role in the global artificial intelligence industry and Huang's close relationship with President Donald Trump , whose administration has eased some restrictions on the company's sales of advanced chips to China .

There has been no public evidence establishing that Huang knowingly acted on behalf of Chinese interests, knew of Alice Huang's alleged intelligence connections or altered his positions on U.S. export policy because of her.
In an internal message sent to Nvidia staff, Jensen Huang acknowledged Sunday that he had been unfaithful to his wife but did not identify anyone involved.
Newsweek has not independently confirmed the reporting.
Nvidia announced Thursday that Huang had resigned as president, CEO and a member of its board, effective immediately.
Foreign Ministry spokesperson Guo Jiakun said Monday that "the so-called Chinese spy allegation is unsubstantiated" and "nothing but smears against China."
Commerce Department was investigating whether Megaspeed was helping China obtain restricted AI chips.
The company has denied wrongdoing, saying it complies with applicable export controls and that investigations found no evidence of illegal activity.

extraction.body: The abrupt resignation of Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang on Thursday comes as Democrats prepare to take control of Congress following sweeping victories in the midterm elections last week. Judging by their reactions to his exit, which followed revelations of multiple affairs, including one with a suspected Chinese intelligence operative, Democrats intend to pursue answers well beyond his departure from the company. The national security implications loom large, given Nvidia's central role in the global artificial intelligence industry and Huang's close relationship with President Donald Trump , whose administration has eased some restrictions on the company's sales of advanced chips to China . Representative Joe Morelle, a New York Democrat, called Huang's resignation a "wake-up call." "Well, it sounds like [Huang] admitted to more than one inappropriate relationship, so I think he did what was appropriate given the circumstances," Morelle told Newsweek on Thursday. "It's really a wake-up call in what is a critical position he has, and obviously in terms of national security and economic security." Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer, meanwhile, made clear that Huang's resignation would not end congressional scrutiny of the matter. "Despite Jensen Huang's resignation, Congress must demand answers from Mr. Huang and others at Nvidia about how they may have put U.S. national security at risk," the New York Democrat wrote on X Thursday. Schumer also demanded answers from the Trump administration about what it knew of Huang's relationship with a suspected Chinese intelligence asset and how it responded. But the controversy extends beyond corporate leadership. The New York Times reported that U.S. intelligence officials had identified Alice Huang, a Chinese business executive with whom Huang developed a relationship, as a potential intelligence operative for Beijing, raising questions about whether foreign intelligence services sought to influence a powerful executive involved in shaping U.S. technology policy. With Democrats preparing to assume control of Congress, the scandal could also intensify scrutiny of the Trump administration's handling of intelligence warnings and its relationship with Jensen Huang. Nvidia announced Thursday that Huang had resigned as president, CEO and a member of its board, effective immediately. The company appointed longtime Chief Financial Officer Colette Kress as interim CEO and said its board had begun searching for a permanent successor. Jensen Huang's exit followed reports that he had engaged in an extramarital affair with Alice Huang (no relation), whom U.S. intelligence reportedly identified as having been recruited by China's Ministry of State Security. According to the Times , the alleged intelligence operation sought information about American AI technology and potentially aimed to influence Nvidia to advocate for greater Chinese access to advanced U.S. chips. Alice Huang is a Chinese national who served as managing director of Singapore-based Megaspeed, a company whose purchases of Nvidia chips had already drawn scrutiny from U.S. officials. Megaspeed and its affiliates purchased more than $4.8 billion worth of Nvidia technology since June 2024, according to the Times . The Times previously reported that the U.S. Commerce Department was investigating whether Megaspeed was helping China obtain restricted AI chips. The company has denied wrongdoing, saying it complies with applicable export controls and that investigations found no evidence of illegal activity. In an internal message sent to Nvidia staff, Jensen Huang acknowledged Sunday that he had been unfaithful to his wife but did not identify anyone involved. The Times subsequently reported Wednesday that he had also engaged in an affair with Kimberly Powell , Nvidia's vice president of healthcare and one of his direct reports. Reuters, citing two people familiar with the matter, reported Thursday that Huang had a third affair, this time with another Nvidia employee.. Newsweek has not independently confirmed the reporting. China has rejected the espionage allegations. Foreign Ministry spokesperson Guo Jiakun said Monday that "the so-called Chinese spy allegation is unsubstantiated" and "nothing but smears against China." Nvidia's board said Sunday it had opened an independent investigation into the matter, adding it had "no reason to believe that either national security or NVIDIA secrets were compromised." There has been no public evidence establishing that Huang knowingly acted on behalf of Chinese interests, knew of Alice Huang's alleged intelligence connections or altered his positions on U.S. export policy because of her. Trump said Monday that Huang had told him he "absolutely had no idea that the person in question was a spy,” adding that he believed him. Senator Elizabeth Warren, a Massachusetts Democrat, said Thursday that Huang's resignation did not eliminate the need for accountability. "Jensen Huang's decision to resign from NVIDIA does not absolve him, other executives, or the company as a whole of responsibility for putting our national security at risk or for any potential violations of our laws," Warren wrote on X. Senator Mark Warner of Virginia, a senior Democrat on the Senate Intelligence Committee, raised broader concerns about the influence of technology executives on American national security policy. "I think it also raises a question, where we have these companies that are so powerful, whether it's Jensen Huang or Elon Musk, that they literally are driving national security policy," Warner told Newsweek . "I think we have to question whether that is in the best systems in this country." Huang has been a prominent advocate for allowing American chipmakers to compete in China, arguing that shutting U.S. companies out of the market would strengthen Chinese competitors. His lobbying helped persuade the Trump administration to loosen some restrictions on Nvidia's sales to China. Trump subsequently announced an arrangement allowing the company to sell its H200 chips to approved Chinese customers, with the U.S. government receiving 25 percent of the proceeds. Those commercial and political relationships are now attracting fresh scrutiny as lawmakers seek to determine whether sensitive information was compromised and whether the administration responded appropriately to intelligence about Huang's relationship. Asked whether Huang should testify, the South Dakota Republican said, "I think that it would make sense because of the, again, the nature of the association and the governments and the national security interests, what we're talking about here." Huang's resignation leaves Nvidia facing two major challenges: finding a successor to the executive who co-founded the company in 1993—Trump on Thursday floated former Apple CEO Tim Cook —and navigating congressional and federal scrutiny of his reported relationship with a suspected Chinese intelligence operative. House Foreign Affairs Committee Chairman Brian Mast said Thursday that Huang had agreed to testify before Congress, with lawmakers still negotiating a date for his appearance, Bloomberg reported. Also Thursday, three Republican House committee chairs requested a closed-door interview on December 1, warning that they could issue a subpoena if Huang did not agree. The Senate Banking Committee has separately requested his testimony in early December. The company said Sunday its independent investigation will examine the available information , while Trump said Monday that the FBI was also looking into the matter. Meanwhile, Democrats' demands for answers suggest the controversy could remain a focus of congressional oversight even after Huang's departure. And with Republicans also expressing interest in hearings, the former Nvidia chief may find that leaving the company does little to end the questions surrounding his conduct, his influence over U.S. technology policy and what the Trump administration knew.

Nvidia has been one of the strongest voices in Washington lobbying against curbs on Chinese companies' access to compute that relies on US chips in data centers located outside China, US media outlet The Information reported on Monday.

Representative Bill Foster, a Democratic co-sponsor with Republican Bill Huizenga of the Chip Security Act, wrote that "it's time to get it across the finish line" in an X post Monday that shared the news that Nvidia's board of directors had launched a probe into Huang's alleged targeting by a "foreign intelligence effort".

Republican Senator Pete Ricketts on Monday cited national security concerns surrounding Nvidia's relationship with Singapore firm Megaspeed as he called for the Match Act, which he sponsored, to be passed.

AFP-Yonhap There is growing momentum to pass a slate of major new export control bills targeting China, in the wake of the Democrats' takeover of the US Congress and scrutiny over American chip giant Nvidia following CEO Jensen Huang's admission of an extramarital affair. Leading US politicians have been quick to jump on the news to put pressure on the White House and other lawmakers to approve three bills covering advanced semiconductor chips and chipmaking equipment. At the center of their demands is the inclusion of the three bills in the National Defense Authorization Act (NDAA), the annual defense authorization bill. "There are provisions currently in the Senate version of the NDAA that will restrict chip access to China that I strongly support," House Democratic leader Hakeem Jeffries told reporters at a press conference on Monday US time. "I think we're going to work hard to make sure that those provisions make it into the final version of the NDAA." Jeffries is poised to become Speaker of the House once the new Congress is sworn in on January 3. The Senate's version of the NDAA already includes all three proposed measures: the Chip Security Act, which would crack down on chip smuggling, the AI Overwatch Act, which would give Congress greater oversight over advanced chip exports, and the Match Act, which would compel US allies to stop selling chipmaking equipment to China. Sponsors of all three bills from both US parties have issued statements in recent days calling for NDAA inclusion. Republican Senator Pete Ricketts on Monday cited national security concerns surrounding Nvidia's relationship with Singapore firm Megaspeed as he called for the Match Act, which he sponsored, to be passed. Republican Senator Jim Banks and Democratic Senator Elizabeth Warren, the cosponsors of the AI Overwatch Act, also cited the Nvidia scandal in a joint statement on Monday calling for passage of their bill. "It is time for Congress to take decisive action to pass key bills like the AI Overwatch Act in the NDAA that will cut off the various pathways through which China accesses advanced chips," they said. Representative Bill Foster, a Democratic co-sponsor with Republican Bill Huizenga of the Chip Security Act, wrote that "it's time to get it across the finish line" in an X post Monday that shared the news that Nvidia's board of directors had launched a probe into Huang's alleged targeting by a "foreign intelligence effort". Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang speaks at the company-wide convention at their T17 and T18 plots in Shilin-Beitou Technology Park, Taipei, May 27. US President Donald Trump has yet to speak out in favor of the bills. However, there are now signs that the administration is moving to engage with the legislative branch on the measures. On Monday, Chairman of the House Foreign Affairs Committee Brian Mast revealed that the White House has added provisions to the AI Overwatch Act that would target Chinese access to US chips through overseas data centers. According to US media outlet Punchbowl News, administration officials have also provided technical feedback on the Match Act, though the engagement remains short of an endorsement. Beijing has repeatedly denounced the three export control bills as efforts by US lawmakers to weaponize trade and tech issues. AFP-Yonhap There is growing momentum to pass a slate of major new export control bills targeting China, in the wake of the Democrats' takeover of the US Congress and scrutiny over American chip giant Nvidia following CEO Jensen Huang's admission of an extramarital affair.

Leading US politicians have been quick to jump on the news to put pressure on the White House and other lawmakers to approve three bills covering advanced semiconductor chips and chipmaking equipment.
At the center of their demands is the inclusion of the three bills in the National Defense Authorization Act (NDAA), the annual defense authorization bill.

"There are provisions currently in the Senate version of the NDAA that will restrict chip access to China that I strongly support," House Democratic leader Hakeem Jeffries told reporters at a press conference on Monday US time.

"I think we're going to work hard to make sure that those provisions make it into the final version of the NDAA." Jeffries is poised to become Speaker of the House once the new Congress is sworn in on January 3.

The Senate's version of the NDAA already includes all three proposed measures: the Chip Security Act, which would crack down on chip smuggling, the AI Overwatch Act, which would give Congress greater oversight over advanced chip exports, and the Match Act, which would compel US allies to stop selling chipmaking equipment to China.
Sponsors of all three bills from both US parties have issued statements in recent days calling for NDAA inclusion.

Republican Senator Pete Ricketts on Monday cited national security concerns surrounding Nvidia's relationship with Singapore firm Megaspeed as he called for the Match Act, which he sponsored, to be passed.

Republican Senator Jim Banks and Democratic Senator Elizabeth Warren, the cosponsors of the AI Overwatch Act, also cited the Nvidia scandal in a joint statement on Monday calling for passage of their bill.

"It is time for Congress to take decisive action to pass key bills like the AI Overwatch Act in the NDAA that will cut off the various pathways through which China accesses advanced chips," they said.

Representative Bill Foster, a Democratic co-sponsor with Republican Bill Huizenga of the Chip Security Act, wrote that "it's time to get it across the finish line" in an X post Monday that shared the news that Nvidia's board of directors had launched a probe into Huang's alleged targeting by a "foreign intelligence effort".
Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang speaks at the company-wide convention at their T17 and T18 plots in Shilin-Beitou Technology Park, Taipei, May 27.
AFP-Yonhap Huang has long argued against strengthened chip export controls on China, citing the need for US companies to compete in the Chinese market.

Nvidia has been one of the strongest voices in Washington lobbying against curbs on Chinese companies' access to compute that relies on US chips in data centers located outside China, US media outlet The Information reported on Monday.
US President Donald Trump has yet to speak out in favor of the bills.
However, there are now signs that the administration is moving to engage with the legislative branch on the measures.

On Monday, Chairman of the House Foreign Affairs Committee Brian Mast revealed that the White House has added provisions to the AI Overwatch Act that would target Chinese access to US chips through overseas data centers.
According to US media outlet Punchbowl News, administration officials have also provided technical feedback on the Match Act, though the engagement remains short of an endorsement.
Beijing has repeatedly denounced the three export control bills as efforts by US lawmakers to weaponize trade and tech issues.
Foreign Ministry spokesman Guo Jiakun on Monday described the latest espionage allegations involving Nvidia as unfounded and intended to smear Beijing.

Elizabeth Warren (D-Mass.) called for legislation targeting "various pathways through which China accesses advanced chips."

passages: China warned the United States on Friday against putting additional export controls on semiconductors in the wake of the scandal surrounding AI chip giant Nvidia.
I’m in favour of limiting those exports,” House speaker Mike Johnson was quoted as saying.

Reports allege the Commerce Department under Secretary Howard Lutnick may have failed to act on suspicions that Megaspeed was helping reroute restricted Nvidia technology to China.

sources.title: Democrats Demand Answers Over Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang's Alleged China Spy Scandal - Newsweek
passages: The abrupt resignation of Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang on Thursday comes as Democrats prepare to take control of Congress following sweeping victories in the midterm elections last week.

Judging by their reactions to his exit, which followed revelations of multiple affairs, including one with a suspected Chinese intelligence operative, Democrats intend to pursue answers well beyond his departure from the company.
"Despite Jensen Huang's resignation, Congress must demand answers from Mr.
Huang and others at Nvidia about how they may have put U.S. national security at risk," the New York Democrat wrote on X Thursday.

"I think it also raises a question, where we have these companies that are so powerful, whether it's Jensen Huang or Elon Musk, that they literally are driving national security policy," Warner told Newsweek .
Meanwhile, Democrats' demands for answers suggest the controversy could remain a focus of congressional oversight even after Huang's departure.

The national security implications loom large, given Nvidia's central role in the global artificial intelligence industry and Huang's close relationship with President Donald Trump , whose administration has eased some restrictions on the company's sales of advanced chips to China .

There has been no public evidence establishing that Huang knowingly acted on behalf of Chinese interests, knew of Alice Huang's alleged intelligence connections or altered his positions on U.S. export policy because of her.
In an internal message sent to Nvidia staff, Jensen Huang acknowledged Sunday that he had been unfaithful to his wife but did not identify anyone involved.
Newsweek has not independently confirmed the reporting.
Nvidia announced Thursday that Huang had resigned as president, CEO and a member of its board, effective immediately.
Foreign Ministry spokesperson Guo Jiakun said Monday that "the so-called Chinese spy allegation is unsubstantiated" and "nothing but smears against China."
Commerce Department was investigating whether Megaspeed was helping China obtain restricted AI chips.
The company has denied wrongdoing, saying it complies with applicable export controls and that investigations found no evidence of illegal activity.

AFP-Yonhap There is growing momentum to pass a slate of major new export control bills targeting China, in the wake of the Democrats' takeover of the US Congress and scrutiny over American chip giant Nvidia following CEO Jensen Huang's admission of an extramarital affair. Leading US politicians have been quick to jump on the news to put pressure on the White House and other lawmakers to approve three bills covering advanced semiconductor chips and chipmaking equipment. At the center of their demands is the inclusion of the three bills in the National Defense Authorization Act (NDAA), the annual defense authorization bill. "There are provisions currently in the Senate version of the NDAA that will restrict chip access to China that I strongly support," House Democratic leader Hakeem Jeffries told reporters at a press conference on Monday US time. "I think we're going to work hard to make sure that those provisions make it into the final version of the NDAA." Jeffries is poised to become Speaker of the House once the new Congress is sworn in on January 3. The Senate's version of the NDAA already includes all three proposed measures: the Chip Security Act, which would crack down on chip smuggling, the AI Overwatch Act, which would give Congress greater oversight over advanced chip exports, and the Match Act, which would compel US allies to stop selling chipmaking equipment to China. Sponsors of all three bills from both US parties have issued statements in recent days calling for NDAA inclusion. Republican Senator Pete Ricketts on Monday cited national security concerns surrounding Nvidia's relationship with Singapore firm Megaspeed as he called for the Match Act, which he sponsored, to be passed. Republican Senator Jim Banks and Democratic Senator Elizabeth Warren, the cosponsors of the AI Overwatch Act, also cited the Nvidia scandal in a joint statement on Monday calling for passage of their bill. "It is time for Congress to take decisive action to pass key bills like the AI Overwatch Act in the NDAA that will cut off the various pathways through which China accesses advanced chips," they said. Representative Bill Foster, a Democratic co-sponsor with Republican Bill Huizenga of the Chip Security Act, wrote that "it's time to get it across the finish line" in an X post Monday that shared the news that Nvidia's board of directors had launched a probe into Huang's alleged targeting by a "foreign intelligence effort". Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang speaks at the company-wide convention at their T17 and T18 plots in Shilin-Beitou Technology Park, Taipei, May 27. AFP-Yonhap Huang has long argued against strengthened chip export controls on China, citing the need for US companies to compete in the Chinese market. Nvidia has been one of the strongest voices in Washington lobbying against curbs on Chinese companies' access to compute that relies on US chips in data centers located outside China, US media outlet The Information reported on Monday. US President Donald Trump has yet to speak out in favor of the bills. However, there are now signs that the administration is moving to engage with the legislative branch on the measures. On Monday, Chairman of the House Foreign Affairs Committee Brian Mast revealed that the White House has added provisions to the AI Overwatch Act that would target Chinese access to US chips through overseas data centers. According to US media outlet Punchbowl News, administration officials have also provided technical feedback on the Match Act, though the engagement remains short of an endorsement. Beijing has repeatedly denounced the three export control bills as efforts by US lawmakers to weaponize trade and tech issues. Foreign Ministry spokesman Guo Jiakun on Monday described the latest espionage allegations involving Nvidia as unfounded and intended to smear Beijing.

Huang, Powell and a representative of Nvidia's board did not respond to requests for comment, while Alice Huang could not be reached.
The revelation came hours after Huang resigned from the chipmaking giant he had led for 33 years, amid a scandal involving a woman suspected by U.S. intelligence of working for China.
Reuters did not identify the newly reported employee and said attempts to contact her had been unsuccessful.

Huang's departure raises questions about the future leadership of one of the world's most influential artificial intelligence companies, whose chips and investments have played a central role in the industry's expansion.
Following Huang's resignation, Nvidia appointed Chief Financial Officer Colette Kress as interim CEO while its board searches for a permanent replacement.

passages: Bitcoin price traded at USD 69,215.2 at 12:37:26 Berlin time on November 13, 2026, according to Investing.com .
The cryptocurrency was below the psychologically important USD 70,000 level after a volatile session, with the source showing a daily range of USD 67,731.2 to USD 71,485.5.
The report also cited persistent ETF outflows and said US spot Bitcoin ETFs recorded almost USD 300 million in outflows on November 11.
A recovery above that level would improve the short-term market tone, but it would not by itself establish a lasting trend reversal.
Conversely, continued ETF withdrawals or stronger-than-expected inflation data could keep liquidity and leverage under pressure.
These are market-risk considerations, not a directional trading recommendation.
Bitcoin's circulating supply was listed at 20.11 million coins against a maximum supply of 21 million.
Higher inflation has increased market expectations for a more restrictive Federal Reserve policy.
That matters for Bitcoin because higher yields and a stronger US dollar can reduce the appeal of non-yielding, risk-sensitive assets.
The Morningstar report quoted analysts who identified ETF flows and forthcoming US economic data as important factors for the next market move.
Further Bitcoin coverage is available on the Bitcoin topic page .

(NVDA), weighed on the asset. BTC prices slumped nearly 7% over the past day, falling to $68,529.96 at the time of writing. Meanwhile, Ethereum (ETH) prices slipped to $1,912.54. See what 10M+ investors are talking about. Get the Stocktwits Daily Rip for what retail is watching right now, free to your inbox According to market commentator The Kobeissi Letter, the selling pressure led to a loss of about $150 billion in crypto markets over 48 hours. Although Bitcoin is falling to its lowest level in months, some experts believe that now is a good time to enter. Crypto analyst Michaël van de Poppe said in a post on X that he has been buying BTC, outlining five reasons for his move. He noted that the "terrible sentiment" around the underlying asset means it is hard for prices to keep declining, adding that while there have been multiple events for the asset price to crash, it hasn't yet and markets are simply witnessing a 20% correction. He also pointed out that this is a support area, "just barely beneath the 200-Day MA and ideal for liquidity." The analyst said that Bitcoin had already bottomed on the Friday prior to the SpaceX IPO and that he "wouldn't be surprised" if the present scenario was at the same cadence. "Fifthly: Nasdaq is already up a lot, meaning that there's a gap between Bitcoin and the Nasdaq. It doesn't take long for this gap to close, which is why I've been buying Bitcoin today," he said. Meanwhile, Anthony Pompliano, Founder and CEO of Professional Capital Management, said in a post on X, "Bitcoin is falling to prices we haven't seen since…..3 months ago. Everyone relax, so you can realize that AI and bitcoin are one big trade now." However, long-time crypto critic Peter Schiff is not convinced. In a post on X, he implored investors to think about how Bitcoin has been trading relative to 2021. "Think about this, HOLDers. Bitcoin just traded at a lower price than it traded in November 2021. How many of you who owned Bitcoin back then expected it to be below the Nov. 2021 high more than five years later? Bitcoin is in a long-term bear market. The long-term trend is down," he argued. Rich Rosenblum, co-founder of crypto market maker GSR, told Bloomberg that the volatility in the AI trade and continued U.S. dollar strength have impacted some long Bitcoin positions negatively, while the red-hot inflation data and changes in Nvidia Corp.'s (NVDA) leadership amid Jensen Huang's resignation are also weighing on risk assets. Dean Chen, an analyst at crypto exchange Bitunix, also said in a note Thursday, as per Bloomberg, "Bitcoin is showing signs of a changing market structure, with selling pressure concentrated in derivatives while spot market activity remains comparatively resilient." Meanwhile, futures cumulative volume delta, a measure that tracks how aggressive buyers or sellers are in the futures market, has turned deeply negative, he noted, while adding that open interest has also declined. "Taken together, these indicators suggest that leveraged exposure is cooling, but market positioning remains mixed," Chen reportedly said. Crypto-linked equities fell alongside cryptocurrencies late Thursday. Strategy (MSTR), Bitmine Immersion Technologies (BMNR), Strive (ASST), Coinbase Global Inc. (COIN), and Robinhood Markets Inc. (HOOD) all saw their shares decline in the overnight trade. Strategy also faces pressure after MSCI Inc. said it would remove the company from its global indexes after the Nov. 30 rebalancing, likely prompting an exodus from passive funds. Caroline Mauron, co-founder of Orbit Markets, told Bloomberg that MSCI's decision to drop Strategy, which is the largest corporate buyer of BTC, from its global equity benchmarks has also been a factor affecting the cryptocurrency. Although Bitcoin is falling to its lowest level in months, some experts believe that now is a good time to enter.
Crypto analyst Michaël van de Poppe said in a post on X that he has been buying BTC, outlining five reasons for his move.

He noted that the "terrible sentiment" around the underlying asset means it is hard for prices to keep declining, adding that while there have been multiple events for the asset price to crash, it hasn't yet and markets are simply witnessing a 20% correction.
He also pointed out that this is a support area, "just barely beneath the 200-Day MA and ideal for liquidity."
The analyst said that Bitcoin had already bottomed on the Friday prior to the SpaceX IPO and that he "wouldn't be surprised" if the present scenario was at the same cadence.
"Fifthly: Nasdaq is already up a lot, meaning that there's a gap between Bitcoin and the Nasdaq. It doesn't take long for this gap to close, which is why I've been buying Bitcoin today," he said.
