extraction.body: The Federal Aviation Administration lifted its nationwide ground stop at 6:16 p.m. Mountain time Friday, ending a halt on departures from every U.S. airport that lasted more than four hours, and Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy blamed overloaded, aging communications equipment for the failure. "We use 1980s little copper lines. It's an old system that went down and went down everywhere. It got overloaded," Duffy told reporters at the White House, ABC News reported . "Our switches, our routers, actually got overloaded with data," he said, according to NBC News . Duffy said "all of the new equipment that we put in, none of that went down," and called for emergency funding from Congress to replace the system. "This is an emergency," he said. "I want $50 billion." Congress approved $12.5 billion for air traffic control upgrades last year. "The FAA Command Center nationwide ground stop has been cancelled," the agency said in an advisory . Recovery will be gradual. "I believe that it's going to take us some time to get back to capacity," Duffy said, adding that "hopefully tomorrow we are going to start to see far better movement." As of 7:39 p.m., 215 departures from Denver International Airport had been canceled and 336 delayed Friday, according to the flight-tracking service FlightAware . Another 183 arrivals had been canceled and 308 delayed. Nationally, FlightAware counted 6,755 cancellations of flights within, into or out of the United States. Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin said investigators had not found signs of an attack but had not ruled one out. "It appears that this was mechanically driven. However, we're still looking, so we're not going to rule that out," Mullin said, ABC News reported. Microsoft said it had no indication the ground stop was related to its own recent service disruption, and the company behind the FAA's new SMART air traffic management tool said the ground stop "is not based on or a result of the SMART system," NBC News reported. The ground stop took effect at 1:53 p.m., as the Kiowa County Press reported earlier Friday . The FAA had blamed a "temporary telecommunications outage" affecting the Air Route Traffic Control Centers, which manage high-altitude traffic between airports. Colorado is handled by the Denver center in Longmont. The first sign of trouble in FAA records came in Chicago. At 1:17 p.m., about 35 minutes before the nationwide order, the FAA halted flights headed to Chicago Midway International Airport from across the country, citing an equipment outage, according to an FAA advisory . Shortly before the nationwide order, a notice from the National Weather Service hinted at the trouble. At 1:44 p.m., the Weather Service office that serves the Boston area reported that data from the FAA's weather radar at Boston Logan International Airport had been restored, and that "Boston Center reported teleco issues actively being worked." Boston Center is the FAA facility that handles high-altitude traffic over New England, and "teleco" is shorthand for telecommunications. The notice warned that further interruptions were possible. Disruptions are expected to continue into Saturday. United Airlines, which operates a hub at Denver, said it planned to cancel most of its remaining Friday flights, with exceptions for some international flights, ABC News reported . JetBlue said it was canceling all remaining Friday flights except Europe-bound departures from New York and Boston. "We expect disruptions to continue into tomorrow, including additional cancellations," JetBlue said in a statement. After the nationwide stop ended, the FAA briefly held United flights bound for Chicago O'Hare International Airport and, at the airline's request, Alaska Airlines flights bound for Seattle and San Diego, according to FAA advisories. Some airlines are waiving change fees. United told passengers they can reschedule without change fees or fare differences on a United flight departing between November 12 and November 20, in the same cabin and between the same cities, and Delta is allowing free changes for Friday and Saturday travel, ABC News reported . Travelers should check with their airline before leaving for the airport. The FAA posts current airport conditions at nasstatus.faa.gov . While the stop was in effect, flights already in the air were allowed to land, and a limited number of flights over the ocean were cleared to leave, including Pacific-bound flights from San Francisco, flights to and from Hawaii and some transatlantic flights from Boston, according to ABC News. Nationwide ground stops are rare. The last one came in January 2023, when the failure of the FAA's Notice to Air Missions system held departures across the country for about 90 minutes. Before that, the FAA cleared the skies after the September 11, 2001, terrorist attacks. Use these section links to keep reading beyond the latest front-page stories. extraction.body: The Federal Aviation Administration said Friday night that airplane departures can resume after the agency lifted a nationwide ground stop that Trump administration officials blamed on “overloaded,” “outdated” systems. Even with the order being lifted, the airlines will not be able to return to normal operations immediately because so many of their planes and crews are out of position. The FAA had grounded all flights nationwide Friday afternoon, causing hundreds of flights to be diverted. Officials cited “extraordinary circumstances” caused by communications problems at regional air traffic control centers. Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin told reporters at the White House that the introduction of some new technology into an old air traffic control system overwhelmed it. The nationwide ground stop was the first since January 2023 , when a key FAA computer system malfunctioned, and the second since the aftermath of the Sept. 11, 2001, attacks. There was no indication the communications failure was related to a cyberattack. The consequences were profound, disrupting potentially thousands of planned flights through at least late Friday night and upending travel plans for passengers. “It’s frustrating. This certainly sounds like it’s going to be more than the usual run-of-the-mill delay. I look forward to finding out why,” said Jeff Dubner, a Washington attorney whose Alaska Airlines flight home from Los Angeles was already half an hour late and taxiing to the runway when the plane came to a halt. International flights were being handled on a case-by-case basis, according to Mullin, with some seen taking off Friday evening. The uncertainty left travelers scrambling to find alternatives. Amtrak's ticketing system appeared to be down. Several hundred users reported the outage on Down Detector Friday evening. Ticketing agents with Southwest Airlines were roaming the Terminal 1 departures hall Friday afternoon trying to answer passenger questions. But there wasn't much information to share. Christin Barber, a traveler at SAN, said her travel plans are unclear. "I'm going to go to Denver first for a couple of days because I have a funeral to attend tomorrow, And then I'm going on home to Albany, New York," Barber said. "I don't know what to do at this point." A San Diego Airport official said in a statement that "arriving flights will continue to land as space allows." Asked whether Mullin could rule out a cyberattack or rogue artificial intelligence incident, he said: “There’s nothing completely certain right now. It doesn’t appear that way.” He said there are no “footprints” showing an attack and that it appears to be “mechanically driven,” adding that officials were still looking for the cause. At least 827 flights were diverted so far as a result. As of 7:05 p.m. EST, 670 flights were sent back to the airport from where they originally took off, while 157 were redirected to a different airport, according to Cirium, an aviation analytics company. The airports where many of the flights ended up being diverted included Washington Dulles International Airport, Los Angeles International Airport, Cincinnati/Northern Kentucky International Airport and Nashville International Airport. Some 11,000 flights carrying more than 1.5 million passengers were scheduled to take off from airports in the U.S. after 4 p.m. EST, raising the likelihood of more cancelations and flight diversions. At Chicago O’Hare Airport on Friday afternoon, travelers passing through security learned about the ground stop when they looked up at screens that showed flight delays across the board. Some called friends or family members, debating whether to stay the night in Chicago or find another way to their destinations. Amber McQuilkin, 27, sat on a bench, disappointed that she might miss a trip with friends to New York for the League of Legends world finals. Her friends, she said, had already arrived there. “There’s not really any information being passed to me,” said the Seattle software engineer, who took a week of vacation for the trip. “I contemplated just abandoning the flight and driving, but then the more I thought about it, the more I’m like, that would be miserable.” Austin Curtis and his wife were rethinking their trip from South Bend, Indiana, to a friend’s baby shower in Denver after getting delayed during a layover in Chicago. NBA, NHL and college teams were left stranded as they tried to reach their destinations. Meanwhile, NFL teams were left to wonder whether the issue would be resolved in time to travel to their games this weekend. Cargo flights were also delayed by the ground stop. FedEx, the world’s largest cargo airline, said it is prepared to activate contingency plans to keep any possible disruptions at a minimum. U.S. airlines move about 61,000 tons of goods – from letters to packages -- to and from more than 220 countries daily, according to the industry trade group Airlines for America. Despite the nationwide FAA ground stop, SpaceX launched its Starship rocket from Texas on Friday afternoon on its latest test flight. Mullin had said investigators will look at whether there is any link to the FAA's nationwide rollout of a new artificial intelligence system to help identify problems and reroute planes. But that system operates out of one location near Washington, D.C., and just sends recommendations to the air traffic control centers. The government has been working to overhaul the outdated technology that air traffic controllers rely on since Congress approved $12.5 billion for the project last year. Miles of old copper wires have been replaced with fiber optic lines and old radio systems are gradually being replaced at airports across the country. But much work remains. Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy has said that another $30 billion will be needed to complete the work, and the White House has begun lobbying Congress to approve it. The problem appeared similar to a regional air traffic control communication outage in September that snarled hundreds of flights across the Northeast, aviation safety expert Steve Arroyo said, except this time on a nationwide scale. It may be linked to the outdated technology used by air traffic controllers. “If you don’t have that ability, whether it’s because the old wires that they have are just run down or for whatever reason, you’ve got to stop airplanes on the ground,” said Arroyo, who is a former United Airlines pilot. “And not put them in the air where you’re going to risk not being able to communicate with them.” Friday’s ground stop was different than the one after Sept. 11 because planes were not being told to land immediately and pilots likely were able to communicate with ground controllers at airports, Arroyo said. extraction.body: The Federal Aviation Administration lifted a nationwide ground stop Friday after more than four hours, following a communications outage that disrupted air travel across the country. Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy told reporters Friday evening that aging air traffic control equipment became overloaded with data, causing instability in radar information and communications with aircraft. The disruption prompted the FAA to halt departures nationwide out of an abundance of caution. The FAA said earlier Friday that the ground stop was issued due to “extraordinary circumstances and for reasons of safety” related to “communication issues.” Speaking at a news conference, Duffy said the problems began at 3:36 p.m. ET, when air traffic control facilities across the country experienced “instability for our radar” and communications. He attributed the disruption to aging analog telecommunications equipment, including switches and routers that became overloaded. "It's the old hardware that went down," Duffy said, adding that newer equipment installed under the Trump administration was not affected, before renewing calls for Congress to provide additional funding to modernize the nation's legacy equipment. Earlier this week, Duffy told Politico that the administration was lobbying Congress to secure $30 billion funding to upgrade air traffic control. “You will have more of them unless the American people and the Congress tell us to build, and I can’t wait for that,” Duffy said, warning of potential future ground stops. Duffy said more than 3,500 aircraft were already in the air en route to U.S. airports nationwide when Friday’s ground stop was issued. He emphasized that the FAA had not lost all radar or telecommunications capabilities and continued allowing critical flights, including medical evacuations and shipments of lifesaving medications. When the FAA issued its initial alert, the agency said international flights arriving in the U.S. would “be managed on a case-by-case basis.” The agency did not indicate how long the earlier ground stop would last, only stating that planes should not depart “until further notice.” The agency said in a statement to MS NOW earlier Friday that communication issues were “impacting multiple Air Route Traffic Control Centers” and that FAA technicians were investigating. Duffy shared the same statement on his X account. A Justice Department source told MS NOW that officials did not track any potential connection to terrorism and described the problem as a “frequency issue.” Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin insisted Friday evening that passengers were never in danger and the FAA acted out of caution. There was there was never any lives at risk,” Mullin said. We did it out of an abundance of caution." Mullin said officials had found “zero evidence" that the outage was caused by a cyberattack or rogue artificial intelligence, though he stopped short of definitively ruling out either possibility. He also assured the public that the Federal Emergency Management Agency had activated its centers to assist stranded travelers, including those who might need access to medication. He said FEMA was coordinating with airports, cities and states to address passengers' needs. Duffy cautioned that returning to normal flight operations “is going to be slow," with airlines prioritizing larger flights depending on crew availability. "It's going to take us some time to unwind what's happened this afternoon," Duffy said, adding that he expects operations to improve Saturday and return to normal ahead of Thanksgiving travel. Two people at the FAA confirmed that Friday’s earlier ground stop was only the second nationwide ground stop since the Sept. The previous nationwide ground stop was in 2023. President Donald Trump had not publicly addressed the nationwide ground stop as of shortly before 9 p.m. ET, though Duffy said the president had been in frequent contact with him and Mullin throughout the disruption. "I know he is fully engaged because he has communicated with the both of us multiple times from the point that it happened to moments before I came out," Duffy said. Jim Himes, the ranking Democrat on the House Intelligence Committee, said earlier Friday he had not been told what caused the FAA ground stop. As a member of the Gang of Eight, Himes would typically be briefed if the incident involved a national security threat. Maria Cantwell, the top Democrat on the Senate Commerce, Science and Transportation Committee, said the committee plans to review “technology issues related to how planes communicate through primary frequencies, backup frequencies and other issues.” At Denver International Airport, where journalists and Democrats were departing Friday afternoon after attending a conference on the party’s future, Gov. Jason Crow, D-Colo., told MS NOW they were still learning details about the ground stop. Cory Booker, D-N.J., described the situation as a “significant breach or breakdown.” “Whether this is a breach or a breakdown, either one is unacceptable,” Booker said. “We need to learn from this, fix it and prevent it from ever happening again.” Several airports issued announcements Friday afternoon advising travelers that departing flights were being held and urging them to consult with their airlines for travel plans. Both American Airlines and Delta said flights already in the air would continue to their destinations. A traveler at Jacksonville International Airport in Florida who was scheduled to fly to Atlanta told MS NOW that their pilot said their departure would be delayed by at least seven hours. An MS NOW video editor reported that American Airlines representatives at Newark Liberty International Airport told passengers they would not have updates for seven hours. Another passenger at Los Angeles International Airport who boarded a flight for San Jose told MS NOW the pilot announced around 1:15. p.m. local time that the flight would be delayed by about 90 minutes. According to FlightAware, a flight tracking website, there were more than 9,500 delays as of about 9:25 p.m.

sources.title: FBI probes whether a software update caused the FAA ground stop - Startup Fortune
passages: Bloomberg reported that the FBI doesn't believe the outage was a cyberattack or criminal act, and that one line of inquiry is whether a software update caused it.
An update is a far more ordinary explanation than a hack, and in some ways a more uncomfortable one, because it means a national system can be taken down by its own maintenance.

The FAA then ordered a nationwide ground stop, telling airlines that "all departing traffic should remain groundstopped until further notice" and citing "extraordinary circumstances and reasons of safety." Planes already in the air were allowed to land, and international arrivals were handled case by case.
Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy said the fault hit every one of the FAA's en route air traffic control centers, and CBS News counted about 8,000 delays and 400 cancellations within hours.
Investigators haven't named the update, its author or a restart time.

passages: Microsoft outage: The tech giant is still working on its servers to restore the services after a massive outage hit Outlook, Teams, Copilot and several Microsoft 365 applications across multiple regions.
The disruptions started in the early hours of November 13 leaving users in several countries struggling to access emails, join meetings and use Microsoft's cloud-based productivity tools.
The Microsoft outage has affected many services.

Outlook and Exchange Online have experienced some of the most significant problems, with users reporting difficulties accessing inboxes, sending emails and connecting through desktop, web and mobile applications.
Users and IT administrators can check the Microsoft 365 Service Health dashboard for updates.
Now with many services experiencing massive downtime, there are also concerns about the possible cyberattack.
However, Microsoft has clarified that the disruption is not related to a cybersecurity incident.
There is also no indication of a hacking attack, and no cybercriminal group has claimed responsibility at the moment.

Some servers unexpectedly became unavailable after failing automated health checks reducing the infrastructure available to handle incoming requests.
The initial attempts to restore services have not gone entirely as planned.
Microsoft said some servers brought back online became unresponsive again when user traffic returned.
This has forced its engineering teams to restore capacity gradually while redistributing network traffic and investigating alternative recovery measures.
Microsoft has not provided a confirmed timeline for the complete restoration of its services.

But while Meta (META.O) has consistently showed strong ad revenues – a move that “easily justifies” its investments according to Evercore analyst Mark Mahaney – Microsoft’s key cloud business Azure has been slowing down.

Microsoft “did not recommit to (its Azure second-half outlook) the same way that it did 90 days ago.
“Meta’s ability to use AI to sustainably drive both engagement and pricing growth is a rarity in its (and the industry’s) history,” MoffettNathanson analysts said.
Microsoft was on track to erase about $182 billion off its market cap.

The chief executives of both the companies defended their heavy investments on artificial intelligence on Wednesday, days after Chinese upstart DeepSeek unveiled a breakthrough in cheap AI that shook the technology industry. But while Meta (META.O) has consistently showed strong ad revenues – a move that “easily justifies” its investments according to Evercore analyst Mark Mahaney – Microsoft’s key cloud business Azure has been slowing down. The Windows maker missed market estimates for quarterly revenue growth at Azure and gave a third-quarter forecast for the business that was below expectations, even after it promised a rebound for the unit in the second half of its fiscal year. “The second-half re-acceleration story for Azure is not playing out,” Barclays analyst Raimo Lenschow said. “The company overly focused on AI workloads at the expense of core Azure. It will take time to fix this, which means the Azure growth acceleration the market had been hoping for has to wait for a little longer.” For Facebook-parent Meta, a better-than-expected 21 per cent jump in revenue helped ease investor fears around Zuckerberg’s plans to spend as much as $65 billion this year on AI, even as its first-quarter forecast was muted. And Meta might have more benefits to show from AI than anyone,” Rosenblatt analyst Barton Crockett wrote. At least 15 brokerages raised their price targets on Meta, which has a 12-month forward price-to-earnings ratio of about 26.22. The company looked set to add more than $80 billion to its market value on Thursday. “Meta’s ability to use AI to sustainably drive both engagement and pricing growth is a rarity in its (and the industry’s) history,” MoffettNathanson analysts said. extraction.body: A romantic relationship between a CEO and a vice president who reports directly to him could create a serious conflict of interest. When that relationship is allegedly undisclosed and the executive holds authority over the subordinate's career, compensation, and responsibilities, it becomes a governance problem , not a personal one. The New York Times, citing five people who worked at Nvidia and spoke anonymously, reported that Jensen Huang allegedly had an extramarital relationship with Kimberly Powell, Nvidia's vice president of health care, who reportedly reports to him. Both Huang and Powell are married to other people, according to the Times. Two of the five anonymous sources told the Times that Huang and Powell were captured on video appearing affectionate at a San Jose hotel during Nvidia's GTC developer conference in March. The Times stated it had not viewed the video, and its existence should not be treated as established. The responses from all three parties were notable mostly for what they were not. Nvidia declined to comment to the Times. Powell did not respond to a request for comment. When the Times reached Huang directly, he said "I don't think you should be talking to me directly" and ended the call. Huang did not expressly deny the allegation in that exchange. This allegation is distinct from the separate matter in which Huang acknowledged being unfaithful to his wife in a message to Nvidia employees, according to the BBC. That admission concerned a different alleged relationship, with Alice Huang. U.S. officials reportedly assessed Alice Huang to be a Chinese intelligence asset , an assessment China has denied. Nvidia's board retained Wachtell, Lipton, Rosen and Katz to conduct an independent investigation into that matter, according to CNBC. Whether the scope of that investigation covers the Powell allegation is not public. Nvidia's own code of conduct, as characterized in Times reporting, instructs employees to avoid situations that create conflicts of interest, including those involving personal relationships, and states that the company investigates misconduct reports promptly. A reporting relationship between a CEO and a vice president is exactly what those rules exist to prevent. The available evidence does not confirm whether Nvidia's policies include explicit provisions for the chief executive, but the conflict-of-interest framework applies broadly to the company's workforce. The allegation and the footage described by anonymous sources both remain without independent confirmation. Whether the alleged relationship affected Powell's career trajectory, pay, or responsibilities at Nvidia has not been publicly confirmed. Powell joined Nvidia in 2008 and advanced to vice president of government health care after earlier roles in AI business development . No reporting establishes a connection between that progression and the alleged relationship. Nvidia shares fell more than 3% in after-hours trading after the Times published its report, according to CNBC, though that decline likely reflects the cumulative weight of multiple ongoing concerns. The more consequential question is not on a stock ticker. Five people inside Nvidia allegedly knew enough about a reported relationship between the CEO and a direct report to speak with a reporter. Whether any internal process addressed that situation before a law firm was retained for a separate investigation is not established by the available reporting. Nvidia's board faces a governance structure that was not built to scrutinize the person who built the company, and that gap is exactly what an independent review should now examine.

extraction.body: A romantic relationship between a CEO and a vice president who reports directly to him could create a serious conflict of interest. When that relationship is allegedly undisclosed and the executive holds authority over the subordinate's career, compensation, and responsibilities, it becomes a governance problem , not a personal one. The New York Times, citing five people who worked at Nvidia and spoke anonymously, reported that Jensen Huang allegedly had an extramarital relationship with Kimberly Powell, Nvidia's vice president of health care, who reportedly reports to him. Both Huang and Powell are married to other people, according to the Times. Two of the five anonymous sources told the Times that Huang and Powell were captured on video appearing affectionate at a San Jose hotel during Nvidia's GTC developer conference in March. The Times stated it had not viewed the video, and its existence should not be treated as established. The responses from all three parties were notable mostly for what they were not. Nvidia declined to comment to the Times. Powell did not respond to a request for comment. When the Times reached Huang directly, he said "I don't think you should be talking to me directly" and ended the call. Huang did not expressly deny the allegation in that exchange. This allegation is distinct from the separate matter in which Huang acknowledged being unfaithful to his wife in a message to Nvidia employees, according to the BBC. That admission concerned a different alleged relationship, with Alice Huang. U.S. officials reportedly assessed Alice Huang to be a Chinese intelligence asset , an assessment China has denied. Nvidia's board retained Wachtell, Lipton, Rosen and Katz to conduct an independent investigation into that matter, according to CNBC. Whether the scope of that investigation covers the Powell allegation is not public. Nvidia's own code of conduct, as characterized in Times reporting, instructs employees to avoid situations that create conflicts of interest, including those involving personal relationships, and states that the company investigates misconduct reports promptly. A reporting relationship between a CEO and a vice president is exactly what those rules exist to prevent. The available evidence does not confirm whether Nvidia's policies include explicit provisions for the chief executive, but the conflict-of-interest framework applies broadly to the company's workforce. The allegation and the footage described by anonymous sources both remain without independent confirmation. Whether the alleged relationship affected Powell's career trajectory, pay, or responsibilities at Nvidia has not been publicly confirmed. Powell joined Nvidia in 2008 and advanced to vice president of government health care after earlier roles in AI business development . No reporting establishes a connection between that progression and the alleged relationship. Nvidia shares fell more than 3% in after-hours trading after the Times published its report, according to CNBC, though that decline likely reflects the cumulative weight of multiple ongoing concerns. The more consequential question is not on a stock ticker. Five people inside Nvidia allegedly knew enough about a reported relationship between the CEO and a direct report to speak with a reporter. Whether any internal process addressed that situation before a law firm was retained for a separate investigation is not established by the available reporting. Nvidia's board faces a governance structure that was not built to scrutinize the person who built the company, and that gap is exactly what an independent review should now examine.

And because of that, we shut the system down,” he added. Earlier Friday, Duffy said in a social media post that the stoppage was due to “a communication issue impacting all Air Route Traffic Control Centers” and that the FAA’s technicians are looking into the matter. A notice from the FAA said the ground stop was being imposed “due to extraordinary circumstances and for reasons of safety”. Duffy said that more than 3,500 airplanes were in the air when the ground stop was issued. Mullin said in a news conference that preliminary investigations into the stoppage did not indicate that it was tied to a “nefarious attack”. “There’s no indication as of yet that this was a nefarious attack against it. It’s just a telecommunications outage as of right now,” he told reporters. As news of the airspace reopening trickled down to airline passengers, not all greeted the news with joy. A woman at John F Kennedy airport in New York who gave her name as simply Lola said she was frustrated. She had already rebooked her flight to Atlanta for another day and was going home. “I don’t like it,” she said. Amid the earlier confusion at US airports, the California governor, Gavin Newsom, called the Trump administration to offer more clarity to passengers who are trying to get to their destinations. “Americans are stuck at airports across the country. They deserve answers, clear updates, and a plan to get home safely. Instead, the Trump Administration is correcting reporters on AI’s “preferred name”. These are not serious people,” Newsom wrote in a post on X, in reference to Mullin correcting a reporter’s use of the term AI earlier in the day. In an interview on CNN, US congressman Ro Khanna said that he is waiting to be briefed on what exactly led to the technical issues and sparked the ground stoppage and for more public-facing communications from the transportation secretary. “There’s a lot of nervousness,” Khanna said of the feeling among passengers. “We’re waiting to be briefed in Congress about what, exactly, has happened. We just need communication from them. If they were there every hour briefing the American public, it would help and give us a sense of a timeline.” According to CNN, the FAA told airlines that the outages are the result of router malfunctions that are believed to have originated at Chicago Midway international airport and rippled across the rest of the US. Amid the uncertainty, San Francisco international airport announced in a social media post that flights bound for Hawaii and Asia were cleared to depart. John F Kennedy airport posted on its social media that travelers should confirm flight status with the airline before heading to the airport. British Airways cancelled a flight to New York that had been due to take off from Heathrow at 10.30pm on Friday night, and a spokesperson for Manchester airport confirmed three US-bound flights scheduled to leave on Saturday morning – all operated by Virgin Atlantic – were likely to be affected if the issue was not resolved soon. A ground-stop order by the FAA requires that aircraft remain on the ground and bars them from taking off. Planes already in the air are usually allowed to remain in the air. This is the third time all departing flights have been grounded in the US. The first time was on 9/11; the other was in January 2023, when the FAA paused all ⁠domestic departures for less than two hours after a pilot notification system malfunctioned. The FAA has more than 14,000 air traffic controllers who handle the more than 44,000 flights that take off from airports across the US each day, according to FAA data. Last week, the FAA announced that the first digital air traffic control towers in the US were officially operational in Alaska and Florida, as part of a modernization project intended to reduce flight delays and improve the flow of air traffic. Last year, ​Congress ​approved $12.5bn to fix ​the FAA’s ageing communications system, and ​on Friday ‌the FAA ​and ​White House asked Congress for another $30.1bn to address other issues.

Open-weight artificial intelligence could lose one of its most influential supporters following the board-led ouster of Nvidia co-founder Jensen Huang, potentially changing the direction of an industry in which the chipmaker has championed alternatives to closed AI systems. The push for openly available AI model weights is one of several efforts Huang helped organize that could suffer after his resignation following his admission of an extramarital affair, TechCrunch argued . Nvidia makes open-weight models available alongside open-source tools for AI agents and security. These models give businesses more choices and can help reduce costs. In July, Huang coordinated a letter in favor of open-weight models that attracted hundreds of signatures. The effort followed reported lobbying by Anthropic and OpenAI for restrictions on Chinese open-weight models. TechCrunch identified Microsoft CEO Satya Nadella as another prominent supporter, though the outlet observed that Nadella hasn't organized the industry around the issue as visibly as Huang. Beyond supporting open-weight models, Huang helped finance the infrastructure needed to power AI. According to Bloomberg reporting cited in the analysis, Nvidia had committed to $750 billion in deals by July in which its investments helped companies expand and purchase its chips. That expansion has consequences for the energy grid: Data centers need electricity to run processors and cooling equipment. While AI can help optimize clean energy systems, the infrastructure behind it also consumes substantial amounts of electricity and water. Forbes reported that nearly half of the year's approximately $80 billion in data center bond offerings carried high-risk "junk" ratings, TechCrunch noted. Nvidia also agreed in August to guarantee $105 billion in funding for an OpenAI facility in Ohio, CNBC reported . Alongside its infrastructure investments, Nvidia has pursued technical approaches to AI safety. Its Open Agent Safety Platform attracted more than 100 participating companies, creating a largely open-source effort to address misbehaving AI agents. The initiative followed incidents involving OpenAI and Anthropic agents accessing others' networks or engaging in other misconduct. Huang advocated industry-led safety measures. TechCrunch posited that his departure weakens that approach by removing its most visible champion. Another initiative looks to move some AI work onto personal computers. Huang recruited PC manufacturers to develop high-end systems designed to run agents locally, targeting creators, developers, and other users already familiar with the technology. Those machines are scheduled to debut for the 2026 holiday shopping season. Nvidia's planned $12.9 billion acquisition of Hugging Face, a major hosting platform for open-weight models, is scheduled to close in the first half of 2027, subject to regulatory approval. Huang's push for open-weight AI touches on questions about safety, energy use, and access to computing hardware. • Trump called AI danger talk a "hoax" during a phone call to Huang. • Huang said AI must cause "pain and suffering" before helping the climate. • Anthropic's Dario Amodei urged an AI slowdown and outside access to check model safety practices. • OpenAI's Sam Altman said the upsides justify some AI misuse , diverging from Anthropic. extraction.body: Michael Dell described Jensen Huang as a "visionary of the AI age." Deutsche Telekom CEO Tim Höttges said a photo with the Nvidia CEO produced more media coverage for his company than its iPhone launch. During the keynote of his annual Dreamforce conference, Salesforce's Marc Benioff said, "Jensen, we're all following you, bro," as the two paced through the audience. Follow CNBC's live coverage of Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang's resignation His fame extended way beyond tech. In May, Huang joined President Donald Trump on Air Force One for a trip to China to meet with President Xi Jinping . Three months later, Huang gathered six of the biggest names at the Nasdaq to announce on CNBC a proposed $500 billion artificial intelligence buildout plan, cementing his central role at the intersection of Wall Street and Silicon Valley. As Nvidia became the first company to rip past a $5 trillion market cap, bending the laws of physics with its advanced graphics processing units and pushing the AI boom to seemingly endless bounds, the now 63-year-old Huang, clad in a black leather jacket, traversed the globe as the face of the brand powering the next industrial revolution. Over the past week it all came crashing down. Following two reported extramarital affairs — one with an alleged Chinese spy and another with an employee — Huang is leaving the company he co-founded 33 years ago in crisis, and thrusting the AI market into chaos. The board is now left to pick a successor for a company that's been run by a singular figure with no second-in-command. Chief Financial Officer Colette Kress has been named interim CEO. Harvey Jones has been appointed chairman. Nvidia has not responded to multiple requests for comment. "How companies handle a crisis determines their future," former Cisco CEO John Chambers, now a startup investor, told CNBC's " Fast Money " on Wednesday. "How they handle this will determine if they're a great company and a great leadership team beyond one person." It had been a tumultuous stretch for Nvidia, even before the Huang saga led the board to launch an investigation of the CEO's behavior and the potential national security implications. The stock is on pace for its sixth straight weekly drop, which would be the longest losing streak since 2012. That includes a 9% slump last week after the midterm elections resulted in sweeping Democratic victories in both chambers of Congress, and the passage of dozens of ballot measures that could slow the buildout of new data centers. Nvidia is scheduled to report quarterly results on Tuesday, and expectations remain high, with analysts projecting 92% year-over-year revenue growth to $109.2 billion, according to LSEG. That's up 18-fold from the same quarter in 2022, just before OpenAI launched ChatGPT and kicked off the generative AI era. It's a historic level of growth for any business, and particularly notable for a company that spent most of its first few decades as a niche technology provider for video games. Huang founded Nvidia to make chips for computer graphics, both for video games and rendering. In the early 2000s, he and other executives saw an opportunity to put GPUs to work for computationally intense projects. That technology eventually turned Nvidia into the most important player in AI and a key American asset for national defense. In the process, Huang became the ultimate decider, choosing how, when and where GPUs get allocated. The biggest buyers were the hyperscalers — Amazon, Google , Meta and Microsoft — which needed the chips to build their own AI services and make them available to cloud customers. OpenAI , meanwhile, was snapping up GPUs for its powerful models and consumer apps. Oracle gobbled up billions of dollars worth of GPUs, going heavily into debt in the process. Elon Musk's xAI, now part of SpaceX , did the same to build its Grok model, before eventually starting to rent out excess capacity to Anthropic and Google. Huang wanted the world standardizing on Nvidia. Last year he demanded that Oracle buy additional Nvidia networking hardware if it wanted allocation to its state-of-the-art Grace Blackwell chips, said two people familiar with the deal who asked not to be named because the negotiations were private. In August, Nvidia said it will provide up to $105 billion in financing for an OpenAI data center in Ohio that could be the largest of its kind in the world. "He created the product that started the industry," said Chris Miglino, CEO of neocloud Axe Compute . " Without his leadership we may be many years behind where we are today with AI chip technology, which is the driving force behind the neocloud market." When it comes to investing cash in fledgling startups, Huang is known to host entrepreneurs at Nvidia's Silicon Valley headquarters. While there could be 30 Nvidia employees in the room for the pitch meeting, only Huang asks questions, according to people with knowledge of the matter, who requested anonymity because they're not authorized to speak publicly about it. One source told CNBC that key aspects of project finance are so reliant on Huang's sign-off that, when he travels, those involved in the deal are forced to wait for his plane to land before learning if they can go forward or if terms have to be renegotiated. Huang's ambitions extended well beyond the U.S. He wanted to be a force in China, which became a difficult market for Nvidia during the Biden administration and was virtually off-limits after Trump implemented strict export controls in his second term. Huang's aggressive pursuit of China may have been his undoing. The woman, with whom the Nvidia CEO had a romantic affair, was identified by U.S. intelligence as having been recruited by China's Ministry of State Security to gather information on Huang, according to people briefed on the intelligence cited by The New York Times. She has business ties to Megaspeed International, a Singapore-based cloud computing firm and an Nvidia customer that's facing scrutiny over suspicions that it facilitated billions of dollars of restricted Nvidia chips to China. U.S. lawmakers are up in arms, with many demanding investigations as well as Huang's resignation. Senate Banking Committee member Kevin Cramer , R-N.D., vocalized his concerns on Wednesday. "What bothers me at the end of it is what we don't know is what she knows about him that can be utilized," Cramer told CNBC, right before Huang resigned and referring to the affair. "This is a guy that's right now so vulnerable to extortion, blackmail. I just don't think, as a national security matter, we can run the risk." sources.title: Jensen Huang’s exit puts Nvidia’s support for open source in question
passages: Without Huang, the concern among open source community members is that whoever takes over will be more cautious.
Nvidia has named CFO Colette Kress as interim CEO.
It’s not clear how Kress will approach the Hugging Face deal or support for the open model ecosystem, but founder-driven priorities tend to get a downgrade when leadership changes.
Huang’s departure also comes as Nvidia has yet to finalize a deal to acquire open source platform Hugging Face for $13 billion .
Still, supporting open source isn’t simply a passion project Huang pursued out of idealism.
It’s increasingly central to Nvidia’s business strategy.
Huang has been a staunch supporter of open source AI, framing the ecosystem as good for safety, innovation, diffusion, and sovereignty.
Huang’s influence extended beyond Nvidia’s investments and product roadmap.
He also emerged as one of the most prominent voices pushing back against Washington’s efforts to restrict the open AI ecosystem.

Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang resigned Thursday after he admitted to an affair with an alleged Chinese spy, raising concerns about U.S. national security and the motives behind the executive’s support for softer chip export controls on China.
Nvidia also agreed to pay $6 billion for a non-exclusive license for open AI coding startup Poolside’s technology.
The question now is whether that commitment can survive without the man who made it a priority.

Within Nvidia, Huang pushed for the development of the Nemotron family of open-weight AI models built for long-running agentic AI systems and reasoning workloads — potential competitors to closed frontier models.

Huang also backed companies that would make American open models more competitive, investing in startups like Reflection AI and Thinking Machines Lab.
TechCrunch has reached out to Nvidia for comment.

extraction.body: The open source community just lost one of its strongest advocates. Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang resigned Thursday after he admitted to an affair with an alleged Chinese spy, raising concerns about U.S. national security and the motives behind the executive’s support for softer chip export controls on China. Huang has been a staunch supporter of open source AI, framing the ecosystem as good for safety, innovation, diffusion, and sovereignty. And as frontier AI labs increasingly move to reduce their reliance on Nvidia and build their own chips, supporting open source is also a good way for the company to diversify its customer base by selling chips to nation-states, enterprises, and any organization that wants to own its own models. Still, Huang’s resignation raises questions about whether Nvidia will carry on his legacy by continuing to support the open model community. Jensen no longer being CEO would be very very bad for the open model cause in the US. Huang’s departure also comes as Nvidia has yet to finalize a deal to acquire open source platform Hugging Face for $13 billion . Hugging Face CEO Clem Delangue said in a post on X that the company would continue to fight for open source , whatever happens next. Nvidia also agreed to pay $6 billion for a non-exclusive license for open AI coding startup Poolside’s technology. Within Nvidia, Huang pushed for the development of the Nemotron family of open-weight AI models built for long-running agentic AI systems and reasoning workloads — potential competitors to closed frontier models. One company insider told TechCrunch that they don’t expect a change in leadership to have an impact on Nemotron development. Huang also backed companies that would make American open models more competitive, investing in startups like Reflection AI and Thinking Machines Lab. Huang’s influence extended beyond Nvidia’s investments and product roadmap. He also emerged as one of the most prominent voices pushing back against Washington’s efforts to restrict the open AI ecosystem. Earlier this year, Huang wrote an open letter signed by 25 companies, including Microsoft, Meta, IBM, and Palantir, urging the U.S. government not to over-restrict open-weight AI models, many of which come from China. The impetus for that letter was Washington’s debate over how the U.S. should respond to allegations that Chinese AI labs are stealing intellectual property from American counterparts like Anthropic and OpenAI, both of which have reportedly appealed directly to Washington on the matter, urging stronger protections. That combination of Huang’s personal visibility and Nvidia’s market power made him the strongest counterweight to arguments from closed-model providers like Anthropic and OpenAI, which have advocated for greater restrictions on advanced AI models due to safety reasons. Without Huang, the concern among open source community members is that whoever takes over will be more cautious. Nvidia has named CFO Colette Kress as interim CEO. It’s not clear how Kress will approach the Hugging Face deal or support for the open model ecosystem, but founder-driven priorities tend to get a downgrade when leadership changes. Huang’s exit could also strengthen the arguments of those in Washington who are arguing for tougher restrictions on Chinese AI companies, particularly as the scandal surrounding his relationship with Alice Huang, the Megaspeed executive and alleged spy, puts renewed scrutiny on his efforts to loosen chip export controls. Restrictions on open-weight models from China could kneecap competition for American companies, the most powerful of which have kept their models closed. Still, supporting open source isn’t simply a passion project Huang pursued out of idealism. It’s increasingly central to Nvidia’s business strategy. As some of Nvidia’s biggest customers, including Google and OpenAI, develop their own chips, Nvidia has an incentive to cultivate a much broader ecosystem of AI developers and customers. More players training, fine-tuning, and running models mean more GPUs sold, and less dependence on a handful of frontier labs. Huang may be gone, but Nvidia still needs an open AI ecosystem. The question now is whether that commitment can survive without the man who made it a priority. TechCrunch has reached out to Nvidia for comment. This article has been updated with information from an Nvidia employee. extraction.body: Nvidia’s former chief executive Jensen Huang (젠슨 황) has stepped down following a board decision, raising expectations that a significant vacuum could emerge across the AI industry.On Tuesday, tech media outlet TechCrunch said the matter goes beyond a simple management scandal and could shake Nvidia’s role in driving AI policy and coordinating the industry.The key point is that Huang has served as a leading external channel for the AI industry, beyond his role as Nvidia CEO. Nvidia has pushed multiple agendas at once, including open-weight models, safety for AI agents, AI PCs and data centre investment structures, rather than acting only as a semiconductor supplier. Huang’s exit is seen as removing the central axis that connected and drove these agendas at the same time.First, some have raised the possibility that momentum behind open-weight models could weaken. Huang is seen as one of the most active advocates for the need for open-weight models in discussions with the tech industry and policymakers. Nvidia has provided not only its own models but also open-source technology tied to agents and AI security, and it has already agreed to acquire Hugging Face for $12.9 billion. The deal is expected to close in the first half of next year, subject to regulatory approval.After reports in July that Anthropic and OpenAI had asked the Trump administration to ban Chinese open-weight models, Huang organised an industry-wide letter of support. He advanced the argument that open-weight models give companies choice and lower costs. But a key variable is that there may be no clear figure to lead this push in an organised way at the industry level going forward.Debates on regulating AI agents could also be affected. Huang has publicly argued several times this year that, while security incidents involving AI agents have been revealed, the industry does not yet need regulation and safety issues can be solved through technology. He rallied the industry again as it was reviewing whether it needed an audit framework or a supervisory body similar to financial industry regulators. Nvidia brought together more than 100 companies to launch an Open Agent Safety Platform. The open-source-based project set out the goal of reducing problems involving agents that go out of control.The industry’s view of AI could also change. Huang has defined AI as an engineering system that produces products and stressed it can be controlled like other engineering systems. That contrasts with a trend among some large AI labs to highlight model autonomy or the possibility of consciousness. TechCrunch said Huang’s exit would, for the time being, weaken the voice representing that opposing view.Nvidia’s strategy in the AI PC market is also being put to the test. Huang recently persuaded several PC manufacturers to join Nvidia’s CPU strategy. He has also prepared a premium line of AI PCs that run AI agents on the device itself. The new products are due for release ahead of the year-end shopping season.The issue is that Huang’s personal symbolism has played an important role in product marketing. TechCrunch said Huang was no longer a suitable figure to promote these devices as an alternative to the Mac mini. It said Huang’s exit introduced a variable into efforts to build awareness for the new products and into strategies to expand the market.Confidence in AI data centre investment and financing structures could also be shaken. As a data centre construction boom continued, Huang directly designed large-scale financial structures centred on Nvidia. Critics have also raised claims that Nvidia approved circular transactions in which it supports customer expansion through equity investment and those customers then buy Nvidia chips. Citing a Bloomberg report, the outlet said the company had committed about $750 billion in such transactions through July.In August, Nvidia decided to provide support akin to loss compensation for $105 billion in funding for an OpenAI data centre in Ohio, and in the same month major private equity firms and financial companies including Apollo, BlackRock, Blackstone, Brookfield, Goldman Sachs and KKR decided to invest up to $500 billion in data centre construction. Huang has promised that Nvidia GPUs can serve as collateral that guarantees value preservation, presenting Nvidia as “investable infrastructure”.The issue is that Huang’s exit could affect confidence in these financing ideas themselves. Wall Street is already worried about the possibility of a sharp drop in Nvidia’s share price and the fallout, while fatigue over AI infrastructure investment has also grown. TechCrunch wrote, “Nvidia has ultimately lost its top salesman, and the AI industry has lost its strongest ‘hype man’.”After Huang’s exit, Nvidia now faces the task of building new leadership beyond a founder-centric management system. External variables also remain, including the possibility of additional political investigations. Whether Nvidia can replace Huang’s personal influence and maintain leadership of the AI industry has emerged as a key point to watch for the industry.

passages: Without Huang, the concern among open source community members is that whoever takes over will be more cautious.
Nvidia has named CFO Colette Kress as interim CEO.
It’s not clear how Kress will approach the Hugging Face deal or support for the open model ecosystem, but founder-driven priorities tend to get a downgrade when leadership changes.
Huang’s departure also comes as Nvidia has yet to finalize a deal to acquire open source platform Hugging Face for $13 billion .
Still, supporting open source isn’t simply a passion project Huang pursued out of idealism.
It’s increasingly central to Nvidia’s business strategy.
Huang has been a staunch supporter of open source AI, framing the ecosystem as good for safety, innovation, diffusion, and sovereignty.
Huang’s influence extended beyond Nvidia’s investments and product roadmap.
He also emerged as one of the most prominent voices pushing back against Washington’s efforts to restrict the open AI ecosystem.

Nvidia also agreed to pay $6 billion for a non-exclusive license for open AI coding startup Poolside’s technology.
The question now is whether that commitment can survive without the man who made it a priority.

extraction.body: The open source community just lost one of its strongest advocates. Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang resigned Thursday after he admitted to an affair with an alleged Chinese spy, raising concerns about U.S. national security and the motives behind the executive’s support for softer chip export controls on China. Huang has been a staunch supporter of open source AI, framing the ecosystem as good for safety, innovation, diffusion, and sovereignty. And as frontier AI labs increasingly move to reduce their reliance on Nvidia and build their own chips, supporting open source is also a good way for the company to diversify its customer base by selling chips to nation-states, enterprises, and any organization that wants to own its own models. Still, Huang’s resignation raises questions about whether Nvidia will carry on his legacy by continuing to support the open model community. Jensen no longer being CEO would be very very bad for the open model cause in the US. Huang’s departure also comes as Nvidia has yet to finalize a deal to acquire open source platform Hugging Face for $13 billion . Hugging Face CEO Clem Delangue said in a post on X that the company would continue to fight for open source , whatever happens next. Nvidia also agreed to pay $6 billion for a non-exclusive license for open AI coding startup Poolside’s technology. Within Nvidia, Huang pushed for the development of the Nemotron family of open-weight AI models built for long-running agentic AI systems and reasoning workloads — potential competitors to closed frontier models. One company insider told TechCrunch that they don’t expect a change in leadership to have an impact on Nemotron development. Huang also backed companies that would make American open models more competitive, investing in startups like Reflection AI and Thinking Machines Lab. Huang’s influence extended beyond Nvidia’s investments and product roadmap. He also emerged as one of the most prominent voices pushing back against Washington’s efforts to restrict the open AI ecosystem. Earlier this year, Huang wrote an open letter signed by 25 companies, including Microsoft, Meta, IBM, and Palantir, urging the U.S. government not to over-restrict open-weight AI models, many of which come from China. The impetus for that letter was Washington’s debate over how the U.S. should respond to allegations that Chinese AI labs are stealing intellectual property from American counterparts like Anthropic and OpenAI, both of which have reportedly appealed directly to Washington on the matter, urging stronger protections. That combination of Huang’s personal visibility and Nvidia’s market power made him the strongest counterweight to arguments from closed-model providers like Anthropic and OpenAI, which have advocated for greater restrictions on advanced AI models due to safety reasons. Without Huang, the concern among open source community members is that whoever takes over will be more cautious. Nvidia has named CFO Colette Kress as interim CEO. It’s not clear how Kress will approach the Hugging Face deal or support for the open model ecosystem, but founder-driven priorities tend to get a downgrade when leadership changes. Huang’s exit could also strengthen the arguments of those in Washington who are arguing for tougher restrictions on Chinese AI companies, particularly as the scandal surrounding his relationship with Alice Huang, the Megaspeed executive and alleged spy, puts renewed scrutiny on his efforts to loosen chip export controls. Restrictions on open-weight models from China could kneecap competition for American companies, the most powerful of which have kept their models closed. Still, supporting open source isn’t simply a passion project Huang pursued out of idealism. It’s increasingly central to Nvidia’s business strategy. As some of Nvidia’s biggest customers, including Google and OpenAI, develop their own chips, Nvidia has an incentive to cultivate a much broader ecosystem of AI developers and customers. More players training, fine-tuning, and running models mean more GPUs sold, and less dependence on a handful of frontier labs. Huang may be gone, but Nvidia still needs an open AI ecosystem. The question now is whether that commitment can survive without the man who made it a priority. TechCrunch has reached out to Nvidia for comment. extraction.body: Nvidia’s former chief executive Jensen Huang (젠슨 황) has stepped down following a board decision, raising expectations that a significant vacuum could emerge across the AI industry.On Tuesday, tech media outlet TechCrunch said the matter goes beyond a simple management scandal and could shake Nvidia’s role in driving AI policy and coordinating the industry.The key point is that Huang has served as a leading external channel for the AI industry, beyond his role as Nvidia CEO. Nvidia has pushed multiple agendas at once, including open-weight models, safety for AI agents, AI PCs and data centre investment structures, rather than acting only as a semiconductor supplier. Huang’s exit is seen as removing the central axis that connected and drove these agendas at the same time.First, some have raised the possibility that momentum behind open-weight models could weaken. Huang is seen as one of the most active advocates for the need for open-weight models in discussions with the tech industry and policymakers. Nvidia has provided not only its own models but also open-source technology tied to agents and AI security, and it has already agreed to acquire Hugging Face for $12.9 billion. The deal is expected to close in the first half of next year, subject to regulatory approval.After reports in July that Anthropic and OpenAI had asked the Trump administration to ban Chinese open-weight models, Huang organised an industry-wide letter of support. He advanced the argument that open-weight models give companies choice and lower costs. But a key variable is that there may be no clear figure to lead this push in an organised way at the industry level going forward.Debates on regulating AI agents could also be affected. Huang has publicly argued several times this year that, while security incidents involving AI agents have been revealed, the industry does not yet need regulation and safety issues can be solved through technology. He rallied the industry again as it was reviewing whether it needed an audit framework or a supervisory body similar to financial industry regulators. Nvidia brought together more than 100 companies to launch an Open Agent Safety Platform. The open-source-based project set out the goal of reducing problems involving agents that go out of control.The industry’s view of AI could also change. Huang has defined AI as an engineering system that produces products and stressed it can be controlled like other engineering systems. That contrasts with a trend among some large AI labs to highlight model autonomy or the possibility of consciousness. TechCrunch said Huang’s exit would, for the time being, weaken the voice representing that opposing view.Nvidia’s strategy in the AI PC market is also being put to the test. Huang recently persuaded several PC manufacturers to join Nvidia’s CPU strategy. He has also prepared a premium line of AI PCs that run AI agents on the device itself. The new products are due for release ahead of the year-end shopping season.The issue is that Huang’s personal symbolism has played an important role in product marketing. TechCrunch said Huang was no longer a suitable figure to promote these devices as an alternative to the Mac mini. It said Huang’s exit introduced a variable into efforts to build awareness for the new products and into strategies to expand the market.Confidence in AI data centre investment and financing structures could also be shaken. As a data centre construction boom continued, Huang directly designed large-scale financial structures centred on Nvidia. Critics have also raised claims that Nvidia approved circular transactions in which it supports customer expansion through equity investment and those customers then buy Nvidia chips. Citing a Bloomberg report, the outlet said the company had committed about $750 billion in such transactions through July.In August, Nvidia decided to provide support akin to loss compensation for $105 billion in funding for an OpenAI data centre in Ohio, and in the same month major private equity firms and financial companies including Apollo, BlackRock, Blackstone, Brookfield, Goldman Sachs and KKR decided to invest up to $500 billion in data centre construction. Huang has promised that Nvidia GPUs can serve as collateral that guarantees value preservation, presenting Nvidia as “investable infrastructure”.The issue is that Huang’s exit could affect confidence in these financing ideas themselves. Wall Street is already worried about the possibility of a sharp drop in Nvidia’s share price and the fallout, while fatigue over AI infrastructure investment has also grown. TechCrunch wrote, “Nvidia has ultimately lost its top salesman, and the AI industry has lost its strongest ‘hype man’.”After Huang’s exit, Nvidia now faces the task of building new leadership beyond a founder-centric management system. External variables also remain, including the possibility of additional political investigations. Whether Nvidia can replace Huang’s personal influence and maintain leadership of the AI industry has emerged as a key point to watch for the industry.

sources.title: FAA lifts nationwide ground stop that blocked takeoffs for hours
passages: Takeoffs from airports throughout the US largely stopped on Friday after the FAA issued a national ground stop at 3:44PM ET “due to extraordinary circumstances and for reasons of safety,” while planes in the air will be allowed to land.

extraction.body: Takeoffs from airports throughout the US largely stopped on Friday after the FAA issued a national ground stop at 3:44PM ET “due to extraordinary circumstances and for reasons of safety,” while planes in the air will be allowed to land. The FAA tweeted just after 5PM ET that, “There has been a temporary telecommunications outage - out of an abundance of caution all flights have been halted. Every flight has been accounted for and international flights will be handled on a case by case basis.” More than four hours after the stop was issued, officials announced it was lifted at 8:15PM ET and that flights will resume. It’s unclear how many flights will be able to take off and when, as they now face problems of overloaded airports and flight crews that have run out of time to operate the planes, meaning many people will be stuck where they are for the time being and more flights will be delayed or canceled. In a press conference announcing that the stop had been lifted, Transportation Secretary Ryan Duffy blamed an aging air traffic control system that he is pursuing funds to replace, saying that the TRACONs (Terminal Radar Approach Control) in the air traffic control centers “started to have inconsistency in the data from the radars and the communications from airplanes.” He said that the devices that had the issue were analog telecom devices, where the switches / routers “got overloaded with data” and started to show inconsistency. An earlier report from CBS News cited multiple sources who said that an update to the air traffic control system’s private communications network, operated by L3Harris, caused a system reboot and the subsequent outage. The flight tracking site FlightAware lists 9,124 US flights as delayed and 5,901 flights canceled as of 8:39PM ET. According to CNN, the last nationwide ground stop in 2023 lasted for about 90 minutes after the NOTAM (Notice to Air Missions) system for pilots went down, and the last one prior to that was after the attacks on September 11th, 2001. Air Space Intelligence (ASI), the company that designed the system and was awarded a 12-year $875 million contract in June to deploy it, denied any connection, tweeting “The current ground stop is not based on or a result of the SMART system, any product of ASI or our integration with FAA and ATC.” Jon Ostrower of The Air Current reports that the outage began with the Chicago air traffic control center, followed by centers in Boston, Washington, New York, and Minneapolis, and as the FAA issued a ground stop for aircraft flying east, more facilities began reporting problems.

extraction.body: The US federal aviation regulator has lifted a nationwide ground stop for all airports. Trump administration officials blame "overloaded" and "outdated" systems for the hourslong halt to departures. The US Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) canceled a ground stop on all national flights hours after stopping departures at US airports on Friday. "We have old switches, old routers, we use 1980s old copper lines. We use an old system," US Secretary of Transportation Sean Duffy said. "It was a legacy network problem." Even with the order being lifted, airlines will not be able to immediately return to normal operations as many of their planes and crews are out of position. "It's going to be slow," Duffy told reporters at the White House. Officials said they think the system will be back to normal in time for Thanksgiving on November 26, one of the busiest times to travel in the US. It was the first nationwide ground stop since January 2023, when the FAA dealt with a system outage. Prior to that, the last ground stop was after the September 11, 2001 terror attacks . US Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin said there was no indication the communications breakdown resulted from a cyberattack or artificial intelligence and that the ⁠public ​was ​never ​in danger. Over 4,500 flights were canceled Friday and about 700 for Saturday and over 10,000 flights within, into, or out of the United States were delayed, according to the FlightAware aviation tracker. "All departing traffic should remain groundstopped until further notice," the FAA had said earlier Friday. The agency said the ground stop was "due to extraordinary circumstances and reasons for safety." The FAA cited a temporary telecommunication outage and said, "Every flight has been accounted for and international flights will be handled on a case by case basis." The agency said flights were halted "out of abundance of caution." In a post on X, Duffy said the stop was due to a communication issue impacting all Air Route Traffic Control Centers. "FAA technicians are investigating the issue. We will provide immediate updates as we have them," he wrote. The FAA ground stop order came a day after Duffy asked Congress for $30 billion to upgrade and modernize the US Air Traffic Control System. "This investment is critical to complete the modernization of our national airspace — delivering a resilient telecommunications backbone for air traffic controllers, modern hardware and software, state-of-the-art control towers, and world-class airport infrastructure," Duffy and Office of Management and Budget Director Russell Vought wrote in a letter to lawmakers. The European Organisation for the Safety of Air Navigation, Eurocontrol, urged airlines to issue delay notices for flights that had initially been unable to take off. Eurocontrol had earlier said that all flights departing for US airports from its 42 member states were suspended following a request from the FAA. It has since removed that note from its website. Canada's air navigation service provider, NAV Canada, said it is closely monitoring the US ground stop and later said, "It was implementing traffic management measures at Toronto Pearson, Montreal-Trudeau, Calgary and Vancouver to safely manage traffic volumes." "Travelers should expect delays and check with their airline. Our systems are operating normally," NAV Canada added.

extraction.body: Takeoffs from airports throughout the US largely stopped on Friday after the FAA issued a national ground stop at 3:44PM ET “due to extraordinary circumstances and for reasons of safety,” while planes in the air will be allowed to land. The FAA tweeted just after 5PM ET that, “There has been a temporary telecommunications outage - out of an abundance of caution all flights have been halted. Every flight has been accounted for and international flights will be handled on a case by case basis.” More than four hours after the stop was issued, officials announced it was lifted at 8:15PM ET and that flights will resume. It’s unclear how many flights will be able to take off and when, as they now face problems of overloaded airports and flight crews that have run out of time to operate the planes, meaning many people will be stuck where they are for the time being and more flights will be delayed or canceled. In a press conference announcing that the stop had been lifted, Transportation Secretary Ryan Duffy blamed an aging air traffic control system that he is pursuing funds to replace, saying that the TRACONs (Terminal Radar Approach Control) in the air traffic control centers “started to have inconsistency in the data from the radars and the communications from airplanes.” He said that the devices that had the issue were analog telecom devices, where the switches / routers “got overloaded with data” and started to show inconsistency. An earlier report from CBS News cited multiple sources who said that an update to the air traffic control system’s private communications network, operated by L3Harris, caused a system reboot and the subsequent outage. The flight tracking site FlightAware lists 9,124 US flights as delayed and 5,901 flights canceled as of 8:39PM ET. According to CNN, the last nationwide ground stop in 2023 lasted for about 90 minutes after the NOTAM (Notice to Air Missions) system for pilots went down, and the last one prior to that was after the attacks on September 11th, 2001. Air Space Intelligence (ASI), the company that designed the system and was awarded a 12-year $875 million contract in June to deploy it, denied any connection, tweeting “The current ground stop is not based on or a result of the SMART system, any product of ASI or our integration with FAA and ATC.” Jon Ostrower of The Air Current reports that the outage began with the Chicago air traffic control center, followed by centers in Boston, Washington, New York, and Minneapolis, and as the FAA issued a ground stop for aircraft flying east, more facilities began reporting problems.

extraction.body: The US federal aviation regulator has lifted a nationwide ground stop for all airports. Trump administration officials blame "overloaded" and "outdated" systems for the hourslong halt to departures. The US Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) canceled a ground stop on all national flights hours after stopping departures at US airports on Friday. "We have old switches, old routers, we use 1980s old copper lines. We use an old system," US Secretary of Transportation Sean Duffy said. "It was a legacy network problem." Even with the order being lifted, airlines will not be able to immediately return to normal operations as many of their planes and crews are out of position. "It's going to be slow," Duffy told reporters at the White House.
