The US government on Thursday said it had obtained court authorization to seize or restrain use of over $1.2 billion stolen during last month's $6.3 billion Binance heist, as part of a larger effort to disrupt North Korea's ongoing cryptocurrency theft.

The court also allowed the takedown of cloud-based infrastructure used in a Democratic People’s Republic of Korea (DPRK) social engineering scheme called “FaceStealer” that has amassed more than $400 million in the last 18 months.

It’s called FaceStealer because it involved secretly recorded webcam videos. Victims are typically people working in the cryptocurrency and web3 industries, along with open source software developers and maintainers who DPRK hackers target in the hope of accessing the software repositories they control as the first step towards creating supply chain attacks.
The FBI said it had seized more than 900 webcam videos belonging to these tech workers.
First, the North Koreans send targets an invitation to join a video meeting. Those invitations come from hijacked accounts that the next intended victim may find familiar or credible.

“You're going to think it's real because it's going to be based on either conversations or interests you've expressed in the past with this actual person,” said special agent Jeremy Robertson, who oversees counterintelligence and cyber investigations at FBI Los Angeles.
“They're going to then send you a link to catch up, and it's usually a calendar invite, and it's going to have some typo-squatted URLs in there,” he told reporters on Thursday.

The URL directs the victim to a fake Zoom or Teams meeting, and the cybercriminals record the target’s webcam video while playing a phony, prerecorded video of the person who purportedly sent the meeting invite.
Sometimes the hackers also use deepfake videos of well-known individuals in the cryptocurrency and web3 industries, we’re told.

“When you log in, whoever invited you – your friend or business associate – is going to be on the screen, but you're not going to hear any audio,” Robertson said. “But you're going to see their face, you're going to see them looking around, you're going to see them mouthing some words, and then in the text box you're going to receive some instructions.”

The text box tells the victim that the person on the other end of the video call can’t hear them, they need to upgrade their software for the audio to work properly, and it sends a link to the supposed fix.
Clicking to access the “fix” installs cryptocurrency-stealing malware on the victim’s computer and sends their contact list to the digital thieves to perpetuate the scam.

The FBI attributes FaceStealer to a North Korea-linked group tracked as Sapphire Sleet , which is widely regarded as a Lazarus Group offshoot. Sapphire Sleet is also known as UNC1069, Stardust Chollima, APT38, and BlueNoroff.

“The actors behind this activity, commonly referred to as Sapphire Sleet and other associated names, are part of a broader North Korean effort to generate revenue for the regime, to steal virtual assets, and gain access to networks and trusted online ecosystems,” Brett Leatherman, assistant director of the FBI's Cyber Division, told reporters. “North Korean hackers are increasingly blending cyber intrusion, social engineering, and emerging technologies such as deep fakes to make their impersonation efforts more convincing and scalable.”

The FBI also provided an update on its efforts to recover the stolen assets from the October 29 attack on Binance. The agency previously blamed the $6.3 billion heist on TraderTraitor, a North Korean hacking operation also linked to Lazarus Group.

Last week, Binance revealed the attackers laid the groundwork for their “ sophisticated, multi-stage campaign ” back in June, and said it involved social engineering during fake job interviews, malware downloads, compromised internal AI tooling, endpoint takeover, and an “advanced transaction-authorization method.”

Since the theft, federal investigators and private-sector partners have helped freeze more than $2.7 billion in stolen assets. The Justice Department's court authorization covers more than $1.2 billion of that haul.®

sources.title: FBI disrupts crypto theft scheme by North Korean hacking group; billions stolen so far
passages: The FBI said it has disrupted a highly tailored, hard-to-detect cryptocurrency theft scheme by a North Korean hacking group that has managed to steal billions across the world in recent years.
Before the operation was disrupted, the scheme resulted in the theft of more than $400 million over an 18-month period.

Federal authorities said they have worked closely with private companies to recover the stolen funds, freezing more than $2.7 million and obtaining court approval to seize or restrict access to $1.2 billion of that amount.
FBI officials say the funds are used to bankroll its "rogue regime and illicit weapons program through cryptocurrency theft" and the videos are employed to impersonate and target more victims.
FBI officials said efforts to trace, freeze, seize and forfeit the stolen virtual assets are ongoing.

“Cryptocurrency unfortunately has become fertile ground for North Korea to defraud victims and fund its malign activities,” Bill Essayli, the top federal prosecutor for Los Angeles, said in a written statement.

extraction.body: The FBI said it has disrupted a highly tailored, hard-to-detect cryptocurrency theft scheme by a North Korean hacking group that has managed to steal billions across the world in recent years. The hackers have aggressively targeted people in the cryptocurrency and Web3 industries, as well as workers in the development and maintenance of open-source software, the FBI said in a written statement. Web3, in general, describes internet applications that interact with a blockchain — a digital ledger that stores data. On Thursday, the FBI and Department of Justice announced the disruption of a cloud-based infrastructure used by the North Korean hackers, resulting in the seizure of more than 900 webcam videos of victims working in the crypto and Web3 industries worldwide. Before the operation was disrupted, the scheme resulted in the theft of more than $400 million over an 18-month period. FBI officials say the funds are used to bankroll its "rogue regime and illicit weapons program through cryptocurrency theft" and the videos are employed to impersonate and target more victims. “North Korea’s government bankrolls its rogue regime and illicit weapons program through cryptocurrency theft,” said Principal Deputy Assistant Atty. "The FBI attributes this activity to the North Korean hacking group commonly referred to in the private sector as Sapphire Sleet, UNC1069, Stardust Chollima, APT38, and BlueNoroff," the FBI said in a written statement. “Cryptocurrency unfortunately has become fertile ground for North Korea to defraud victims and fund its malign activities,” Bill Essayli, the top federal prosecutor for Los Angeles, said in a written statement. “Today’s seizure shows that America will continue the fight against rogue states who financially gain from cybercrime.” The federal agency said the hackers used several tactics to compromise victims, including a sophisticated social engineering scheme dubbed "FaceStealer." The scheme involves hijacking LinkedIn, Telegram, Slack and Discord accounts of people known to the victim, then impersonating those people to make contact and lure the victims into video calls using Zoom, Microsoft Teams and Google Meets. "Their objective is compromise of the software supply chain. By infiltrating accounts of trusted developers and maintainers, the threat actors can potentially distribute malicious code through widely used software, impacting millions of downstream users," the FBI said in its written statement. FBI Cyber Branch Operations Director Brett Leatherman said in a statement that the "North Korean regime relies on proceeds from large-scale cryptocurrency theft to fund its illicit weapons program, stealing billions of dollars in recent years." Separately from the FaceStealer scheme, members of the North Korean military, referred by the FBI as "TraderTraitor," stole more than $6 billion in cryptocurrency from the world's largest crypto exchange Binance on Oct. Binance said it has replaced the stolen assets to its customers, but not recovered the stolen loot. Federal authorities said they have worked closely with private companies to recover the stolen funds, freezing more than $2.7 million and obtaining court approval to seize or restrict access to $1.2 billion of that amount. FBI officials said efforts to trace, freeze, seize and forfeit the stolen virtual assets are ongoing.

passages: The FBI disrupted an elaborate North Korean hacking campaign that used secretly recorded videos of victims to impersonate them in online meetings, in a scheme that officials said Thursday has netted more than $400 million in stolen cryptocurrency and threatened widely used software.

Separately, the Justice Department announced court authorization to seize or restrain more than $1.2 billion stolen from Binance, the cryptocurrency exchange hit by a roughly $6.3 billion theft last month .

“What we’ve seen over the last six months is a significant evolution in both the scale and sophistication of this operation,” said Justin Moore, director of adversary operations at Arctic Wolf, one of the firms that has assisted the FBI in its efforts to track the operation.
“Today, we’ve identified more than 677 targets across 58 countries.

We’ve also seen the group’s social engineering playbook expand well beyond fake meetings into document-sharing platforms, identity verification requests, media content, and other trusted business workflows.”
The FBI attributed the theft to North Korea’s TraderTraitor group.
“This is not something we can patch,” Robertson said, calling it a “very, very convincing” social engineering scheme.
The FaceStealer operations build on relationships victims already trust.
Invitations arrive through genuine accounts that hackers have taken over on services including Telegram, LinkedIn, Slack and Discord, officials say.
Access to earlier conversations allows the attackers to make their messages sound familiar, Jeremy Robertson, special agent in charge at the FBI’s Los Angeles Field Office, told reporters.
A meeting link directs the target to a website designed to look like Zoom or Microsoft Teams.

extraction.body: The FBI disrupted an elaborate North Korean hacking campaign that used secretly recorded videos of victims to impersonate them in online meetings, in a scheme that officials said Thursday has netted more than $400 million in stolen cryptocurrency and threatened widely used software. The operation , dubbed FaceStealer, tricks people into joining fake video calls with what appear to be familiar contacts, then installing malicious software disguised as a fix for an audio problem. Hackers use the resulting access to steal funds, take over accounts and approach the victim’s friends and colleagues. Authorities seized cloud infrastructure used in the campaign and more than 900 webcam videos of victims. The FBI also said hackers broke into the computer of a developer who maintains widely used software, then used that access to add malicious code that could reach people downloading it. The attack was detected and stopped before it widely spread. Separately, the Justice Department announced court authorization to seize or restrain more than $1.2 billion stolen from Binance, the cryptocurrency exchange hit by a roughly $6.3 billion theft last month . Officials said the two campaigns likely involved different North Korean actors. The FaceStealer operations build on relationships victims already trust. Invitations arrive through genuine accounts that hackers have taken over on services including Telegram, LinkedIn, Slack and Discord, officials say. Access to earlier conversations allows the attackers to make their messages sound familiar, Jeremy Robertson, special agent in charge at the FBI’s Los Angeles Field Office, told reporters. A meeting link directs the target to a website designed to look like Zoom or Microsoft Teams. Inside, the target sees a recording of someone they recognize. The attackers sometimes add other apparent participants, making the meeting more convincing. A message then tells the person their audio is not working and supplies instructions to fix it. Those steps — which can include running a script or pasting commands into the computer’s terminal — instead install malware capable of recording keystrokes, capturing screens and giving the hackers continued access. Meanwhile, the fake meeting records the new victim’s webcam. That footage, combined with stolen accounts and contact lists, helps the hackers repeat the process with someone else. The campaign highlights a unique degree of scale and creativity on the part of Pyongyang’s cryptocurrency theft operations that have not been publicly outlined before. “This is not something we can patch,” Robertson said, calling it a “very, very convincing” social engineering scheme. The targeting has also reached developers who maintain open-source software, which other organizations use to build their own applications. Earlier this year, a maintainer of a JavaScript software library joined a fake Teams meeting featuring someone they recognized and followed instructions that infected their computer, officials said. “What we’ve seen over the last six months is a significant evolution in both the scale and sophistication of this operation,” said Justin Moore, director of adversary operations at Arctic Wolf, one of the firms that has assisted the FBI in its efforts to track the operation. “Today, we’ve identified more than 677 targets across 58 countries. We’ve also seen the group’s social engineering playbook expand well beyond fake meetings into document-sharing platforms, identity verification requests, media content, and other trusted business workflows.” In the separate Binance case, public and private sector efforts have frozen more than $2.7 billion. The $1.2 billion covered by court orders is part of that total and not an additional recovery. A senior DOJ official said the government now has custody of the funds covered by those orders. Returning them would generally involve court proceedings to determine ownership, though the official cautioned it was too early to say exactly how that process would unfold. Binance previously said attackers used a fake job interview to compromise an engineer’s computer before reaching systems used to approve cryptocurrency transfers. The FBI attributed the theft to North Korea’s TraderTraitor group. Recovering more of the money is becoming harder as the hackers divide it into smaller amounts and distribute it among laundering networks, the senior DOJ official said. “These actors have gotten very good at laundering,” the official said. “They’ve learned from their past efforts and our efforts to interdict them.” NEXT STORY: Nvidia spying allegations test Washington’s defenses against tech espionage

The U.S. Department of Justice announced two separate but connected actions against North Korea ‘s cryptocurrency theft operations. The press release covers the seizure of infrastructure behind a social engineering scheme called FaceStealer and court-authorized seizures tied to the $6 billion Binance theft of October 29. Together, the two moves put more than $1.2 billion back under law enforcement control.

“Today the Department of Justice announced coordinated actions against the Democratic People’s Republic of North Korea (DPRK) government’s schemes to fund its regime through the massive theft of cryptocurrency.” states the press release published by DoJ. “These actions include the seizure of cloud-based infrastructure used in the FaceStealer social engineering scheme that has resulted in the theft of more than $400 million worth of cryptocurrency and the court-authorized seizure and restraint of more than $1.2 billion worth of cryptocurrency recently stolen from Binance, a virtual currency exchange.”

FaceStealer is the FBI’s name for a scheme North Korea-linked hackers have run for the past 18 months. The same actors go by Sapphire Sleet , BlueNoroff , APT38 and several other tracking names depending on who is writing the report. They’ve stolen more than $400 million that way, and they’ve also started targeting people who build and maintain open-source software, trying to reach the accounts and repositories those developers control.

The process is quite specific. The hackers send meeting invitations from accounts they have already stolen. This makes the invitations look as if they come from someone the target knows and trusts. During the meeting, they play a recorded video of a previous victim or use a deepfake showing a well-known person in the cryptocurrency or Web3 industry. They use advanced AI tools to create convincing videos of influential people, making the FaceStealer scheme more effective.

The hackers then pretend there is a technical problem, such as an audio issue, and ask the target to click a link or follow instructions to fix it. This leads to the installation of malware. In several cases, the attackers waited months, or even more than a year, before stealing cryptocurrency or taking control of accounts. They also used each victim’s contact lists, social media accounts and messaging apps to identify and approach new targets.
Under a federal warrant, the FBI seized more than 900 webcam videos recorded from FaceStealer victims.

“The FBI today published a report providing greater detail on the mechanics of the FaceStealer scheme, including best practices to protect against this scheme and steps victims can take in the event of a compromise. Additionally, the FBI created a website, www.fbi.gov/facestealer , to serve as a centralized hub for resources and information on the scheme.” continues the press release. “The effort to disrupt the FaceStealer campaign was led by Assistant U.S. Attorney Khaldoun Shobaki for the Central District of California and the FBI’s Los Angeles Field Office.”
The operation to seize the infrastructure was led by the U.S. Attorney’s Office for the Central District of California and the FBI’s Los Angeles Field Office.

The mechanics are specific. The hackers send meeting invitations from accounts stolen from earlier victims, so the invite looks like it comes from someone the target knows. Once in the meeting, the hackers play a pre-recorded video of a previous victim or use a deepfake of a well-known person in crypto or Web3 to simulate trusted contacts.

“The North Korean hackers also use super intelligence (SI) to develop deepfake videos of well-known and influential individuals often in the cryptocurrency and web3 industries that make the FaceStealer scheme even more effective.” FBI continues. “Here again, they use the deepfake videos in the meetings with targets to gain the target’s trust.”

Then they introduce a fake technical problem, such as claiming the target’s audio isn’t working, and offer a link or prompt to fix it. The fix installs malware. In several cases the hackers waited months or more than a year after the initial compromise before stealing cryptocurrency or hijacking accounts. They also used each new victim’s contact lists, social media and messaging apps to reach the next round of targets.

The FBI seized more than 900 webcam videos from FaceStealer victims under a federal warrant. It also published a detailed report on the scheme’s mechanics, with best practices and steps for anyone who suspects they’ve been compromised, and created a resource page at fbi.gov/facestealer. The infrastructure seizure was led by the Central District of California and the FBI’s Los Angeles Field Office.

“The North Korean regime relies on proceeds from large-scale cryptocurrency theft to fund its illicit weapons program, stealing billions of dollars in recent years,” said FBI Cyber Branch Operations Director Brett Leatherman. “North Korean cyber actors have used the FaceStealer scheme to aggressively target individuals in the cryptocurrency and Web3 sectors through deceptive social engineering tactics, resulting in the theft of more than $400 million in the last 18 months. The FBI remains committed to identifying, disrupting, and imposing cost on North Korean actors targeting the virtual asset community.”

Separately, the DOJ has been working since October 29 to freeze and recover the $6 billion stolen from Binance by North Korea’s TraderTraitor unit. Combined government and private-sector efforts have frozen more than $2.7 billion so far, and the DOJ has court authorization to seize or restrain more than $1.2 billion of that. The Criminal Division’s Computer Crime and Intellectual Property Section called it freezing about half of the historic breach before it got beyond law enforcement reach.

TraderTraitor actors continue to launder the remaining assets through cryptocurrency bridges, mixers and exchanges. The FBI, the U.S. Secret Service and IRS Criminal Investigation last week issued a joint cyber alert naming the addresses the actors are using and urging cryptocurrency service providers to block any transactions involving those addresses or funds derived from them.

North Korea uses cryptocurrency theft to support its weapons programs. The U.S. Department of Justice (DOJ) has repeatedly highlighted this link. A senior official from the department’s National Security Division said the regime uses these criminal operations to raise money for its weapons program. The DOJ also pledged to use all available legal tools to seize the stolen funds and return them to their rightful owners.

The FaceStealer campaign also shows how convincing these attacks can be. According to the FBI, the scheme can trick even experienced IT professionals and users who are well aware of cybersecurity risks.

“Efforts to trace, freeze, seize, and forfeit the stolen virtual assets are ongoing, as TraderTraitor actors continue to launder such assets through various cryptocurrency bridges, mixers, and exchanges.” concludes the press release. “For example, last week, the FBI, in coordination with its law enforcement partners at the U.S. Secret Service (USSS) and the Internal Revenue Service (IRS-CI), issued a Cyber Alert attributing the theft and urging VASPs to block transactions with or derived from cryptocurrency addresses TraderTraitor actors are using to launder the stolen Binance assets.”

extraction.body: ‘FaceStealer’ scam tied to $400M+ theft, 900+ webcam recordings The US government on Thursday said it had obtained court authorization to seize or restrain use of over $1.2 billion stolen during last month's $6.3 billion Binance heist, as part of a larger effort to disrupt North Korea's ongoing cryptocurrency theft. The court also allowed the takedown of cloud-based infrastructure used in a Democratic People’s Republic of Korea (DPRK) social engineering scheme called “FaceStealer” that has amassed more than $400 million in the last 18 months. It’s called FaceStealer because it involved secretly recorded webcam videos. Victims are typically people working in the cryptocurrency and web3 industries, along with open source software developers and maintainers who DPRK hackers target in the hope of accessing the software repositories they control as the first step towards creating supply chain attacks. The FBI said it had seized more than 900 webcam videos belonging to these tech workers. First, the North Koreans send targets an invitation to join a video meeting. Those invitations come from hijacked accounts that the next intended victim may find familiar or credible. “You're going to think it's real because it's going to be based on either conversations or interests you've expressed in the past with this actual person,” said special agent Jeremy Robertson, who oversees counterintelligence and cyber investigations at FBI Los Angeles. “They're going to then send you a link to catch up, and it's usually a calendar invite, and it's going to have some typo-squatted URLs in there,” he told reporters on Thursday. The URL directs the victim to a fake Zoom or Teams meeting, and the cybercriminals record the target’s webcam video while playing a phony, prerecorded video of the person who purportedly sent the meeting invite. Sometimes the hackers also use deepfake videos of well-known individuals in the cryptocurrency and web3 industries, we’re told. “When you log in, whoever invited you – your friend or business associate – is going to be on the screen, but you're not going to hear any audio,” Robertson said. “But you're going to see their face, you're going to see them looking around, you're going to see them mouthing some words, and then in the text box you're going to receive some instructions.” The text box tells the victim that the person on the other end of the video call can’t hear them, they need to upgrade their software for the audio to work properly, and it sends a link to the supposed fix. The FBI attributes FaceStealer to a North Korea-linked group tracked as Sapphire Sleet , which is widely regarded as a Lazarus Group offshoot. extraction.body: The FBI disrupted an elaborate North Korean hacking campaign that used secretly recorded videos of victims to impersonate them in online meetings, in a scheme that officials said Thursday has netted more than $400 million in stolen cryptocurrency and threatened widely used software. The operation , dubbed FaceStealer, tricks people into joining fake video calls with what appear to be familiar contacts, then installing malicious software disguised as a fix for an audio problem. Hackers use the resulting access to steal funds, take over accounts and approach the victim’s friends and colleagues. Authorities seized cloud infrastructure used in the campaign and more than 900 webcam videos of victims. The FBI also said hackers broke into the computer of a developer who maintains widely used software, then used that access to add malicious code that could reach people downloading it. The attack was detected and stopped before it widely spread. Separately, the Justice Department announced court authorization to seize or restrain more than $1.2 billion stolen from Binance, the cryptocurrency exchange hit by a roughly $6.3 billion theft last month . Officials said the two campaigns likely involved different North Korean actors. The FaceStealer operations build on relationships victims already trust. Invitations arrive through genuine accounts that hackers have taken over on services including Telegram, LinkedIn, Slack and Discord, officials say. Access to earlier conversations allows the attackers to make their messages sound familiar, Jeremy Robertson, special agent in charge at the FBI’s Los Angeles Field Office, told reporters. A meeting link directs the target to a website designed to look like Zoom or Microsoft Teams. Inside, the target sees a recording of someone they recognize. The attackers sometimes add other apparent participants, making the meeting more convincing. A message then tells the person their audio is not working and supplies instructions to fix it. Those steps — which can include running a script or pasting commands into the computer’s terminal — instead install malware capable of recording keystrokes, capturing screens and giving the hackers continued access. Meanwhile, the fake meeting records the new victim’s webcam. That footage, combined with stolen accounts and contact lists, helps the hackers repeat the process with someone else. The campaign highlights a unique degree of scale and creativity on the part of Pyongyang’s cryptocurrency theft operations that have not been publicly outlined before. “This is not something we can patch,” Robertson said, calling it a “very, very convincing” social engineering scheme. The targeting has also reached developers who maintain open-source software, which other organizations use to build their own applications. Earlier this year, a maintainer of a JavaScript software library joined a fake Teams meeting featuring someone they recognized and followed instructions that infected their computer, officials said. “What we’ve seen over the last six months is a significant evolution in both the scale and sophistication of this operation,” said Justin Moore, director of adversary operations at Arctic Wolf, one of the firms that has assisted the FBI in its efforts to track the operation. “Today, we’ve identified more than 677 targets across 58 countries. We’ve also seen the group’s social engineering playbook expand well beyond fake meetings into document-sharing platforms, identity verification requests, media content, and other trusted business workflows.” In the separate Binance case, public and private sector efforts have frozen more than $2.7 billion. The $1.2 billion covered by court orders is part of that total and not an additional recovery. A senior DOJ official said the government now has custody of the funds covered by those orders. Returning them would generally involve court proceedings to determine ownership, though the official cautioned it was too early to say exactly how that process would unfold. Binance previously said attackers used a fake job interview to compromise an engineer’s computer before reaching systems used to approve cryptocurrency transfers. The FBI attributed the theft to North Korea’s TraderTraitor group. Recovering more of the money is becoming harder as the hackers divide it into smaller amounts and distribute it among laundering networks, the senior DOJ official said. “These actors have gotten very good at laundering,” the official said. “They’ve learned from their past efforts and our efforts to interdict them.” NEXT STORY: Nvidia spying allegations test Washington’s defenses against tech espionage

The U.S. Department of Justice announced two separate but connected actions against North Korea ‘s cryptocurrency theft operations. The press release covers the seizure of infrastructure behind a social engineering scheme called FaceStealer and court-authorized seizures tied to the $6 billion Binance theft of October 29. Together, the two moves put more than $1.2 billion back under law enforcement control.

“Today the Department of Justice announced coordinated actions against the Democratic People’s Republic of North Korea (DPRK) government’s schemes to fund its regime through the massive theft of cryptocurrency.” states the press release published by DoJ. “These actions include the seizure of cloud-based infrastructure used in the FaceStealer social engineering scheme that has resulted in the theft of more than $400 million worth of cryptocurrency and the court-authorized seizure and restraint of more than $1.2 billion worth of cryptocurrency recently stolen from Binance, a virtual currency exchange.”

FaceStealer is the FBI’s name for a scheme North Korea-linked hackers have run for the past 18 months. The same actors go by Sapphire Sleet , BlueNoroff , APT38 and several other tracking names depending on who is writing the report. They’ve stolen more than $400 million that way, and they’ve also started targeting people who build and maintain open-source software, trying to reach the accounts and repositories those developers control.

The process is quite specific. The hackers send meeting invitations from accounts they have already stolen. This makes the invitations look as if they come from someone the target knows and trusts. During the meeting, they play a recorded video of a previous victim or use a deepfake showing a well-known person in the cryptocurrency or Web3 industry. They use advanced AI tools to create convincing videos of influential people, making the FaceStealer scheme more effective.

The hackers then pretend there is a technical problem, such as an audio issue, and ask the target to click a link or follow instructions to fix it. This leads to the installation of malware. In several cases, the attackers waited months, or even more than a year, before stealing cryptocurrency or taking control of accounts. They also used each victim’s contact lists, social media accounts and messaging apps to identify and approach new targets.
Under a federal warrant, the FBI seized more than 900 webcam videos recorded from FaceStealer victims.

“The FBI today published a report providing greater detail on the mechanics of the FaceStealer scheme, including best practices to protect against this scheme and steps victims can take in the event of a compromise. Additionally, the FBI created a website, www.fbi.gov/facestealer , to serve as a centralized hub for resources and information on the scheme.” continues the press release. “The effort to disrupt the FaceStealer campaign was led by Assistant U.S. Attorney Khaldoun Shobaki for the Central District of California and the FBI’s Los Angeles Field Office.”
The operation to seize the infrastructure was led by the U.S. Attorney’s Office for the Central District of California and the FBI’s Los Angeles Field Office.

The mechanics are specific. The hackers send meeting invitations from accounts stolen from earlier victims, so the invite looks like it comes from someone the target knows. Once in the meeting, the hackers play a pre-recorded video of a previous victim or use a deepfake of a well-known person in crypto or Web3 to simulate trusted contacts.

“The North Korean hackers also use super intelligence (SI) to develop deepfake videos of well-known and influential individuals often in the cryptocurrency and web3 industries that make the FaceStealer scheme even more effective.” FBI continues. “Here again, they use the deepfake videos in the meetings with targets to gain the target’s trust.”

Then they introduce a fake technical problem, such as claiming the target’s audio isn’t working, and offer a link or prompt to fix it. The fix installs malware. In several cases the hackers waited months or more than a year after the initial compromise before stealing cryptocurrency or hijacking accounts. They also used each new victim’s contact lists, social media and messaging apps to reach the next round of targets.

The FBI seized more than 900 webcam videos from FaceStealer victims under a federal warrant. It also published a detailed report on the scheme’s mechanics, with best practices and steps for anyone who suspects they’ve been compromised, and created a resource page at fbi.gov/facestealer. The infrastructure seizure was led by the Central District of California and the FBI’s Los Angeles Field Office.

“The North Korean regime relies on proceeds from large-scale cryptocurrency theft to fund its illicit weapons program, stealing billions of dollars in recent years,” said FBI Cyber Branch Operations Director Brett Leatherman. “North Korean cyber actors have used the FaceStealer scheme to aggressively target individuals in the cryptocurrency and Web3 sectors through deceptive social engineering tactics, resulting in the theft of more than $400 million in the last 18 months. The FBI remains committed to identifying, disrupting, and imposing cost on North Korean actors targeting the virtual asset community.”

Separately, the DOJ has been working since October 29 to freeze and recover the $6 billion stolen from Binance by North Korea’s TraderTraitor unit. Combined government and private-sector efforts have frozen more than $2.7 billion so far, and the DOJ has court authorization to seize or restrain more than $1.2 billion of that. The Criminal Division’s Computer Crime and Intellectual Property Section called it freezing about half of the historic breach before it got beyond law enforcement reach.

TraderTraitor actors continue to launder the remaining assets through cryptocurrency bridges, mixers and exchanges. The FBI, the U.S. Secret Service and IRS Criminal Investigation last week issued a joint cyber alert naming the addresses the actors are using and urging cryptocurrency service providers to block any transactions involving those addresses or funds derived from them.

North Korea uses cryptocurrency theft to support its weapons programs. The U.S. Department of Justice (DOJ) has repeatedly highlighted this link. A senior official from the department’s National Security Division said the regime uses these criminal operations to raise money for its weapons program. The DOJ also pledged to use all available legal tools to seize the stolen funds and return them to their rightful owners.

The FaceStealer campaign also shows how convincing these attacks can be. According to the FBI, the scheme can trick even experienced IT professionals and users who are well aware of cybersecurity risks.

“Efforts to trace, freeze, seize, and forfeit the stolen virtual assets are ongoing, as TraderTraitor actors continue to launder such assets through various cryptocurrency bridges, mixers, and exchanges.” concludes the press release. “For example, last week, the FBI, in coordination with its law enforcement partners at the U.S. Secret Service (USSS) and the Internal Revenue Service (IRS-CI), issued a Cyber Alert attributing the theft and urging VASPs to block transactions with or derived from cryptocurrency addresses TraderTraitor actors are using to launder the stolen Binance assets.”

extraction.body: Passengers wait at Midway Airport as a nationwide ground stop brings flights to a halt. UPDATE: The Federal Aviation Administration has lifted the nationwide ground stop, but flight disruptions are expected to linger into the weekend. The Federal Aviation Administration released a new statement following a rare ground stop issued at all airports across the country. Stream NBC 5 for free, 24/7, wherever you are. In its original alert, the FAA said the ground stop was issued "due to extraordinary circumstances and for reasons of safety." In a newer statement, the agency said the alert followed "communication issues impacting multiple Air Route Traffic Control Centers." "FAA technicians are investigating the issue. We will provide updates," the FAA said in its statement. In a later message, the FAA said the issue stemmed from "a temporary telecommunications outage." "Out of an abundance of caution all flights have been halted. Every flight has been accounted for and international flights will be handled on a case by case basis," the statement read. A nationwide ground stop is exceptionally rare, experts say, with only one other such alert issued since 9/11. That ground stop took place in 2023 , when the FAA suffered an outage of the system that sends messages to pilots. According to the advisory from the FAA Friday, all aircraft operators were told "by order of the Federal Aviation Command Center" that airports were ground stopped and all departing traffic should remain grounded "until further notice." "Inbound flights will be managed on a case by case basis," the alert stated. Moments earlier, both major airports in Chicago were listed under a ground stop due to an "equipment outage." It remained unclear if that outage was connected to the ground stop, however. U.S. Secretary of Transportation Sean Duffy confirmed the ground stop, saying it was under investigation. The @FAAnews issued a nationwide ground stop for all U.S. airports following a communication issue impacting all Air Route Traffic Control Centers. FAA technicians are investigating the issue. We will provide immediate updates as we have them. U.S. Secretary of Homeland Security Markwayne Mullin Mullin said there was "no indication as of yet that this was a nefarious attack against us." "We were wanting to assure all the American people this isn't a safety to the American people or another 9/11," Mullin said. "I think that's what a lot of people are trying to make the comparison to, and that's not the case." The communications problems don’t appear to be linked to the FAA’s new AI-powered system the agency is rolling out to help predict problems in the sky, according to Mullin. The FAA’s SMART system is based in a single location near Washington, D.C., where a team of experts analyzes flight schedules, weather forecasts and hundreds of other streams of data. Then that office sends recommendations to the FAA’s command center that relays them to controllers across the country for consideration. The company that designed the system, ASI, said “the current ground stop is not based on or a result of the SMART system, any product of ASI or our integration with FAA and ATC.” More than 200 flights were delayed at Chicago's airports Friday afternoon. As of 3:11 p.m., the Chicago Department of Aviation reported 213 delays at O'Hare International Airport and another 55 at Midway International Airport. Former United Airlines pilot and aviation expert Steve Arroyo said the problem appeared similar to a regional air traffic control communication outage in September that snarled hundreds of flights across the Northeast, except this time on a nationwide scale. Arroyo said it could be linked to the outdated technology used by air traffic controllers. “If you don’t have that ability, whether it’s because the old wires that they have are just run down or for whatever reason, you’ve got to stop airplanes on the ground,” said Arroyo. “And not put them in the air where you’re going to risk not being able to communicate with them.” While still early in the investigation, multiple officials from multiple agencies told NBC News there is no indication that the incident has been caused by malicious activity. They said they haven’t seen the type of activity that would normally be associated with a cyber attack incident but cautioned that it is still early in the investigation and that information could still change. Three senior officials said there’s nothing that indicates a connection between the FAA incident and Thursday's Microsoft outage. Check back for more on this developing story.

extraction.body: At 12:54 p.m. Pacific on Friday, the FAA ordered every departing flight in America to stay exactly where it was, a move the agency had pulled only twice before: on September 11, 2001, and one January morning in 2023. The official reason, as of this writing, is a "temporary telecommunications outage" somewhere in the web of radios and radar that keeps airliners from meeting each other at 35,000 feet. That's a plausible explanation and, let's be honest, barely an explanation at all. The stop also landed just days after the agency took a new AI air-traffic planning tool nationwide, and the Homeland Security secretary says he isn't ruling anything out, though so far nothing ties the two together and officials say they see no sign of an attack. So here's what's known, what isn't, and which of the theories ricocheting around your feed deserve a raised eyebrow versus a full eye-roll (details current as of mid-afternoon Pacific on Friday, Nov. 13). The FAA's Air Traffic Control System Command Center posted the advisory at 12:54 p.m. Pacific, ordering all airports ground-stopped "due to extraordinary circumstances and for reasons of safety," according to the SF Standard . About 20 minutes later, Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy took to X to blame "a communication issue impacting all Air Route Traffic Control Centers," which, as ABC News explains, are the 22 facilities responsible for everything flying above 18,000 feet. He offered neither a cause nor an estimate of when flights would resume. The scale is hard to overstate. Roughly 11,000 flights were still scheduled to depart when the order came down, per aviation analytics firm Cirium, as CNBC reported. Flightradar24 counted 4,042 airborne flights bound for U.S. airports at that moment, all of which were allowed to land, and by press time Afar was citing FlightAware figures of more than 10,000 delays and 1,948 cancellations, both still climbing. So what actually broke? The aviation newsletter The Air Current reported, via Fast Company , that the command center told airlines radio frequencies and radar capabilities were affected and that it had no information on timing or cause. One pilot told Yahoo News the trouble started at Kansas City Center, which covers the middle of the country, and spread from there; that's a single account, not an FAA finding. ABC News noted both Chicago airports had already been grounded earlier in the afternoon for an equipment outage, and Newsweek counts this as only the third nationwide ground stop ever. Every Bay Area airport got caught in it. KQED confirmed that planes weren't departing from SFO, Oakland, San José Mineta or Sacramento, that SFO spokesperson Doug Yakel said inbound flights would keep landing, and that the Governor's Office said the state was "closely monitoring" the ground stop. Long ground stops can also leave crews at risk of reaching legal duty-hour limits. There was a sliver of good news by midafternoon. The SF Standard reported that Pacific-bound flights at SFO were cleared to resume about two hours in, with a plane lifting off around 2:30 p.m. and stranded travelers cheering a second takeoff before 3. The same report said the FAA later extended the broader stop to 8:30 p.m. Pacific, and that San José's airport told travelers it didn't know when operations would return to normal. SFO had already been having a day, with FAA wind-and-weather delays in place before any of this started, and SFist noticed the FAA's own status page was still blaming a 138-minute average delay on wind, with no mention of the national shutdown. A nationwide outage on top of the weather delays feels like piling on. The administration's message has been consistent, if thin. Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin told reporters there was "no indication as of yet that this was a nefarious attack against us," per The Hill , though he also said officials aren't "ruling out anything at this point," as GeekWire quoted him. Multiple officials from multiple agencies told NBC News they hadn't seen the kind of activity normally associated with a cyberattack, while cautioning it's early. Bloomberg, as relayed by MS NOW , reported the FBI doesn't believe a cyberattack or criminality was involved. Here's the awkward part. An airline source told CNN that controllers were on a crisis call with still no clear answer on the cause, and a congressional official told Scripps News that neither the White House nor the Pentagon knew what had happened. The cause remained unclear even as officials said they had seen no signs of a cyberattack. For what it's worth, Mullin said President Trump had been briefed, according to CNN . Here's the sequence, as best it can be pieced together. The FAA began using SMART, short for Strategic Management of Airspace, Routes and Trajectories, in a "limited mode" around Washington in September, per Bloomberg via AviationPros , then expanded it to all 22 centers, according to Airways , which cites a November 10 FAA statement. The SF Standard describes the expansion as coming a day before the outage, so the exact date is murky, but every account puts it ahead of Friday. SMART is an AI air-traffic planning tool, a different layer from the radios and radar reportedly affected Friday. Mullin said officials weren't "ruling out anything at this point," while the tool's maker said the stop "is not based on or a result of the SMART system," per NBC News . SMART had gone nationwide before Friday's stop, but whether the two are connected remains unclear. Nature abhors a vacuum, and the internet abhors an unexplained outage. As of this writing, we couldn't find any named public figure putting a specific accusation of sabotage or cover-up on the record; what we found instead was a lot of "just asking questions," which is how these things usually start. Everything in this section is unverified, and we've labeled it accordingly. The claim: Iran, or another adversary, took down air traffic control. Where it comes from: the U.S. and Israel went to war with Iran on February 28, and in April the FBI, CISA and NSA warned that Iran-affiliated hackers were disrupting American critical infrastructure, TechCrunch reported. Colin Clarke of the Soufan Group told Yahoo News he'd fielded several texts asking "This is the Iranians, right?" while saying he'd seen no evidence cyberterrorism was behind the stop. The reality check: officials say there's no indication of an attack, and Google threat analyst John Hultquist observed back in March that Iranian hackers often "fabricate and exaggerate their effects," per Defense One . And in 2023, the last nationwide stop also set off cyberattack fears before the FAA concluded contract workers had accidentally deleted files, as NPR reported. The dull explanation has a strong track record here, though "strong" is not the same as "always." The claim: the FAA's new AI system broke the airspace. Where it comes from: the timing laid out above, plus Mullin's refusal to rule it out, which GeekWire also reported. The reality check: Air Space Intelligence said the stop "is not based on or a result of the SMART system," in a statement NBC News quoted, and the FAA has said SMART makes recommendations facilities can accept or decline and can't take control of an aircraft, per Airways . On paper, a scheduling advisor shouldn't be able to knock out radios and radar, which are different layers of the system, though "on paper" has not been the FAA's strongest argument this year. Of course, a company denying fault is also what companies do, which is why the investigation matters. The claim: the FAA stoppage, Thursday's Microsoft 365 outage and a Friday-afternoon National Weather Service outage are one coordinated event. Where it comes from: the NWS said it was dealing with nationwide internet and communications problems, Reuters reported, and WND put "Coincidence?" in its headline over a roundup of social posts while acknowledging there was no confirmed link. Polymarket and Mario Nawfal flagged the weather outage alongside the ground stop, and Gunther Eagleman's post is a representative sample: 🚨 NOW: The National Weather Service is reportedly confirming a NATIONWIDE RADAR OUTAGE. This comes less than an hour after the FAA grounded every departing flight in America over a communication issue at every Air Route Traffic Control Center. That means TWO NATIONWIDE SYSTEMS went down on the same afternoon. Nobody has said yet whether the two are connected, and Americans deserve a straight answer fast. Washington needs to tell us exactly what is going on. — Gunther Eagleman™ (@GuntherEagleman) November 13, 2026 To be fair to the poster, the post doesn't claim a hack; it asks for answers, which is a reasonable thing to want. It does lean on the words "radar outage," which is slightly misleading: per News9 , the NWS problem involved its national radar website and other online products, and local offices kept issuing warnings and forecasts, as KESQ noted. The reality check: three senior officials told NBC News there's nothing to indicate a connection to the Microsoft outage, and Mullin dismissed the idea with "Those are separate issues," per Ticker News . IVN reports Microsoft attributed its outage to a network capacity upgrade followed by a network change, with no sign of malicious activity. What no one we found has addressed directly is the Weather Service overlap, and the SF Standard noted officials haven't confirmed whether those two outages are related, so that one is an open question rather than a conspiracy. The strongest version of the skeptic's argument goes like this: early official reads are sometimes wrong, and "no evidence of an attack" is only as good as the FAA's ability to see one. On that second point, the Government Accountability Office reported September 21 that the FAA hadn't completed formal risk assessments for seven of eight spectrum-dependent systems it reviewed and lacked comprehensive real-time detection of jamming and spoofing, so some incidents can only be investigated after someone reports them, per AvWeb . The agency concurred with all nine of the watchdog's recommendations, according to the GAO . To be clear, that report describes vulnerabilities, not an incident, and no one has tied it to Friday's stop. But it's the best evidence anywhere in this story that "we found nothing" and "nothing happened" are different statements. It cuts both ways, though: in each of the recent incidents we found, the dull explanation, a deleted file or a blown circuit, beat the dramatic one. Air traffic control wobbles have been the story of the past 18 months. In spring 2025, the Philadelphia facility that handles Newark's airspace lost radar for 90 seconds and radios for 30 on April 28, with several more outages in the following weeks, according to UPI . Newark's approach control had been moved to Philadelphia in July 2024 to address chronic understaffing, per AeroCorner . This year has been no better. On August 6, a dual equipment failure at the Minneapolis center knocked out radar and voice communications for roughly two hours and triggered ground stops across multiple states, according to AeroCorner . On September 21, a blown circuit in Philadelphia led to more than 1,000 canceled flights nationwide after FAA Administrator Bryan Bedford said officials discovered the backup line had already been cut, as ABC7 reported, with PhillyVoice reporting the FAA blamed an Amtrak crew for the damage. So much for redundancy. Which brings us to the money and the politics. Congress has approved $12.5 billion for the air traffic control overhaul, and the figure cited for what's still needed has ranged from about $20 billion in September reporting from AeroCorner to $30 billion in remarks from Duffy, per Scripps News . Sen. Tammy Duckworth, the top Democrat on the aviation subcommittee, said "The safety of our skies is built on redundancies" and promised to demand answers, according to CNN , while the Senate Commerce Committee's Republican staff said the stoppage underscores the need to modernize the centers, per Yahoo News . Quick note first: this is general information, not legal advice. Under DOT's automatic refund rule, a passenger whose flight is canceled or significantly changed is entitled to a refund if they don't accept the alternative flight or travel credit the airline offers, according to KOMO . "Significant" means a change of more than three hours domestically or six internationally, as Good Morning America explains, and the money is supposed to arrive without you asking, within seven days for a credit card and 20 days for other payment methods, per CNN via WHDH . The rule doesn't turn on whose fault the cancellation was, and there's no separate cash payout for the inconvenience itself, the way European passengers get, according to DeepArrival . Meals and hotels are murkier. Most major airlines have committed to give passengers meals after a long wait and hotel rooms for overnight disruptions, KOMO reports, but those promises live in each carrier's own customer-service plan and, as we understand it, generally apply when the airline is at fault. A nationwide FAA-ordered stop is about as far from "the airline's fault" as it gets, so check your carrier's plan before assuming a hotel voucher is coming; that's our read, not a ruling. Then there's the tarmac. DOT rules bar U.S. airlines from letting domestic flights sit on the tarmac more than three hours without offering passengers a chance to deplane (four hours for international), and require food and water after two hours, with exceptions for safety, security or air traffic control reasons, according to DOT . Whether a nationwide ground stop falls under the air-traffic-control exception is a question we expect lawyers will enjoy. For now, if you're stuck on a plane for hours, ask the crew what the plan is. The stop was extended to 8:30 p.m. Pacific per the SF Standard's reporting, though Latin Times reported it remained in effect with no lift timeline as of 5:45 p.m. Eastern, and Live and Let's Fly predicts Saturday will be messy even after departures resume. Beyond the logistics, keep an eye out for a named cause from the FAA or DOT, Duckworth's promised demand for answers, and whether anyone ever addresses the Weather Service overlap. Until then, check your airline's app, resist the urge to "just head to the airport," and be a little skeptical of anyone on X who sounds certain about anything at 3 p.m. on a Friday. Every Bay Area airport got caught in it. KQED confirmed that planes weren't departing from SFO, Oakland, San José Mineta or Sacramento, that SFO spokesperson Doug Yakel said inbound flights would keep landing, and that the Governor's Office said the state was "closely monitoring" the ground stop. Long ground stops can also leave crews at risk of reaching legal duty-hour limits.

There was a sliver of good news by midafternoon. The SF Standard reported that Pacific-bound flights at SFO were cleared to resume about two hours in, with a plane lifting off around 2:30 p.m. and stranded travelers cheering a second takeoff before 3. The same report said the FAA later extended the broader stop to 8:30 p.m. Pacific, and that San José's airport told travelers it didn't know when operations would return to normal.

SFO had already been having a day, with FAA wind-and-weather delays in place before any of this started, and SFist noticed the FAA's own status page was still blaming a 138-minute average delay on wind, with no mention of the national shutdown. A nationwide outage on top of the weather delays feels like piling on.

The administration's message has been consistent, if thin. Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin told reporters there was "no indication as of yet that this was a nefarious attack against us," per The Hill , though he also said officials aren't "ruling out anything at this point," as GeekWire quoted him. Multiple officials from multiple agencies told NBC News they hadn't seen the kind of activity normally associated with a cyberattack, while cautioning it's early. Bloomberg, as relayed by MS NOW , reported the FBI doesn't believe a cyberattack or criminality was involved.

Here's the awkward part. An airline source told CNN that controllers were on a crisis call with still no clear answer on the cause, and a congressional official told Scripps News that neither the White House nor the Pentagon knew what had happened. The cause remained unclear even as officials said they had seen no signs of a cyberattack.
For what it's worth, Mullin said President Trump had been briefed, according to CNN .

Here's the sequence, as best it can be pieced together. The FAA began using SMART, short for Strategic Management of Airspace, Routes and Trajectories, in a "limited mode" around Washington in September, per Bloomberg via AviationPros , then expanded it to all 22 centers, according to Airways , which cites a November 10 FAA statement. The SF Standard describes the expansion as coming a day before the outage, so the exact date is murky, but every account puts it ahead of Friday.
SMART is an AI air-traffic planning tool, a different layer from the radios and radar reportedly affected Friday.

Mullin said officials weren't "ruling out anything at this point," while the tool's maker said the stop "is not based on or a result of the SMART system," per NBC News . SMART had gone nationwide before Friday's stop, but whether the two are connected remains unclear.

Nature abhors a vacuum, and the internet abhors an unexplained outage. As of this writing, we couldn't find any named public figure putting a specific accusation of sabotage or cover-up on the record; what we found instead was a lot of "just asking questions," which is how these things usually start. Everything in this section is unverified, and we've labeled it accordingly.

The claim: Iran, or another adversary, took down air traffic control. Where it comes from: the U.S. and Israel went to war with Iran on February 28, and in April the FBI, CISA and NSA warned that Iran-affiliated hackers were disrupting American critical infrastructure, TechCrunch reported. Colin Clarke of the Soufan Group told Yahoo News he'd fielded several texts asking "This is the Iranians, right?" while saying he'd seen no evidence cyberterrorism was behind the stop.

The reality check: officials say there's no indication of an attack, and Google threat analyst John Hultquist observed back in March that Iranian hackers often "fabricate and exaggerate their effects," per Defense One . And in 2023, the last nationwide stop also set off cyberattack fears before the FAA concluded contract workers had accidentally deleted files, as NPR reported. The dull explanation has a strong track record here, though "strong" is not the same as "always."
The claim: the FAA's new AI system broke the airspace. Where it comes from: the timing laid out above, plus Mullin's refusal to rule it out, which GeekWire also reported.

The reality check: Air Space Intelligence said the stop "is not based on or a result of the SMART system," in a statement NBC News quoted, and the FAA has said SMART makes recommendations facilities can accept or decline and can't take control of an aircraft, per Airways . On paper, a scheduling advisor shouldn't be able to knock out radios and radar, which are different layers of the system, though "on paper" has not been the FAA's strongest argument this year. Of course, a company denying fault is also what companies do, which is why the investigation matters.

The claim: the FAA stoppage, Thursday's Microsoft 365 outage and a Friday-afternoon National Weather Service outage are one coordinated event. Where it comes from: the NWS said it was dealing with nationwide internet and communications problems, Reuters reported, and WND put "Coincidence?" in its headline over a roundup of social posts while acknowledging there was no confirmed link. Polymarket and Mario Nawfal flagged the weather outage alongside the ground stop, and Gunther Eagleman's post is a representative sample:

🚨 NOW: The National Weather Service is reportedly confirming a NATIONWIDE RADAR OUTAGE. This comes less than an hour after the FAA grounded every departing flight in America over a communication issue at every Air Route Traffic Control Center. That means TWO NATIONWIDE SYSTEMS went down on the same afternoon. Nobody has said yet whether the two are connected, and Americans deserve a straight answer fast. Washington needs to tell us exactly what is going on.
— Gunther Eagleman™ (@GuntherEagleman) November 13, 2026

To be fair to the poster, the post doesn't claim a hack; it asks for answers, which is a reasonable thing to want. It does lean on the words "radar outage," which is slightly misleading: per News9 , the NWS problem involved its national radar website and other online products, and local offices kept issuing warnings and forecasts, as KESQ noted.

The reality check: three senior officials told NBC News there's nothing to indicate a connection to the Microsoft outage, and Mullin dismissed the idea with "Those are separate issues," per Ticker News . IVN reports Microsoft attributed its outage to a network capacity upgrade followed by a network change, with no sign of malicious activity. What no one we found has addressed directly is the Weather Service overlap, and the SF Standard noted officials haven't confirmed whether those two outages are related, so that one is an open question rather than a conspiracy.

The strongest version of the skeptic's argument goes like this: early official reads are sometimes wrong, and "no evidence of an attack" is only as good as the FAA's ability to see one. On that second point, the Government Accountability Office reported September 21 that the FAA hadn't completed formal risk assessments for seven of eight spectrum-dependent systems it reviewed and lacked comprehensive real-time detection of jamming and spoofing, so some incidents can only be investigated after someone reports them, per AvWeb . The agency concurred with all nine of the watchdog's recommendations, according to the GAO .

To be clear, that report describes vulnerabilities, not an incident, and no one has tied it to Friday's stop. But it's the best evidence anywhere in this story that "we found nothing" and "nothing happened" are different statements. It cuts both ways, though: in each of the recent incidents we found, the dull explanation, a deleted file or a blown circuit, beat the dramatic one.

Air traffic control wobbles have been the story of the past 18 months. In spring 2025, the Philadelphia facility that handles Newark's airspace lost radar for 90 seconds and radios for 30 on April 28, with several more outages in the following weeks, according to UPI . Newark's approach control had been moved to Philadelphia in July 2024 to address chronic understaffing, per AeroCorner .

This year has been no better. On August 6, a dual equipment failure at the Minneapolis center knocked out radar and voice communications for roughly two hours and triggered ground stops across multiple states, according to AeroCorner . On September 21, a blown circuit in Philadelphia led to more than 1,000 canceled flights nationwide after FAA Administrator Bryan Bedford said officials discovered the backup line had already been cut, as ABC7 reported, with PhillyVoice reporting the FAA blamed an Amtrak crew for the damage. So much for redundancy.

Which brings us to the money and the politics. Congress has approved $12.5 billion for the air traffic control overhaul, and the figure cited for what's still needed has ranged from about $20 billion in September reporting from AeroCorner to $30 billion in remarks from Duffy, per Scripps News . Sen. Tammy Duckworth, the top Democrat on the aviation subcommittee, said "The safety of our skies is built on redundancies" and promised to demand answers, according to CNN , while the Senate Commerce Committee's Republican staff said the stoppage underscores the need to modernize the centers, per Yahoo News .

Quick note first: this is general information, not legal advice. Under DOT's automatic refund rule, a passenger whose flight is canceled or significantly changed is entitled to a refund if they don't accept the alternative flight or travel credit the airline offers, according to KOMO . "Significant" means a change of more than three hours domestically or six internationally, as Good Morning America explains, and the money is supposed to arrive without you asking, within seven days for a credit card and 20 days for other payment methods, per CNN via WHDH . The rule doesn't turn on whose fault the cancellation was, and there's no separate cash payout for the inconvenience itself, the way European passengers get, according to DeepArrival .

Meals and hotels are murkier. Most major airlines have committed to give passengers meals after a long wait and hotel rooms for overnight disruptions, KOMO reports, but those promises live in each carrier's own customer-service plan and, as we understand it, generally apply when the airline is at fault. A nationwide FAA-ordered stop is about as far from "the airline's fault" as it gets, so check your carrier's plan before assuming a hotel voucher is coming; that's our read, not a ruling.

Then there's the tarmac. DOT rules bar U.S. airlines from letting domestic flights sit on the tarmac more than three hours without offering passengers a chance to deplane (four hours for international), and require food and water after two hours, with exceptions for safety, security or air traffic control reasons, according to DOT . Whether a nationwide ground stop falls under the air-traffic-control exception is a question we expect lawyers will enjoy. For now, if you're stuck on a plane for hours, ask the crew what the plan is.

The stop was extended to 8:30 p.m. Pacific per the SF Standard's reporting, though Latin Times reported it remained in effect with no lift timeline as of 5:45 p.m. Eastern, and Live and Let's Fly predicts Saturday will be messy even after departures resume. Beyond the logistics, keep an eye out for a named cause from the FAA or DOT, Duckworth's promised demand for answers, and whether anyone ever addresses the Weather Service overlap.
Until then, check your airline's app, resist the urge to "just head to the airport," and be a little skeptical of anyone on X who sounds certain about anything at 3 p.m. on a Friday.

coreStoryFacts.text: Air Space Intelligence, the AI tech startup that is a vendor for the FAA on its new SMART system for air traffic control, said its software didn't cause today's nationwide ground stop.

The US grounded all flights for several hours Friday, sparking travel chaos across the vast country, after what government officials said was a major communications outage caused by decades old technology.- Confusion and delays - The stop sparked chaos and misery at airports around the country.

The United States on Friday lifted an hours-long ground stop at the nation's airports, with top officials explaining that the disruption was due to old equipment and not a cyberattack or sweeping Microsoft outage.Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin dismissed speculation about a coordinated cyber assault on the United States, or any link to the Microsoft outage that affected services worldwide.
Bloomberg reported that the FBI doesn't believe the outage was a cyberattack or criminal act, and that one line of inquiry is whether a software update caused it.
An update is a far more ordinary explanation than a hack, and in some ways a more uncomfortable one, because it means a national system can be taken down by its own maintenance.

The FAA then ordered a nationwide ground stop, telling airlines that "all departing traffic should remain groundstopped until further notice" and citing "extraordinary circumstances and reasons of safety." Planes already in the air were allowed to land, and international arrivals were handled case by case.
Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy said the fault hit every one of the FAA's en route air traffic control centers, and CBS News counted about 8,000 delays and 400 cancellations within hours.
Investigators haven't named the update, its author or a restart time.
In January 2023 the FAA's NOTAM system failure stopped departures nationwide for under two hours, and the agency said files were unintentionally deleted during work on its databases.
In July 2024 a faulty CrowdStrike update crashed about 8.5 million Windows machines, by Microsoft's estimate, and Delta alone said it lost around $500 million.
The pattern is the same each time: a small change, a wide blast radius, and no cheap way back.
Planes sat at gates from Chicago to New York on Friday while investigators asked whether a routine software change, not a hacker, knocked out the radios air traffic controllers depend on.
For now the facts are short: no named update, no confirmed cause, and no public timetable from the FAA for getting every departure moving again.

The @FAAnews issued a nationwide ground stop for all U.S. airports following a communication issue impacting all Air Route Traffic Control Centers.
That ground stop took place in 2023 , when the FAA suffered an outage of the system that sends messages to pilots.
More than 200 flights were delayed at Chicago's airports Friday afternoon.
As of 3:11 p.m., the Chicago Department of Aviation reported 213 delays at O'Hare International Airport and another 55 at Midway International Airport.

The United States on Friday lifted an hours-long ground stop at the nation's airports, with top officials explaining that the disruption was due to old equipment and not a cyberattack or sweeping Microsoft outage.Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin dismissed speculation about a coordinated cyber assault on the United States, or any link to the Microsoft outage that affected services worldwide.
Bloomberg reported that the FBI doesn't believe the outage was a cyberattack or criminal act, and that one line of inquiry is whether a software update caused it.
An update is a far more ordinary explanation than a hack, and in some ways a more uncomfortable one, because it means a national system can be taken down by its own maintenance.

The FAA then ordered a nationwide ground stop, telling airlines that "all departing traffic should remain groundstopped until further notice" and citing "extraordinary circumstances and reasons of safety." Planes already in the air were allowed to land, and international arrivals were handled case by case.
Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy said the fault hit every one of the FAA's en route air traffic control centers, and CBS News counted about 8,000 delays and 400 cancellations within hours.
Investigators haven't named the update, its author or a restart time.
In January 2023 the FAA's NOTAM system failure stopped departures nationwide for under two hours, and the agency said files were unintentionally deleted during work on its databases.
In July 2024 a faulty CrowdStrike update crashed about 8.5 million Windows machines, by Microsoft's estimate, and Delta alone said it lost around $500 million.
The pattern is the same each time: a small change, a wide blast radius, and no cheap way back.
Planes sat at gates from Chicago to New York on Friday while investigators asked whether a routine software change, not a hacker, knocked out the radios air traffic controllers depend on.
For now the facts are short: no named update, no confirmed cause, and no public timetable from the FAA for getting every departure moving again.

That ground stop took place in 2023 , when the FAA suffered an outage of the system that sends messages to pilots.
More than 200 flights were delayed at Chicago's airports Friday afternoon.

One pilot told Yahoo News the trouble started at Kansas City Center, which covers the middle of the country, and spread from there; that's a single account, not an FAA finding.
ABC News noted both Chicago airports had already been grounded earlier in the afternoon for an equipment outage, and Newsweek counts this as only the third nationwide ground stop ever.

Pacific on Friday, the FAA ordered every departing flight in America to stay exactly where it was, a move the agency had pulled only twice before: on September 11, 2001, and one January morning in 2023.
The official reason, as of this writing, is a "temporary telecommunications outage" somewhere in the web of radios and radar that keeps airliners from meeting each other at 35,000 feet.

The stop also landed just days after the agency took a new AI air-traffic planning tool nationwide, and the Homeland Security secretary says he isn't ruling anything out, though so far nothing ties the two together and officials say they see no sign of an attack.

On that second point, the Government Accountability Office reported September 21 that the FAA hadn't completed formal risk assessments for seven of eight spectrum-dependent systems it reviewed and lacked comprehensive real-time detection of jamming and spoofing, so some incidents can only be investigated after someone reports them, per AvWeb .
The agency concurred with all nine of the watchdog's recommendations, according to the GAO .

The FAA began using SMART, short for Strategic Management of Airspace, Routes and Trajectories, in a "limited mode" around Washington in September, per Bloomberg via AviationPros , then expanded it to all 22 centers, according to Airways , which cites a November 10 FAA statement.

One law enforcement source told CBS the problem involved radio frequencies and how pilots and controllers talk to each other.

Beyond that, the record is thin. The FAA hasn't confirmed a cause, and nobody has said publicly which update is under suspicion, who wrote it, or whether it was pushed to every center at once. The cost is already large. CBS counted about 3,100 aircraft bound for US airports when the stop began, and within a short time at least 8,000 delays and 400 cancellations. Airlines now face the slower job of repositioning planes and crews, and a delay of a few hours at the centre of the network spreads for a day or more.

Probably not, and officials say so. Microsoft's Exchange Online problems began shortly before 1 p.m. Eastern on Thursday (about 6 p.m. UK time) and spread to Outlook, Teams, SharePoint and Copilot. Asked about a link, Mullin said: "I don't see any reason to connect those two at all. Those are separate issues." ABC News reported that Microsoft said there was no hack behind its outage either.

Still, two systemic failures in 24 hours will feel like one story to anyone who relies on both, and the common thread isn't a shared vendor. It's that each looks like a change that went wrong inside a system too important to fail quietly.

Frankly, we've been here before. In January 2023 the FAA's NOTAM system failure stopped departures nationwide for under two hours, and the agency said files were unintentionally deleted during work on its databases. The pattern is the same each time: a small change, a wide blast radius, and no cheap way back.

If you build software that other businesses run on, the lesson is dull and expensive. Roll changes out to a small slice first. Keep a rollback you've actually tested. Don't let one vendor, one cable or one release train touch every site at the same moment. For now the facts are short: no named update, no confirmed cause, and no public timetable from the FAA for getting every departure moving again.
