See what 10M+ investors are talking about. Get the Stocktwits Daily Rip for what retail is watching right now, free to your inbox
According to market commentator The Kobeissi Letter, the selling pressure led to a loss of about $150 billion in crypto markets over 48 hours.
Although Bitcoin is falling to its lowest level in months, some experts believe that now is a good time to enter.
Crypto analyst Michaël van de Poppe said in a post on X that he has been buying BTC, outlining five reasons for his move.

He noted that the "terrible sentiment" around the underlying asset means it is hard for prices to keep declining, adding that while there have been multiple events for the asset price to crash, it hasn't yet and markets are simply witnessing a 20% correction.
He also pointed out that this is a support area, "just barely beneath the 200-Day MA and ideal for liquidity."
The analyst said that Bitcoin had already bottomed on the Friday prior to the SpaceX IPO and that he "wouldn't be surprised" if the present scenario was at the same cadence.
"Fifthly: Nasdaq is already up a lot, meaning that there's a gap between Bitcoin and the Nasdaq. It doesn't take long for this gap to close, which is why I've been buying Bitcoin today," he said.

Meanwhile, Anthony Pompliano, Founder and CEO of Professional Capital Management, said in a post on X, "Bitcoin is falling to prices we haven't seen since…..3 months ago. Everyone relax, so you can realize that AI and bitcoin are one big trade now."
However, long-time crypto critic Peter Schiff is not convinced. In a post on X, he implored investors to think about how Bitcoin has been trading relative to 2021.

"Think about this, HOLDers. Bitcoin just traded at a lower price than it traded in November 2021. How many of you who owned Bitcoin back then expected it to be below the Nov. 2021 high more than five years later? Bitcoin is in a long-term bear market. The long-term trend is down," he argued.

Rich Rosenblum, co-founder of crypto market maker GSR, told Bloomberg that the volatility in the AI trade and continued U.S. dollar strength have impacted some long Bitcoin positions negatively, while the red-hot inflation data and changes in Nvidia Corp.'s (NVDA) leadership amid Jensen Huang's resignation are also weighing on risk assets.

Dean Chen, an analyst at crypto exchange Bitunix, also said in a note Thursday, as per Bloomberg, "Bitcoin is showing signs of a changing market structure, with selling pressure concentrated in derivatives while spot market activity remains comparatively resilient."

Meanwhile, futures cumulative volume delta, a measure that tracks how aggressive buyers or sellers are in the futures market, has turned deeply negative, he noted, while adding that open interest has also declined. "Taken together, these indicators suggest that leveraged exposure is cooling, but market positioning remains mixed," Chen reportedly said.

Crypto-linked equities fell alongside cryptocurrencies late Thursday. Strategy (MSTR), Bitmine Immersion Technologies (BMNR), Strive (ASST), Coinbase Global Inc. (COIN), and Robinhood Markets Inc. (HOOD) all saw their shares decline in the overnight trade.
Strategy also faces pressure after MSCI Inc. said it would remove the company from its global indexes after the Nov. 30 rebalancing, likely prompting an exodus from passive funds.

Caroline Mauron, co-founder of Orbit Markets, told Bloomberg that MSCI's decision to drop Strategy, which is the largest corporate buyer of BTC, from its global equity benchmarks has also been a factor affecting the cryptocurrency.
On Stocktwits, retail sentiment around BTC was 'extremely bearish' at the time of writing, while it was 'bearish' for ETH.
Sentiment around MSTR was 'extremely bearish,' while ASST, COIN, and HOOD were in 'bearish' territory. Retail sentiment around BMNR improved from 'neutral' to 'bullish' over 24 hours.

The world's largest cryptocurrency dropped 7.2% to trade at $68,143 as of 0900GMT, fluctuating between a 24-hour low of $67,653 and a high of $73,638. It has lost 33.8% since the beginning of this year. The total market capitalization of all cryptocurrencies contracted 5.8% to $2.3 trillion. Ethereum, the second-largest cryptocurrency, also slid 6.5% over the last 24 hours to trade around $1,610. Treasury yields surged following stronger-than-expected US inflation data, while persistent price pressures were compounded by elevated oil prices. Hawkish comments from Federal Reserve officials further fueled market concerns, with some policymakers suggesting a 50-basis-point rate increase may be warranted. Meanwhile, Democrats secured victory in the November midterm elections, gaining control of both chambers of the US Congress starting next year. The election outcome raised investor expectations of increased regulatory scrutiny of the crypto industry.

He also pointed out that this is a support area, "just barely beneath the 200-Day MA and ideal for liquidity." The analyst said that Bitcoin had already bottomed on the Friday prior to the SpaceX IPO and that he "wouldn't be surprised" if the present scenario was at the same cadence. "Fifthly: Nasdaq is already up a lot, meaning that there's a gap between Bitcoin and the Nasdaq. It doesn't take long for this gap to close, which is why I've been buying Bitcoin today," he said. Meanwhile, futures cumulative volume delta, a measure that tracks how aggressive buyers or sellers are in the futures market, has turned deeply negative, he noted, while adding that open interest has also declined. "Taken together, these indicators suggest that leveraged exposure is cooling, but market positioning remains mixed," Chen reportedly said. (HOOD) all saw their shares decline in the overnight trade. Strategy also faces pressure after MSCI Inc. said it would remove the company from its global indexes after the Nov. 30 rebalancing, likely prompting an exodus from passive funds. Caroline Mauron, co-founder of Orbit Markets, told Bloomberg that MSCI's decision to drop Strategy, which is the largest corporate buyer of BTC, from its global equity benchmarks has also been a factor affecting the cryptocurrency. NVIDIA Founder Jensen Huang's Alleged Spy Associate Alice Huang Was Deeply Tied To Another Chinese Firm With Access To Banned NVIDIA Chips, Says Report

sources.title: Bloomberg details web of Chinese AI companies with smuggled NVIDIA chips linked to Alice Huang - Engadget
passages: A Chinese company with ties to Alice Huang procured NVIDIA AI chips banned in the country, which were then installed at a Shanghai AI facility that also has ties to Alice Huang, according to Bloomberg .

The publication says the documents it has reviewed for its report shows explicit evidence that there's a network of Chinese companies, which have managed to get their hands on NVIDIA chips that weren't supposed to be sold in China, with Huang at the center.
Bloomberg found the hardware details in filings from a company called Shanghai Longteng Intelligent Computing, which was set up by Alice a decade ago.
They were documented as part of the information the company had to submit to the Chinese government, since it was using its servers as a collateral for financing.
The filings also revealed that the company's servers included 52 units made by Super Micro Computer Inc.
Its president is Kang Wei, who is being reported as Alice's husband and the person who introduced her to Jensen Huang .
Former NVIDIA-CEO Jensen Huang is due to testify before Congress this month , and it's likely all of this information will be pored over by officials in the run-up to the event.
To the public, Alice was an executive at Singaporean company Megaspeed, but the reports that had come out since the issue blew up paint a different picture of who she truly was.
Aperia purchased 22 servers from Dell containing NVIDIA H800 chips, which are banned in China.

extraction.body: The NVIDIA chips involved are banned in China. A Chinese company with ties to Alice Huang procured NVIDIA AI chips banned in the country, which were then installed at a Shanghai AI facility that also has ties to Alice Huang, according to Bloomberg . The publication says the documents it has reviewed for its report shows explicit evidence that there's a network of Chinese companies, which have managed to get their hands on NVIDIA chips that weren't supposed to be sold in China, with Huang at the center. To the public, Alice was an executive at Singaporean company Megaspeed, but the reports that had come out since the issue blew up paint a different picture of who she truly was. Bloomberg says the NVIDIA chips listed in the documents it reviewed were sold to Aperia Cloud Services, an NVIDIA Cloud Partner in Singapore. Aperia purchased 22 servers from Dell containing NVIDIA H800 chips, which are banned in China. According to the report, Dell cut off business ties with Aperia in February 2025 due to concerns around the deal. Bloomberg found the hardware details in filings from a company called Shanghai Longteng Intelligent Computing, which was set up by Alice a decade ago. They were documented as part of the information the company had to submit to the Chinese government, since it was using its servers as a collateral for financing. While Alice hasn't been part of Shanghai Longteng since 2017 — and the documents didn't say if she was personally involved in the procurement of the chips — Huang Yu, who was identified as her sister, was the one who took over as majority owner. The filings also revealed that the company's servers included 52 units made by Super Micro Computer Inc. Those units were equipped with NVIDIA's H100 or H200 chips, which can't be sold to Chinese companies without express permission from the US government. The Shanghai AI facility where the smuggled NVIDIA units were installed is called the Yangtze River Delta Project, which Bloomberg says also has ties to Alice Huang. Its president is Kang Wei, who is being reported as Alice's husband and the person who introduced her to Jensen Huang . Alice's company Megaspeed also presented a rendering of the Yangtze River Delta Project to its investors in 2024 and claimed that it was its largest AI facility. Former NVIDIA-CEO Jensen Huang is due to testify before Congress this month , and it's likely all of this information will be pored over by officials in the run-up to the event.

The new details share another link with Alice Huang, whose firm Megaspeed has already been probed for supplying banned NVIDIA AI chips to China. While reports suggest that the US intelligence community is unconvinced that Alice Huang, the associate of NVIDIA CEO Jensen Huang, was a spy, her links to transporting banned GPUs to China are nevertheless present in Bloomberg's analysis of filings with Chinese regulators. In a report , the publication shares that a holding company called Shanghai Longteng Intelligent Computing Data Group Co. ended up gaining access to servers purchased by Aperia Cloud from Dell. Aperia's CEO is facing charges for fraud related to the smuggling of NVIDIA GPUs to China. A Longteng unit (Shanghai Longjie Yaoteng) then used these servers as part of a group of equipment as collateral for financing, says the report, which adds that Alice founded Longteng in 2016 and relinquished shares in 2017. The details about the holding company, which is tied to a Shanghai data center with links to Megaspeed, come as the Southeast Asian nation of Malaysia further tightens GPU rules. Amidst the firestorm created by the former NVIDIA CEO, Minister of Investment, Trade and Industry Datuk Seri Johari Abdul Ghani shared earlier today that his country was evaluating current laws to determine whether they could target GPU re-exports to comply with the US sanctions. US lawmakers are also advancing legislation to prevent Chinese AI companies from accessing restricted chips remotely, with 'footprints' of the banned Blackwell GPUs discovered in forensic analysis of leading Chinese AI models. While Bloomberg also claims that servers manufactured by Super Micro, using the H100 or H200 chips, were also part of the regulatory disclosure, the firm asserted that it did not directly make any such sales. However, the firm's statement claimed that the actions of the indicted were against its rules and policies and in line with US law. passages: Singapore, a hub for billions of dollars' worth of Nvidia sales each year, finds itself increasingly in the crosshairs of Washington's push to stop advanced AI chips from reaching China, as the chipmaker CEO's scandal once again thrusts the city-state into the spotlight.
Nvidia chips can be legally sold to customers in other countries, such as Malaysia or Singapore, and then illicitly resold or re-exported to China.
The alleged transactions in the broader case totaled about $390 million, prosecutors said March last year.
Singapore has faced growing international scrutiny, particularly from the U.S., over its role as a major billing and potential transit hub for Nvidia chips that U.S. officials say have reached China.

Nvidia's revenue linked to Singapore rose to 22% in the fiscal quarter ending July 2025, up from 8% in 2023, with the country's trade ministry estimating chips physically delivered there accounted for less than 1% of the chipmaker's revenue.

Megaspeed, which was spun off from a Chinese gaming company, became Nvidia's largest Southeast Asian customer in less than three years and has bought more than $4.8 billion worth of its chips since June 2024, according to The New York Times, though the company has denied any wrongdoing.
Nvidia appointed Chief Financial Officer Colette Kress as interim CEO while its board searches for a permanent successor.

extraction.body: Singapore, a hub for billions of dollars' worth of Nvidia sales each year, finds itself increasingly in the crosshairs of Washington's push to stop advanced AI chips from reaching China, as the chipmaker CEO's scandal once again thrusts the city-state into the spotlight. The Southeast Asian nation said Thursday that it had barred Alice Huang, the businesswoman at the center of a scandal that catalyzed the end of Jensen Huang's run as Nvidia CEO, from re-entering the country. A fifth person was handed 41 charges on Friday in a Singapore fraud case involving computer servers that might have contained Nvidia chips and were exported to Malaysia. The alleged transactions in the broader case totaled about $390 million, prosecutors said March last year. The investigations into several companies and key officials, including Megaspeed International, began in February 2025 and remained ongoing as of Thursday. Authorities have been examining whether servers exported through Singapore to Malaysia without entering the domestic market were subsequently rerouted to another destination, contrary to declarations made in Singapore, the Ministry of Home Affairs said in a statement late Thursday. Singapore has faced growing international scrutiny, particularly from the U.S., over its role as a major billing and potential transit hub for Nvidia chips that U.S. officials say have reached China. The U.S. has imposed export restrictions on Nvidia's most cutting-edge AI chips to China since 2022 to curb Beijing's surging AI development. Nvidia's revenue linked to Singapore rose to 22% in the fiscal quarter ending July 2025, up from 8% in 2023, with the country's trade ministry estimating chips physically delivered there accounted for less than 1% of the chipmaker's revenue. Experts have pointed to gaps in enforcement of U.S. export restrictions and Singapore's corporate system that make it hard to trace where advanced Nvidia chips ultimately end up. Nvidia chips can be legally sold to customers in other countries, such as Malaysia or Singapore, and then illicitly resold or re-exported to China. Chinese companies can also legally gain remote access to the most advanced AI chips hosted in data centers outside China rather than buying the hardware directly. Chris McGuire, a senior fellow at Council on Foreign Relations and former U.S. national security official, said that Southeast Asia has become "a major hub for chip smuggling and export control circumvention," importing tens of billions of dollars' worth of AI chips per year. Singapore has stepped up efforts to police suspected chip diversion since last year, including investigations involving alleged fraud and money laundering. Authorities acknowledged the potential "blind spots between separate monitoring of trade flows and banking flows," said Alvin Camba, lead scientist and director of research at Lyvi, an Austin-based AI risk assessment firm. Correlating physical shipments with related financial transactions can be "challenging," he added. "Singapore's strong corporate secrecy regulations, which offer extensive protections for foreign investors, can also make it difficult to rapidly identify the true recipients of goods," Camba said. Those challenges can be exploited to "obfuscate financial flows and potentially circumvent global restrictions on technology transfers," he added, urging constant adaptation from regulators. Singapore said it had received limited help from U.S. authorities in its yearlong investigation. Police sought information on Super Micro Computer Inc., a U.S. server supplier relevant to the probe, but the company provided limited cooperation, according to the Thursday statement. The city-state first raised the issue with U.S. authorities in July 2025, and has repeated its request on several occasions since September last year. "Despite these repeated requests, Singapore has to date received limited information or assistance in respect of the company," it said. Police interviewed Alice Huang, a Hong Kong resident who was then Megaspeed's CEO, chairperson and a key controller, in June 2025. In February 2026, authorities concluded that there was insufficient evidence that she had committed offenses related to the declarations under investigation. She was nonetheless barred from re-entering Singapore after being found providing inaccurate information to downplay her role in Megaspeed. The country does not enforce "unilateral export controls" imposed by other countries, the ministry said in Thursday's statement, but it expects companies operating there to take foreign export rules into account in their international business activities. Megaspeed, which was spun off from a Chinese gaming company, became Nvidia's largest Southeast Asian customer in less than three years and has bought more than $4.8 billion worth of its chips since June 2024, according to The New York Times, though the company has denied any wrongdoing. Alice Huang, whom U.S. intelligence identified as a Chinese intelligence asset passing information to Beijing, served as managing director at Megaspeed for eight months in 2023 but has reportedly continued to play a leading role at the company. Jensen Huang has resigned as Nvidia CEO on Thursday, ending 33 years at the helm after revelations that he had two extramarital affairs, plunging the chipmaker at the heart of the global AI boom into crisis. extraction.body: Megaspeed International, which has presented itself as an Nvidia cloud partner, has again come under scrutiny as suspicions grow that restricted Nvidia chips have entered China. 12 that Megaspeed is headquartered in Singapore and has operated subsidiaries and data centres across Southeast Asia.At the centre of the controversy is the relationship between Megaspeed’s former management and Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang (젠슨 황). People connected to U.S. intelligence authorities, cited by the New York Times, identified Alice Huang as a figure recruited by China’s Ministry of State Security to collect information related to Jensen Huang. The Information reported that Alice Huang was involved in helping facilitate shipments of Nvidia chips worth at least $7.5 billion to Chinese companies, based on her ties to Jensen Huang. Nvidia’s board is investigating whether its CEO was targeted by a foreign intelligence agency.Megaspeed was established as 7Road International in 2015. SwiftData, a Singapore entity set up in October 2023, now owns a 100 percent stake. The registered director is Singapore citizen Tan Yong Phong (탄용퐁). Alice Huang served as an executive director for 8 months in 2023 and received 1 Megaspeed share for 1 Singapore dollar on the day she stepped down.The company’s scale expanded sharply over a short period. Megaspeed introduced itself as an Nvidia cloud partner in the Asia-Pacific region and said it provides access to GB200 NVL72 and HGX H100 systems. Assets rose from $75 in 2022 to $33 million in 2023 and about $3 billion in 2024. Revenue increased from $0 in 2023 to $294 million in 2024, but it posted a net loss of about $20 million.Singapore police opened an investigation in October 2025 into the possibility that Megaspeed violated domestic laws. Singapore’s Ministry of Home Affairs, however, denied a Wall Street Journal report that authorities had investigated suspicions of Alice Huang’s links to Chinese intelligence agencies.In Malaysia, Speedmatrix and MS Fusion, which are known to be linked to Megaspeed, use addresses within the same development site. Speedmatrix is known to have purchased advanced AI equipment worth at least $4.8 billion, including systems containing Nvidia chips, from June 2024 to February 2026. A U.S. trade official in 2025 confirmed boxes of unopened Nvidia chips at a Speedmatrix data centre, raising suspicions that the equipment may have been illegally re-exported to China. No conclusive evidence proving illegal diversion was confirmed at the time.MS Fusion, despite having no revenue, agreed in August 2025 to buy a 52.5-acre industrial site in Kota Tinggi for 263.2 million ringgit. It later paid 225.9 million ringgit in overdue charges in September after receiving a default notice from the seller, Crescendo Corp. Malaysian Investment, Trade and Industry Minister Johari Abdul Ghani (조하리 압둘 가니) said the country will ensure it does not become a route to bypass export controls.There is little public information on the Indonesia base. A Jakarta-based entity recorded 242 transactions in customs data through June 2026 involving 3 suppliers and 4 buyers. The transactions included imports of single Nvidia GPU H100 modules. H100 chips have been subject to U.S. licensing requirements for exports to China since August 2022.Megaspeed denies suspicions of illegal transfers of chips to China. The company said that on-site inspections and reviews by the U.S. Commerce Department’s Bureau of Industry and Security, Malaysia’s Ministry of Investment, Trade and Industry, and Nvidia in December 2025 found no evidence of violations.

Nvidia chips can be legally sold to customers in other countries, such as Malaysia or Singapore, and then illicitly resold or re-exported to China.
The alleged transactions in the broader case totaled about $390 million, prosecutors said March last year.
Singapore has faced growing international scrutiny, particularly from the U.S., over its role as a major billing and potential transit hub for Nvidia chips that U.S. officials say have reached China.

Nvidia's revenue linked to Singapore rose to 22% in the fiscal quarter ending July 2025, up from 8% in 2023, with the country's trade ministry estimating chips physically delivered there accounted for less than 1% of the chipmaker's revenue.

Megaspeed, which was spun off from a Chinese gaming company, became Nvidia's largest Southeast Asian customer in less than three years and has bought more than $4.8 billion worth of its chips since June 2024, according to The New York Times, though the company has denied any wrongdoing.
Nvidia appointed Chief Financial Officer Colette Kress as interim CEO while its board searches for a permanent successor.

Nvidia’s Blackwell chips are prohibited from being sold directly in China, which is precisely why this arrangement exists.

extraction.body: Singapore, a hub for billions of dollars' worth of Nvidia sales each year, finds itself increasingly in the crosshairs of Washington's push to stop advanced AI chips from reaching China, as the chipmaker CEO's scandal once again thrusts the city-state into the spotlight. The Southeast Asian nation said Thursday that it had barred Alice Huang, the businesswoman at the center of a scandal that catalyzed the end of Jensen Huang's run as Nvidia CEO, from re-entering the country. A fifth person was handed 41 charges on Friday in a Singapore fraud case involving computer servers that might have contained Nvidia chips and were exported to Malaysia. The alleged transactions in the broader case totaled about $390 million, prosecutors said March last year. The investigations into several companies and key officials, including Megaspeed International, began in February 2025 and remained ongoing as of Thursday. Authorities have been examining whether servers exported through Singapore to Malaysia without entering the domestic market were subsequently rerouted to another destination, contrary to declarations made in Singapore, the Ministry of Home Affairs said in a statement late Thursday. Singapore has faced growing international scrutiny, particularly from the U.S., over its role as a major billing and potential transit hub for Nvidia chips that U.S. officials say have reached China. The U.S. has imposed export restrictions on Nvidia's most cutting-edge AI chips to China since 2022 to curb Beijing's surging AI development. Nvidia's revenue linked to Singapore rose to 22% in the fiscal quarter ending July 2025, up from 8% in 2023, with the country's trade ministry estimating chips physically delivered there accounted for less than 1% of the chipmaker's revenue. Experts have pointed to gaps in enforcement of U.S. export restrictions and Singapore's corporate system that make it hard to trace where advanced Nvidia chips ultimately end up. Nvidia chips can be legally sold to customers in other countries, such as Malaysia or Singapore, and then illicitly resold or re-exported to China. Chinese companies can also legally gain remote access to the most advanced AI chips hosted in data centers outside China rather than buying the hardware directly. Chris McGuire, a senior fellow at Council on Foreign Relations and former U.S. national security official, said that Southeast Asia has become "a major hub for chip smuggling and export control circumvention," importing tens of billions of dollars' worth of AI chips per year. Singapore has stepped up efforts to police suspected chip diversion since last year, including investigations involving alleged fraud and money laundering. Authorities acknowledged the potential "blind spots between separate monitoring of trade flows and banking flows," said Alvin Camba, lead scientist and director of research at Lyvi, an Austin-based AI risk assessment firm. Correlating physical shipments with related financial transactions can be "challenging," he added. "Singapore's strong corporate secrecy regulations, which offer extensive protections for foreign investors, can also make it difficult to rapidly identify the true recipients of goods," Camba said. Those challenges can be exploited to "obfuscate financial flows and potentially circumvent global restrictions on technology transfers," he added, urging constant adaptation from regulators. Singapore said it had received limited help from U.S. authorities in its yearlong investigation. Police sought information on Super Micro Computer Inc., a U.S. server supplier relevant to the probe, but the company provided limited cooperation, according to the Thursday statement. The city-state first raised the issue with U.S. authorities in July 2025, and has repeated its request on several occasions since September last year. "Despite these repeated requests, Singapore has to date received limited information or assistance in respect of the company," it said. Police interviewed Alice Huang, a Hong Kong resident who was then Megaspeed's CEO, chairperson and a key controller, in June 2025. In February 2026, authorities concluded that there was insufficient evidence that she had committed offenses related to the declarations under investigation. She was nonetheless barred from re-entering Singapore after being found providing inaccurate information to downplay her role in Megaspeed. The country does not enforce "unilateral export controls" imposed by other countries, the ministry said in Thursday's statement, but it expects companies operating there to take foreign export rules into account in their international business activities. Megaspeed, which was spun off from a Chinese gaming company, became Nvidia's largest Southeast Asian customer in less than three years and has bought more than $4.8 billion worth of its chips since June 2024, according to The New York Times, though the company has denied any wrongdoing. Alice Huang, whom U.S. intelligence identified as a Chinese intelligence asset passing information to Beijing, served as managing director at Megaspeed for eight months in 2023 but has reportedly continued to play a leading role at the company. Jensen Huang has resigned as Nvidia CEO on Thursday, ending 33 years at the helm after revelations that he had two extramarital affairs, plunging the chipmaker at the heart of the global AI boom into crisis. Nvidia appointed Chief Financial Officer Colette Kress as interim CEO while its board searches for a permanent successor. Got a confidential news tip? We want to hear from you. extraction.body: The Federal Aviation Administration ordered a nationwide ground stop Friday for all airports due to a communication issue affecting air traffic control -- a rare move that thrust the nation's air travel into chaos. In the hours after the ground stop was issued, more than 2,000 flights were canceled and more than 10,000 were delayed as of 6:20 p.m., according to FlightAware, and lawmakers demanded answers about what had happened. The FAA's alert said the stop was "due to extraordinary circumstances and for reasons of safety." Department of Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin sought to reassure the American public, telling reporters Friday evening that there was no indication yet that the incident was a "nefarious attack" and that everyone is safe. "This isn't another 9/11. I cannot repeat that enough," he added. The nationwide ground stop was only the second since 9/11. The last time was in 2023 , when the FAA NOTAM system went down and pilots could not get their pre-departure paperwork. Mullin said the government will look into the root of the problem, but the problem appeared to be "just a telecommunications outage as of now," he told reporters. " As we investigate what caused this, you always got to assume that, as many cyber attacks that take place, that you make that assumption," Mullin said. "But as of right now, that's not known." Shortly after the stop was issued, Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy said in an X statement that it was "due a communication issue impacting all Air Route Traffic Control Centers." "FAA technicians are investigating the issue," he said in an X post. " As we investigate what caused this, you always got to assume that, as many cyber attacks that take place, that you make that assumption," Mullin said. "But as of right now, that's not known." AirSpace Intel, the contractor behind the SMART AI system that has been rolling out at facilities nationwide said in a statement on X that "The current ground stop is not based on or a result of the SMART system, any product of ASI or our integration with FAA and ATC." Mullin said "we're looking at that" when he was asked if there was a link between the rollout and the ground stop. According to Flightradar24, there were 3,100 airborne aircraft bound for U.S. airports earlier amid nationwide ground stop. No additional aircraft are taking off at this time. extraction.body: U.S. air traffic was brought to a standstill Friday after the Federal Aviation Administration ordered a nationwide ground stop for departing flights that lasted more than five hours. The FAA lifted the ground stop at 8:15 p.m. ET, after more than 7,000 flights were canceled and airports across the country became packed with stranded, irritated passengers. The sudden and stunning alert was issued at 3:54 p.m. ET, “due to extraordinary circumstances and for reasons of safety,” the FAA said. It offered no other information beyond stating that “all departing traffic should remain ground stopped until further notice.” Hours later, Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy, in a White House news conference Friday evening, blamed the outage on an outdated air traffic control system in which the routers “got overloaded with data.” By Friday evening, Delta Air Lines, United, American said they were resuming flights. TRACON stands for Terminal Radar Approach Control and is an air traffic control center. “The TRACONS and the centers, we started to have inconsistency in the data from the radars and our communication with airplanes,” Duffy said. That instability was detected at 3:36 p.m., he said. Duffy said the FAA did not lose all telecom or radar capabilities but because of the instability, the ground stop was issued as a cautionary measure. It’ll take time for the airspace to recover from the ground stop as crews and planes are out of place and staffers may have reached on-duty shift limitations. However, Duffy said he anticipates American airspace will catch up before Thanksgiving travel rush. Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin said there was no sign of a cyberattack and the public was never in danger. “FAA was able to handle it. The sudden and stunning alert was issued at 3:54 p.m. ET, “due to extraordinary circumstances and for reasons of safety,” the FAA said. It offered no other information beyond stating that “all departing traffic should remain ground stopped until further notice.”

Hours later, Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy, in a White House news conference Friday evening, blamed the outage on an outdated air traffic control system in which the routers “got overloaded with data.”
By Friday evening, Delta Air Lines, United, American said they were resuming flights.
TRACON stands for Terminal Radar Approach Control and is an air traffic control center.
“The TRACONS and the centers, we started to have inconsistency in the data from the radars and our communication with airplanes,” Duffy said.
That instability was detected at 3:36 p.m., he said.

Department of Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin said there was no indication the nationwide FAA disruption was a “nefarious attack,” saying a telecommunications outage prompted the rare move to issue ground stops at airports across the country. Stream NBC 5 for free, 24/7, wherever you are. The FAA issued a nationwide ground stop Friday afternoon, saying in an initial statement that the move was “due to extraordinary circumstances and for reasons of safety.” In an update, the agency said the alert followed “communication issues impacting multiple Air Route Traffic Control Centers.” The agency later said the issue stemmed from “a temporary telecommunications outage.” Speaking to reporters outside the White House, Mullin repeatedly emphasized that passengers and the public were safe, pushing back on comparisons to the Sept. 11 terrorist attacks. “As I want to make sure we say this again, there's no reason for the public to be afraid or scared for your loved ones,” he said. “This isn't another 9/11. I just can't repeat that enough...This is a telecommunication outage. This is much different.” Officials had not ruled out a cyberattack, but Mullin stressed that they did not yet know the cause and did not want to get ahead of the investigation. “Everybody's safe,” Mullin said. “There is no reason to be concerned about your loved ones if they're flying or anything like that. I just want to make sure everybody's at ease about that. As we investigate what caused this, you always got to assume that as many cyberattacks that take place, that you make that assumption. So, but as of right now, that's not known.” Moments before the nationwide ground stop, both major airports in Chicago were under ground stops due to an “equipment outage.” There was no timeline for restoring normal operations, with Mullin explaining that the outage would “take some time” to resolve. “...So this isn't going to just be resolved and, and turned around within the hour," he said. "This is, this is going to take, take some time. But once again, everybody is safe. The flights are accounted for, and there's no, there should be no fear to the public at all in this.” Only departing flights were affected, while arriving flights were expected to continue to their scheduled airports. One traveler at O’Hare Airport told NBC Chicago that airline employees said their flight was on hold “until further notice,” with no timeline provided for when it might depart. More than 250 flights were delayed between Chicago's O'Hare and Midway airports. “Every flight has been accounted for, and international flights will be handled on a case-by-case basis,” the FAA said. Further details about what caused the nationwide disruption were not immediately clear.

extraction.body: U.S. air traffic was brought to a standstill Friday after the Federal Aviation Administration ordered a nationwide ground stop for departing flights that lasted more than five hours. The FAA lifted the ground stop at 8:15 p.m. ET, after more than 7,000 flights were canceled and airports across the country became packed with stranded, irritated passengers. The sudden and stunning alert was issued at 3:54 p.m. ET, “due to extraordinary circumstances and for reasons of safety,” the FAA said. It offered no other information beyond stating that “all departing traffic should remain ground stopped until further notice.” Hours later, Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy, in a White House news conference Friday evening, blamed the outage on an outdated air traffic control system in which the routers “got overloaded with data.” By Friday evening, Delta Air Lines, United, American said they were resuming flights. TRACON stands for Terminal Radar Approach Control and is an air traffic control center. “The TRACONS and the centers, we started to have inconsistency in the data from the radars and our communication with airplanes,” Duffy said. That instability was detected at 3:36 p.m., he said. Duffy said the FAA did not lose all telecom or radar capabilities but because of the instability, the ground stop was issued as a cautionary measure. It’ll take time for the airspace to recover from the ground stop as crews and planes are out of place and staffers may have reached on-duty shift limitations. However, Duffy said he anticipates American airspace will catch up before Thanksgiving travel rush. Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin said there was no sign of a cyberattack and the public was never in danger. “FAA was able to handle it. We did it out of an abundance of caution,” he said in a news conference from the White House Friday night. Earlier on Friday, he described the issue as a telecommunications outage. At the time of the ground stop, there were over 3,500 airplanes in the air, Duffy said. When the FAA issued the alert, 4,042 flights headed for U.S. destinations were airborne, according to Flightradar24 , a Swedish service that displays real-time aircraft flight tracking information. Friday’s ground stop is perhaps the most severe consequence of what Duffy described as a decades-old air traffic control system using analog equipment, which has led to several issues over the past few years. In May 2025, radar screens at Newark Liberty International Airport’s went black during a 90-second outage. Duffy said the legacy equipment will continue to fail and pushed Congress to approve $50 billion to overhaul the system. Congress last year approved $12.5 billion over five years to upgrade air traffic control, Reuters reported. Mullin said earlier Friday that President Donald Trump was briefed on the ground stop. Mullin said that while authorities cannot rule out a cyberattack, there was no evidence to suggest that. “There’s nothing completely certain right now. It doesn’t appear that way,” he said. Meanwhile, Air Space Intelligence, the AI tech startup that is a vendor for the FAA on its new SMART system for air traffic control, insisted its software was not responsible for the nationwide ground stop. “The current ground stop is not based on or a result of the SMART system, any product of ASI or our integration with FAA and ATC,” the company said in a statement posted to X . Duffy said the SMART system is “completely disconnected” from the equipment that suffered issues Friday. Several hours after the ground stop was announced, a top aviation expert estimated that anywhere from 300,000 to 400,000 passengers were stranded — and it was anybody’s guess when they would get to their destinations. “Daily, we have about 25,000 flights in U.S. domestic markets,” Vikrant Vaze, a Dartmouth professor who specializes in commercial aviation logistics, wrote in an email to NBC News. “I would say we should have around 3,000 to 4,000 flights held up at this time over the past 2 plus hours.” But by 6 p.m., Reagan Washington National Airport in Arlington, Virginia, was at capacity, and Chicago O’Hare International Airport was nearing capacity, meaning there was no place for the planes to park, a source with knowledge told NBC News. There are different layers of communications — high-altitude, midlevel and the towers on the ground. The high-altitude control centers are the ones affected by the outage. At Newark Liberty International Airport in New Jersey, personnel in the control tower said the situation is “a whole mess right now,” according to LiveATC. “We’re running out of space” and “there’s significant gate issues” were comments also heard on the live audio feed. “I’m as much in the dark as everyone else. I’m not getting any information from anybody,” one controller at Newark said, according to the feed. Shortly before the FAA issued its alert, both major airports in Chicago — O’Hare and Midway International Airport — were listed on a ground stop alert due to an “equipment outage,” NBC Chicago reported. Deveren Werne was on an American Airlines jet that was about to take off from Indianapolis to Chicago when suddenly the pilots announced that all flights were grounded. “At first, the pilot announced that there was some kind of radio issue,” Werne, 55, of Greenville, South Carolina, told NBC News in a telephone interview. “Then a little while later, the pilot said something like, ‘There is something going on that’s more serious than that.’” Werne, a consultant who helps manufacturers and other industries adapt AI technology, said he is a frequent flyer and this was a first for him. He said there was “a mixture of emotions” from his fellow passengers on hearing the announcement. “Then I started hearing from other friends who were on planes, including one in Chicago who was stuck on a runway,” Werne said. “Right now, our plane is heading back to the terminal, so at least we’re going to be able to deplane.” Medical flights, such as for organ transplants, were not stopped during the ground stop, Duffy said. Ground stops across the nation are a rarity in U.S. history. After the Sept. 11, 2001, terrorist attacks, the FAA ordered an unprecedented nationwide ground stop. All civilian air traffic across U.S. airspace was halted and airborne planes were ordered to land at the nearest available airports. In January 2023, the FAA grounded all flights for a few hours, blaming a failure in the Notice to Air Missions system, which alerts pilots to a host of potential dangers.

extraction.body: Millions of U.S. travelers were suddenly thrown into limbo Friday afternoon after the FAA announced a nationwide ground stop at all U.S. airports. Hours later, it was lifted, and federal officials used the incident to highlight the need for more funding to update aging systems. Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy initially blamed a communication issue impacting all Air Route Traffic Control Centers. In a White House press briefing later on Friday night, Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin attributed the disruptions to technology upgrades, for “overwhelming” the antiquated equipment. Despite recent hacking incidents of freezers in Europe and U.S. military bases, he said it “doesn’t appear” that a cyberattack was involved though he admitted that “there’s nothing certain right now.” Earlier, he ruled out a terrorist attack and said “This isn’t another 9/11.” Just days before the ground stop, the FAA announced it would deploy an AI tool to help air-traffic controllers During the briefing, Duffy also suggested that the problem was related to old equipment being overloaded. “Our fix gives us a pretty good indication that it was a legacy network problem that went down,” he said. Duffy also called on Congress to provide emergency funding to fix the FAA’s aging systems, saying the Trump administration needs another $30 billion, then putting the price tag at $50 billion. Still, the massive disruption comes as airlines in Europe suffered a wave of phony bomb threats this week. While they all appeared to hoaxes, at least one flight was diverted to a military base in France. Spanish Foreign Minister Jose Manuel Albares said Friday that Europe appeared to be facing “hybrid aggression and a form of psychological warfare.” Meanwhile, consumers are still grappling with the aftermath of a Microsoft outage that shut down email, collaboration and AI functions. The company said Friday it had no indication that the ground stop is related to its global outage. The National Weather Service also said there has been no disruption to its radar systems Friday, denying talk online that it had caused the FAA communications issue. The FAA last issued a nationwide ground stop in 2023, when files related to an alert system for pilots was unintentionally deleted. It delayed thousands of flights, but they resumed soon after the disruption. Earlier this year, flights at New York airports were halted when a contractor accidentally cut a fiber communications line in New Jersey. Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy said technicians investigated a "communication issue," adding that routers within the "incredibly old" air traffic control system became "overloaded with data." "Because of that, we shut them down," Duffy said during a news conference. At the time, he said, there were 3,500 planes in the sky. Duffy also expressed frustration with Congress, as he said President Donald Trump has been asking for at least a year to fully fund a brand new air traffic control system. "How many times does this have to happen before Congress gives the money to fix it?" Duffy said, noting that a complete overhaul would cost approximately $50 billion. "America, when do you want to start building a brand new system?" Duffy said. Department of Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin agreed. He said the lack of funding created a national security threat. "We just saw what took place when we have vulnerabilities and and when we have an old system," he said. "The president has declared this a national emergency and now we have to have Congress act and fund it. This is vitally important that we get this system built. Secretary Duffy has said this multiple times. Our air traffic control system is outdated and it hasn't been a priority from Congress. And, so, this is what happens when Congress kicks the can down the road." Shortly after the ground stop was put in place around 4 p.m. EST, Mullin assured Americans that their safety was not at risk. I want to make sure we say this again -- there is no reason for the public to be afraid or scared for your loved ones," Mullin said. extraction.body: Millions of U.S. travelers were suddenly thrown into limbo Friday afternoon after the FAA announced a nationwide ground stop at all U.S. airports. Hours later, it was lifted, and federal officials used the incident to highlight the need for more funding to update aging systems. Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy initially blamed a communication issue impacting all Air Route Traffic Control Centers. In a White House press briefing later on Friday night, Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin attributed the disruptions to technology upgrades, for “overwhelming” the antiquated equipment. Despite recent hacking incidents of freezers in Europe and U.S. military bases, he said it “doesn’t appear” that a cyberattack was involved though he admitted that “there’s nothing certain right now.” Earlier, he ruled out a terrorist attack and said “This isn’t another 9/11.” Just days before the ground stop, the FAA announced it would deploy an AI tool to help air-traffic controllers During the briefing, Duffy also suggested that the problem was related to old equipment being overloaded. “Our fix gives us a pretty good indication that it was a legacy network problem that went down,” he said. Duffy also called on Congress to provide emergency funding to fix the FAA’s aging systems, saying the Trump administration needs another $30 billion, then putting the price tag at $50 billion. Still, the massive disruption comes as airlines in Europe suffered a wave of phony bomb threats this week. While they all appeared to hoaxes, at least one flight was diverted to a military base in France. Spanish Foreign Minister Jose Manuel Albares said Friday that Europe appeared to be facing “hybrid aggression and a form of psychological warfare.” Meanwhile, consumers are still grappling with the aftermath of a Microsoft outage that shut down email, collaboration and AI functions. The company said Friday it had no indication that the ground stop is related to its global outage. The National Weather Service also said there has been no disruption to its radar systems Friday, denying talk online that it had caused the FAA communications issue. The FAA last issued a nationwide ground stop in 2023, when files related to an alert system for pilots was unintentionally deleted. It delayed thousands of flights, but they resumed soon after the disruption. Earlier this year, flights at New York airports were halted when a contractor accidentally cut a fiber communications line in New Jersey. Jason Ma is the weekend editor at Fortune , where he covers markets, the economy, finance, and housing.

extraction.body: U.S. Secretary of Homeland Security Markwayne Mullin says the FAA groundstop is due to a “telecomunications issue” and that “everyone is safe.” UPDATE: The Federal Aviation Administration has lifted the nationwide ground stop, but flight disruptions are expected to linger into the weekend. Department of Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin said there was no indication the nationwide FAA disruption was a “nefarious attack,” saying a telecommunications outage prompted the rare move to issue ground stops at airports across the country. Stream NBC 5 for free, 24/7, wherever you are. The FAA issued a nationwide ground stop Friday afternoon, saying in an initial statement that the move was “due to extraordinary circumstances and for reasons of safety.” In an update, the agency said the alert followed “communication issues impacting multiple Air Route Traffic Control Centers.” The agency later said the issue stemmed from “a temporary telecommunications outage.” Speaking to reporters outside the White House, Mullin repeatedly emphasized that passengers and the public were safe, pushing back on comparisons to the Sept. 11 terrorist attacks. “As I want to make sure we say this again, there's no reason for the public to be afraid or scared for your loved ones,” he said. “This isn't another 9/11. I just can't repeat that enough...This is a telecommunication outage. This is much different.” Officials had not ruled out a cyberattack, but Mullin stressed that they did not yet know the cause and did not want to get ahead of the investigation. “Everybody's safe,” Mullin said. “There is no reason to be concerned about your loved ones if they're flying or anything like that. I just want to make sure everybody's at ease about that. As we investigate what caused this, you always got to assume that as many cyberattacks that take place, that you make that assumption. So, but as of right now, that's not known.” Moments before the nationwide ground stop, both major airports in Chicago were under ground stops due to an “equipment outage.” There was no timeline for restoring normal operations, with Mullin explaining that the outage would “take some time” to resolve. “...So this isn't going to just be resolved and, and turned around within the hour," he said. "This is, this is going to take, take some time. But once again, everybody is safe. The flights are accounted for, and there's no, there should be no fear to the public at all in this.” Only departing flights were affected, while arriving flights were expected to continue to their scheduled airports. One traveler at O’Hare Airport told NBC Chicago that airline employees said their flight was on hold “until further notice,” with no timeline provided for when it might depart. More than 250 flights were delayed between Chicago's O'Hare and Midway airports. “Every flight has been accounted for, and international flights will be handled on a case-by-case basis,” the FAA said. Further details about what caused the nationwide disruption were not immediately clear.

extraction.body: The Federal Aviation Administration lifted its nationwide ground stop at 6:16 p.m. Mountain time Friday, ending a halt on departures from every U.S. airport that lasted more than four hours, and Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy blamed overloaded, aging communications equipment for the failure. "We use 1980s little copper lines. It's an old system that went down and went down everywhere. It got overloaded," Duffy told reporters at the White House, ABC News reported . "Our switches, our routers, actually got overloaded with data," he said, according to NBC News . Duffy said "all of the new equipment that we put in, none of that went down," and called for emergency funding from Congress to replace the system. "This is an emergency," he said. "I want $50 billion." Congress approved $12.5 billion for air traffic control upgrades last year. "The FAA Command Center nationwide ground stop has been cancelled," the agency said in an advisory . Recovery will be gradual. "I believe that it's going to take us some time to get back to capacity," Duffy said, adding that "hopefully tomorrow we are going to start to see far better movement." As of 7:39 p.m., 215 departures from Denver International Airport had been canceled and 336 delayed Friday, according to the flight-tracking service FlightAware . Another 183 arrivals had been canceled and 308 delayed. Nationally, FlightAware counted 6,755 cancellations of flights within, into or out of the United States. Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin said investigators had not found signs of an attack but had not ruled one out. "It appears that this was mechanically driven. However, we're still looking, so we're not going to rule that out," Mullin said, ABC News reported. Microsoft said it had no indication the ground stop was related to its own recent service disruption, and the company behind the FAA's new SMART air traffic management tool said the ground stop "is not based on or a result of the SMART system," NBC News reported. The ground stop took effect at 1:53 p.m., as the Kiowa County Press reported earlier Friday . The FAA had blamed a "temporary telecommunications outage" affecting the Air Route Traffic Control Centers, which manage high-altitude traffic between airports. Colorado is handled by the Denver center in Longmont. The first sign of trouble in FAA records came in Chicago. At 1:17 p.m., about 35 minutes before the nationwide order, the FAA halted flights headed to Chicago Midway International Airport from across the country, citing an equipment outage, according to an FAA advisory . Shortly before the nationwide order, a notice from the National Weather Service hinted at the trouble. At 1:44 p.m., the Weather Service office that serves the Boston area reported that data from the FAA's weather radar at Boston Logan International Airport had been restored, and that "Boston Center reported teleco issues actively being worked." Boston Center is the FAA facility that handles high-altitude traffic over New England, and "teleco" is shorthand for telecommunications. The notice warned that further interruptions were possible. Disruptions are expected to continue into Saturday. United Airlines, which operates a hub at Denver, said it planned to cancel most of its remaining Friday flights, with exceptions for some international flights, ABC News reported . JetBlue said it was canceling all remaining Friday flights except Europe-bound departures from New York and Boston. "We expect disruptions to continue into tomorrow, including additional cancellations," JetBlue said in a statement. After the nationwide stop ended, the FAA briefly held United flights bound for Chicago O'Hare International Airport and, at the airline's request, Alaska Airlines flights bound for Seattle and San Diego, according to FAA advisories. Some airlines are waiving change fees. United told passengers they can reschedule without change fees or fare differences on a United flight departing between November 12 and November 20, in the same cabin and between the same cities, and Delta is allowing free changes for Friday and Saturday travel, ABC News reported . Travelers should check with their airline before leaving for the airport. The FAA posts current airport conditions at nasstatus.faa.gov . While the stop was in effect, flights already in the air were allowed to land, and a limited number of flights over the ocean were cleared to leave, including Pacific-bound flights from San Francisco, flights to and from Hawaii and some transatlantic flights from Boston, according to ABC News. Nationwide ground stops are rare. The last one came in January 2023, when the failure of the FAA's Notice to Air Missions system held departures across the country for about 90 minutes. Before that, the FAA cleared the skies after the September 11, 2001, terrorist attacks. Use these section links to keep reading beyond the latest front-page stories. extraction.body: The Federal Aviation Administration said Friday night that airplane departures can resume after the agency lifted a nationwide ground stop that Trump administration officials blamed on “overloaded,” “outdated” systems. Even with the order being lifted, the airlines will not be able to return to normal operations immediately because so many of their planes and crews are out of position. The FAA had grounded all flights nationwide Friday afternoon, causing hundreds of flights to be diverted. Officials cited “extraordinary circumstances” caused by communications problems at regional air traffic control centers. Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin told reporters at the White House that the introduction of some new technology into an old air traffic control system overwhelmed it. The nationwide ground stop was the first since January 2023 , when a key FAA computer system malfunctioned, and the second since the aftermath of the Sept. 11, 2001, attacks. There was no indication the communications failure was related to a cyberattack. The consequences were profound, disrupting potentially thousands of planned flights through at least late Friday night and upending travel plans for passengers. “It’s frustrating. This certainly sounds like it’s going to be more than the usual run-of-the-mill delay. I look forward to finding out why,” said Jeff Dubner, a Washington attorney whose Alaska Airlines flight home from Los Angeles was already half an hour late and taxiing to the runway when the plane came to a halt. International flights were being handled on a case-by-case basis, according to Mullin, with some seen taking off Friday evening. The uncertainty left travelers scrambling to find alternatives. Amtrak's ticketing system appeared to be down. Several hundred users reported the outage on Down Detector Friday evening. Ticketing agents with Southwest Airlines were roaming the Terminal 1 departures hall Friday afternoon trying to answer passenger questions. But there wasn't much information to share. Christin Barber, a traveler at SAN, said her travel plans are unclear. "I'm going to go to Denver first for a couple of days because I have a funeral to attend tomorrow, And then I'm going on home to Albany, New York," Barber said. extraction.body: The Federal Aviation Administration lifted a nationwide ground stop Friday after more than four hours, following a communications outage that disrupted air travel across the country. Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy told reporters Friday evening that aging air traffic control equipment became overloaded with data, causing instability in radar information and communications with aircraft. The disruption prompted the FAA to halt departures nationwide out of an abundance of caution. The FAA said earlier Friday that the ground stop was issued due to “extraordinary circumstances and for reasons of safety” related to “communication issues.” Speaking at a news conference, Duffy said the problems began at 3:36 p.m. ET, when air traffic control facilities across the country experienced “instability for our radar” and communications. He attributed the disruption to aging analog telecommunications equipment, including switches and routers that became overloaded. "It's the old hardware that went down," Duffy said, adding that newer equipment installed under the Trump administration was not affected, before renewing calls for Congress to provide additional funding to modernize the nation's legacy equipment. Earlier this week, Duffy told Politico that the administration was lobbying Congress to secure $30 billion funding to upgrade air traffic control. “You will have more of them unless the American people and the Congress tell us to build, and I can’t wait for that,” Duffy said, warning of potential future ground stops. Duffy said more than 3,500 aircraft were already in the air en route to U.S. airports nationwide when Friday’s ground stop was issued. He emphasized that the FAA had not lost all radar or telecommunications capabilities and continued allowing critical flights, including medical evacuations and shipments of lifesaving medications. When the FAA issued its initial alert, the agency said international flights arriving in the U.S. would “be managed on a case-by-case basis.” The agency did not indicate how long the earlier ground stop would last, only stating that planes should not depart “until further notice.” The agency said in a statement to MS NOW earlier Friday that communication issues were “impacting multiple Air Route Traffic Control Centers” and that FAA technicians were investigating. Duffy shared the same statement on his X account. A Justice Department source told MS NOW that officials did not track any potential connection to terrorism and described the problem as a “frequency issue.” Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin insisted Friday evening that passengers were never in danger and the FAA acted out of caution. There was there was never any lives at risk,” Mullin said. We did it out of an abundance of caution." Mullin said officials had found “zero evidence" that the outage was caused by a cyberattack or rogue artificial intelligence, though he stopped short of definitively ruling out either possibility. He also assured the public that the Federal Emergency Management Agency had activated its centers to assist stranded travelers, including those who might need access to medication. He said FEMA was coordinating with airports, cities and states to address passengers' needs. Duffy cautioned that returning to normal flight operations “is going to be slow," with airlines prioritizing larger flights depending on crew availability. "It's going to take us some time to unwind what's happened this afternoon," Duffy said, adding that he expects operations to improve Saturday and return to normal ahead of Thanksgiving travel. Two people at the FAA confirmed that Friday’s earlier ground stop was only the second nationwide ground stop since the Sept. The previous nationwide ground stop was in 2023. President Donald Trump had not publicly addressed the nationwide ground stop as of shortly before 9 p.m. ET, though Duffy said the president had been in frequent contact with him and Mullin throughout the disruption. "I know he is fully engaged because he has communicated with the both of us multiple times from the point that it happened to moments before I came out," Duffy said. Jim Himes, the ranking Democrat on the House Intelligence Committee, said earlier Friday he had not been told what caused the FAA ground stop. As a member of the Gang of Eight, Himes would typically be briefed if the incident involved a national security threat. Maria Cantwell, the top Democrat on the Senate Commerce, Science and Transportation Committee, said the committee plans to review “technology issues related to how planes communicate through primary frequencies, backup frequencies and other issues.” At Denver International Airport, where journalists and Democrats were departing Friday afternoon after attending a conference on the party’s future, Gov. Jason Crow, D-Colo., told MS NOW they were still learning details about the ground stop. Cory Booker, D-N.J., described the situation as a “significant breach or breakdown.” “Whether this is a breach or a breakdown, either one is unacceptable,” Booker said. “We need to learn from this, fix it and prevent it from ever happening again.” Several airports issued announcements Friday afternoon advising travelers that departing flights were being held and urging them to consult with their airlines for travel plans. Both American Airlines and Delta said flights already in the air would continue to their destinations. A traveler at Jacksonville International Airport in Florida who was scheduled to fly to Atlanta told MS NOW that their pilot said their departure would be delayed by at least seven hours. An MS NOW video editor reported that American Airlines representatives at Newark Liberty International Airport told passengers they would not have updates for seven hours. Another passenger at Los Angeles International Airport who boarded a flight for San Jose told MS NOW the pilot announced around 1:15. p.m. local time that the flight would be delayed by about 90 minutes. According to FlightAware, a flight tracking website, there were more than 9,500 delays as of about 9:25 p.m.

extraction.body: The Federal Aviation Administration lifted its nationwide ground stop at 6:16 p.m. Mountain time Friday, ending a halt on departures from every U.S. airport that lasted more than four hours, and Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy blamed overloaded, aging communications equipment for the failure. "We use 1980s little copper lines. It's an old system that went down and went down everywhere. It got overloaded," Duffy told reporters at the White House, ABC News reported . "Our switches, our routers, actually got overloaded with data," he said, according to NBC News . Duffy said "all of the new equipment that we put in, none of that went down," and called for emergency funding from Congress to replace the system. "This is an emergency," he said. "I want $50 billion." Congress approved $12.5 billion for air traffic control upgrades last year. "The FAA Command Center nationwide ground stop has been cancelled," the agency said in an advisory . Recovery will be gradual. "I believe that it's going to take us some time to get back to capacity," Duffy said, adding that "hopefully tomorrow we are going to start to see far better movement." As of 7:39 p.m., 215 departures from Denver International Airport had been canceled and 336 delayed Friday, according to the flight-tracking service FlightAware . Another 183 arrivals had been canceled and 308 delayed. Nationally, FlightAware counted 6,755 cancellations of flights within, into or out of the United States. Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin said investigators had not found signs of an attack but had not ruled one out. "It appears that this was mechanically driven. However, we're still looking, so we're not going to rule that out," Mullin said, ABC News reported. Microsoft said it had no indication the ground stop was related to its own recent service disruption, and the company behind the FAA's new SMART air traffic management tool said the ground stop "is not based on or a result of the SMART system," NBC News reported. The ground stop took effect at 1:53 p.m., as the Kiowa County Press reported earlier Friday . The FAA had blamed a "temporary telecommunications outage" affecting the Air Route Traffic Control Centers, which manage high-altitude traffic between airports. Colorado is handled by the Denver center in Longmont. The first sign of trouble in FAA records came in Chicago. At 1:17 p.m., about 35 minutes before the nationwide order, the FAA halted flights headed to Chicago Midway International Airport from across the country, citing an equipment outage, according to an FAA advisory . Shortly before the nationwide order, a notice from the National Weather Service hinted at the trouble. At 1:44 p.m., the Weather Service office that serves the Boston area reported that data from the FAA's weather radar at Boston Logan International Airport had been restored, and that "Boston Center reported teleco issues actively being worked." Boston Center is the FAA facility that handles high-altitude traffic over New England, and "teleco" is shorthand for telecommunications. The notice warned that further interruptions were possible. Disruptions are expected to continue into Saturday. United Airlines, which operates a hub at Denver, said it planned to cancel most of its remaining Friday flights, with exceptions for some international flights, ABC News reported . JetBlue said it was canceling all remaining Friday flights except Europe-bound departures from New York and Boston. "We expect disruptions to continue into tomorrow, including additional cancellations," JetBlue said in a statement. After the nationwide stop ended, the FAA briefly held United flights bound for Chicago O'Hare International Airport and, at the airline's request, Alaska Airlines flights bound for Seattle and San Diego, according to FAA advisories. Some airlines are waiving change fees. United told passengers they can reschedule without change fees or fare differences on a United flight departing between November 12 and November 20, in the same cabin and between the same cities, and Delta is allowing free changes for Friday and Saturday travel, ABC News reported . Travelers should check with their airline before leaving for the airport. The FAA posts current airport conditions at nasstatus.faa.gov . While the stop was in effect, flights already in the air were allowed to land, and a limited number of flights over the ocean were cleared to leave, including Pacific-bound flights from San Francisco, flights to and from Hawaii and some transatlantic flights from Boston, according to ABC News. Nationwide ground stops are rare. The last one came in January 2023, when the failure of the FAA's Notice to Air Missions system held departures across the country for about 90 minutes. extraction.body: The Federal Aviation Administration said Friday night that airplane departures can resume after the agency lifted a nationwide ground stop that Trump administration officials blamed on “overloaded,” “outdated” systems. Even with the order being lifted, the airlines will not be able to return to normal operations immediately because so many of their planes and crews are out of position. The FAA had grounded all flights nationwide Friday afternoon, causing hundreds of flights to be diverted. Officials cited “extraordinary circumstances” caused by communications problems at regional air traffic control centers. Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin told reporters at the White House that the introduction of some new technology into an old air traffic control system overwhelmed it. The nationwide ground stop was the first since January 2023 , when a key FAA computer system malfunctioned, and the second since the aftermath of the Sept. 11, 2001, attacks. There was no indication the communications failure was related to a cyberattack. The consequences were profound, disrupting potentially thousands of planned flights through at least late Friday night and upending travel plans for passengers. “It’s frustrating. This certainly sounds like it’s going to be more than the usual run-of-the-mill delay. I look forward to finding out why,” said Jeff Dubner, a Washington attorney whose Alaska Airlines flight home from Los Angeles was already half an hour late and taxiing to the runway when the plane came to a halt. International flights were being handled on a case-by-case basis, according to Mullin, with some seen taking off Friday evening. The uncertainty left travelers scrambling to find alternatives. Amtrak's ticketing system appeared to be down. Several hundred users reported the outage on Down Detector Friday evening. Ticketing agents with Southwest Airlines were roaming the Terminal 1 departures hall Friday afternoon trying to answer passenger questions. But there wasn't much information to share. Christin Barber, a traveler at SAN, said her travel plans are unclear. "I'm going to go to Denver first for a couple of days because I have a funeral to attend tomorrow, And then I'm going on home to Albany, New York," Barber said. "I don't know what to do at this point." A San Diego Airport official said in a statement that "arriving flights will continue to land as space allows." Asked whether Mullin could rule out a cyberattack or rogue artificial intelligence incident, he said: “There’s nothing completely certain right now. It doesn’t appear that way.” He said there are no “footprints” showing an attack and that it appears to be “mechanically driven,” adding that officials were still looking for the cause. At least 827 flights were diverted so far as a result. As of 7:05 p.m. EST, 670 flights were sent back to the airport from where they originally took off, while 157 were redirected to a different airport, according to Cirium, an aviation analytics company. The airports where many of the flights ended up being diverted included Washington Dulles International Airport, Los Angeles International Airport, Cincinnati/Northern Kentucky International Airport and Nashville International Airport. Some 11,000 flights carrying more than 1.5 million passengers were scheduled to take off from airports in the U.S. after 4 p.m. EST, raising the likelihood of more cancelations and flight diversions. At Chicago O’Hare Airport on Friday afternoon, travelers passing through security learned about the ground stop when they looked up at screens that showed flight delays across the board. Some called friends or family members, debating whether to stay the night in Chicago or find another way to their destinations. Amber McQuilkin, 27, sat on a bench, disappointed that she might miss a trip with friends to New York for the League of Legends world finals. Her friends, she said, had already arrived there. “There’s not really any information being passed to me,” said the Seattle software engineer, who took a week of vacation for the trip. “I contemplated just abandoning the flight and driving, but then the more I thought about it, the more I’m like, that would be miserable.” Austin Curtis and his wife were rethinking their trip from South Bend, Indiana, to a friend’s baby shower in Denver after getting delayed during a layover in Chicago. NBA, NHL and college teams were left stranded as they tried to reach their destinations. Meanwhile, NFL teams were left to wonder whether the issue would be resolved in time to travel to their games this weekend. Cargo flights were also delayed by the ground stop. FedEx, the world’s largest cargo airline, said it is prepared to activate contingency plans to keep any possible disruptions at a minimum. U.S. airlines move about 61,000 tons of goods – from letters to packages -- to and from more than 220 countries daily, according to the industry trade group Airlines for America. Despite the nationwide FAA ground stop, SpaceX launched its Starship rocket from Texas on Friday afternoon on its latest test flight. Mullin had said investigators will look at whether there is any link to the FAA's nationwide rollout of a new artificial intelligence system to help identify problems and reroute planes. But that system operates out of one location near Washington, D.C., and just sends recommendations to the air traffic control centers. The government has been working to overhaul the outdated technology that air traffic controllers rely on since Congress approved $12.5 billion for the project last year. Miles of old copper wires have been replaced with fiber optic lines and old radio systems are gradually being replaced at airports across the country. But much work remains. passages: The Federal Aviation Administration said Friday night that airplane departures can resume after the agency lifted a nationwide ground stop that Trump administration officials blamed on “overloaded,” “outdated” systems.
Even with the order being lifted, the airlines will not be able to return to normal operations immediately because so many of their planes and crews are out of position.

The FAA had grounded all flights nationwide Friday afternoon, causing hundreds of flights to be diverted. Officials cited “extraordinary circumstances” caused by communications problems at regional air traffic control centers.
Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin told reporters at the White House that the introduction of some new technology into an old air traffic control system overwhelmed it.
The nationwide ground stop was the first since January 2023 , when a key FAA computer system malfunctioned, and the second since the aftermath of the Sept. 11, 2001, attacks.

There was no indication the communications failure was related to a cyberattack. The consequences were profound, disrupting potentially thousands of planned flights through at least late Friday night and upending travel plans for passengers.

“It’s frustrating. This certainly sounds like it’s going to be more than the usual run-of-the-mill delay. I look forward to finding out why,” said Jeff Dubner, a Washington attorney whose Alaska Airlines flight home from Los Angeles was already half an hour late and taxiing to the runway when the plane came to a halt.
International flights were being handled on a case-by-case basis, according to Mullin, with some seen taking off Friday evening.

Ticketing agents with Southwest Airlines were roaming the Terminal 1 departures hall Friday afternoon trying to answer passenger questions. But there wasn't much information to share.
