extraction.body: The Federal Aviation Administration lifted a nationwide ground stop Friday after more than four hours, following a communications outage that disrupted air travel across the country. Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy told reporters Friday evening that aging air traffic control equipment became overloaded with data, causing instability in radar information and communications with aircraft. The disruption prompted the FAA to halt departures nationwide out of an abundance of caution. The FAA said earlier Friday that the ground stop was issued due to “extraordinary circumstances and for reasons of safety” related to “communication issues.” Speaking at a news conference, Duffy said the problems began at 3:36 p.m. ET, when air traffic control facilities across the country experienced “instability for our radar” and communications. He attributed the disruption to aging analog telecommunications equipment, including switches and routers that became overloaded. "It's the old hardware that went down," Duffy said, adding that newer equipment installed under the Trump administration was not affected, before renewing calls for Congress to provide additional funding to modernize the nation's legacy equipment. Earlier this week, Duffy told Politico that the administration was lobbying Congress to secure $30 billion funding to upgrade air traffic control. “You will have more of them unless the American people and the Congress tell us to build, and I can’t wait for that,” Duffy said, warning of potential future ground stops. Duffy said more than 3,500 aircraft were already in the air en route to U.S. airports nationwide when Friday’s ground stop was issued. He emphasized that the FAA had not lost all radar or telecommunications capabilities and continued allowing critical flights, including medical evacuations and shipments of lifesaving medications. When the FAA issued its initial alert, the agency said international flights arriving in the U.S. would “be managed on a case-by-case basis.” The agency did not indicate how long the earlier ground stop would last, only stating that planes should not depart “until further notice.” The agency said in a statement to MS NOW earlier Friday that communication issues were “impacting multiple Air Route Traffic Control Centers” and that FAA technicians were investigating. Duffy shared the same statement on his X account. A Justice Department source told MS NOW that officials did not track any potential connection to terrorism and described the problem as a “frequency issue.” Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin insisted Friday evening that passengers were never in danger and the FAA acted out of caution. There was there was never any lives at risk,” Mullin said. We did it out of an abundance of caution." Mullin said officials had found “zero evidence" that the outage was caused by a cyberattack or rogue artificial intelligence, though he stopped short of definitively ruling out either possibility. He also assured the public that the Federal Emergency Management Agency had activated its centers to assist stranded travelers, including those who might need access to medication. He said FEMA was coordinating with airports, cities and states to address passengers' needs. Duffy cautioned that returning to normal flight operations “is going to be slow," with airlines prioritizing larger flights depending on crew availability. "It's going to take us some time to unwind what's happened this afternoon," Duffy said, adding that he expects operations to improve Saturday and return to normal ahead of Thanksgiving travel. Two people at the FAA confirmed that Friday’s earlier ground stop was only the second nationwide ground stop since the Sept. The previous nationwide ground stop was in 2023. President Donald Trump had not publicly addressed the nationwide ground stop as of shortly before 9 p.m. ET, though Duffy said the president had been in frequent contact with him and Mullin throughout the disruption. "I know he is fully engaged because he has communicated with the both of us multiple times from the point that it happened to moments before I came out," Duffy said. Jim Himes, the ranking Democrat on the House Intelligence Committee, said earlier Friday he had not been told what caused the FAA ground stop. As a member of the Gang of Eight, Himes would typically be briefed if the incident involved a national security threat. Maria Cantwell, the top Democrat on the Senate Commerce, Science and Transportation Committee, said the committee plans to review “technology issues related to how planes communicate through primary frequencies, backup frequencies and other issues.” At Denver International Airport, where journalists and Democrats were departing Friday afternoon after attending a conference on the party’s future, Gov. Jason Crow, D-Colo., told MS NOW they were still learning details about the ground stop. Cory Booker, D-N.J., described the situation as a “significant breach or breakdown.” “Whether this is a breach or a breakdown, either one is unacceptable,” Booker said. “We need to learn from this, fix it and prevent it from ever happening again.” Several airports issued announcements Friday afternoon advising travelers that departing flights were being held and urging them to consult with their airlines for travel plans. Both American Airlines and Delta said flights already in the air would continue to their destinations. A traveler at Jacksonville International Airport in Florida who was scheduled to fly to Atlanta told MS NOW that their pilot said their departure would be delayed by at least seven hours. An MS NOW video editor reported that American Airlines representatives at Newark Liberty International Airport told passengers they would not have updates for seven hours. Another passenger at Los Angeles International Airport who boarded a flight for San Jose told MS NOW the pilot announced around 1:15. p.m. local time that the flight would be delayed by about 90 minutes. According to FlightAware, a flight tracking website, there were more than 9,500 delays as of about 9:25 p.m.

passages: Bloomberg reported that the FBI doesn't believe the outage was a cyberattack or criminal act, and that one line of inquiry is whether a software update caused it.
An update is a far more ordinary explanation than a hack, and in some ways a more uncomfortable one, because it means a national system can be taken down by its own maintenance.

The FAA then ordered a nationwide ground stop, telling airlines that "all departing traffic should remain groundstopped until further notice" and citing "extraordinary circumstances and reasons of safety." Planes already in the air were allowed to land, and international arrivals were handled case by case.
Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy said the fault hit every one of the FAA's en route air traffic control centers, and CBS News counted about 8,000 delays and 400 cancellations within hours.
Investigators haven't named the update, its author or a restart time.
In January 2023 the FAA's NOTAM system failure stopped departures nationwide for under two hours, and the agency said files were unintentionally deleted during work on its databases.
In July 2024 a faulty CrowdStrike update crashed about 8.5 million Windows machines, by Microsoft's estimate, and Delta alone said it lost around $500 million.
The pattern is the same each time: a small change, a wide blast radius, and no cheap way back.
Planes sat at gates from Chicago to New York on Friday while investigators asked whether a routine software change, not a hacker, knocked out the radios air traffic controllers depend on.
For now the facts are short: no named update, no confirmed cause, and no public timetable from the FAA for getting every departure moving again.

passages: Microsoft outage: The tech giant is still working on its servers to restore the services after a massive outage hit Outlook, Teams, Copilot and several Microsoft 365 applications across multiple regions.
The disruptions started in the early hours of November 13 leaving users in several countries struggling to access emails, join meetings and use Microsoft's cloud-based productivity tools.
The Microsoft outage has affected many services.

Outlook and Exchange Online have experienced some of the most significant problems, with users reporting difficulties accessing inboxes, sending emails and connecting through desktop, web and mobile applications.
Users and IT administrators can check the Microsoft 365 Service Health dashboard for updates.
Now with many services experiencing massive downtime, there are also concerns about the possible cyberattack.
However, Microsoft has clarified that the disruption is not related to a cybersecurity incident.
There is also no indication of a hacking attack, and no cybercriminal group has claimed responsibility at the moment.
According to Microsoft's engineering updates, the outage is linked to problems with the server processes responsible for establishing secure connections.
Some servers unexpectedly became unavailable after failing automated health checks reducing the infrastructure available to handle incoming requests.
The initial attempts to restore services have not gone entirely as planned.
Microsoft said some servers brought back online became unresponsive again when user traffic returned.
This has forced its engineering teams to restore capacity gradually while redistributing network traffic and investigating alternative recovery measures.
Microsoft has not provided a confirmed timeline for the complete restoration of its services.

extraction.body: Investors punished Microsoft with a 6 per cent share drop on Thursday as hefty AI bets failed to drive a big increase in its cloud revenue, while Meta rose 4 per cent after CEO Mark Zuckerberg assured Wall Street about growth with promises of a “really big year”. The chief executives of both the companies defended their heavy investments on artificial intelligence on Wednesday, days after Chinese upstart DeepSeek unveiled a breakthrough in cheap AI that shook the technology industry. But while Meta (META.O) has consistently showed strong ad revenues – a move that “easily justifies” its investments according to Evercore analyst Mark Mahaney – Microsoft’s key cloud business Azure has been slowing down. The Windows maker missed market estimates for quarterly revenue growth at Azure and gave a third-quarter forecast for the business that was below expectations, even after it promised a rebound for the unit in the second half of its fiscal year. “The second-half re-acceleration story for Azure is not playing out,” Barclays analyst Raimo Lenschow said. “The company overly focused on AI workloads at the expense of core Azure. It will take time to fix this, which means the Azure growth acceleration the market had been hoping for has to wait for a little longer.” For Facebook-parent Meta, a better-than-expected 21 per cent jump in revenue helped ease investor fears around Zuckerberg’s plans to spend as much as $65 billion this year on AI, even as its first-quarter forecast was muted. And Meta might have more benefits to show from AI than anyone,” Rosenblatt analyst Barton Crockett wrote. At least 15 brokerages raised their price targets on Meta, which has a 12-month forward price-to-earnings ratio of about 26.22. The stock jumped 65 per cent last year, the biggest gain among Big Tech peers. The company looked set to add more than $80 billion to its market value on Thursday. “Meta’s ability to use AI to sustainably drive both engagement and pricing growth is a rarity in its (and the industry’s) history,” MoffettNathanson analysts said. Microsoft was on track to erase about $182 billion off its market cap. About four brokerages trimmed their price targets on the stock, which has lagged its peers with just a 12 per cent gain last year. Microsoft “did not recommit to (its Azure second-half outlook) the same way that it did 90 days ago.

sources.title: Microsoft’s cloud outlook knocks shares, Meta rises on AI payoff signs
passages: Investors punished Microsoft with a 6 per cent share drop on Thursday as hefty AI bets failed to drive a big increase in its cloud revenue, while Meta rose 4 per cent after CEO Mark Zuckerberg assured Wall Street about growth with promises of a “really big year”.

But while Meta (META.O) has consistently showed strong ad revenues – a move that “easily justifies” its investments according to Evercore analyst Mark Mahaney – Microsoft’s key cloud business Azure has been slowing down.
At least 15 brokerages raised their price targets on Meta, which has a 12-month forward price-to-earnings ratio of about 26.22.
Microsoft “did not recommit to (its Azure second-half outlook) the same way that it did 90 days ago.
“Meta’s ability to use AI to sustainably drive both engagement and pricing growth is a rarity in its (and the industry’s) history,” MoffettNathanson analysts said.
Microsoft was on track to erase about $182 billion off its market cap.

extraction.body: Investors punished Microsoft with a 6 per cent share drop on Thursday as hefty AI bets failed to drive a big increase in its cloud revenue, while Meta rose 4 per cent after CEO Mark Zuckerberg assured Wall Street about growth with promises of a “really big year”. The chief executives of both the companies defended their heavy investments on artificial intelligence on Wednesday, days after Chinese upstart DeepSeek unveiled a breakthrough in cheap AI that shook the technology industry. But while Meta (META.O) has consistently showed strong ad revenues – a move that “easily justifies” its investments according to Evercore analyst Mark Mahaney – Microsoft’s key cloud business Azure has been slowing down. The Windows maker missed market estimates for quarterly revenue growth at Azure and gave a third-quarter forecast for the business that was below expectations, even after it promised a rebound for the unit in the second half of its fiscal year. “The second-half re-acceleration story for Azure is not playing out,” Barclays analyst Raimo Lenschow said. “The company overly focused on AI workloads at the expense of core Azure. It will take time to fix this, which means the Azure growth acceleration the market had been hoping for has to wait for a little longer.” For Facebook-parent Meta, a better-than-expected 21 per cent jump in revenue helped ease investor fears around Zuckerberg’s plans to spend as much as $65 billion this year on AI, even as its first-quarter forecast was muted. And Meta might have more benefits to show from AI than anyone,” Rosenblatt analyst Barton Crockett wrote. At least 15 brokerages raised their price targets on Meta, which has a 12-month forward price-to-earnings ratio of about 26.22. The stock jumped 65 per cent last year, the biggest gain among Big Tech peers. The company looked set to add more than $80 billion to its market value on Thursday. “Meta’s ability to use AI to sustainably drive both engagement and pricing growth is a rarity in its (and the industry’s) history,” MoffettNathanson analysts said. Microsoft was on track to erase about $182 billion off its market cap. About four brokerages trimmed their price targets on the stock, which has lagged its peers with just a 12 per cent gain last year. Microsoft “did not recommit to (its Azure second-half outlook) the same way that it did 90 days ago.
